en: The *Vakroktijīvita*, composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Kuntaka.
Chapter One.
[Salutation] to the one who performs the wondrous work of painting the manifold variety of the three worlds.
We praise Śiva, whose sole instrument is the vibration of Śakti.
If phenomena existing within the three worlds are analyzed according to their true nature, that is not at all surprising; for indeed, *kiṃśuka* trees are naturally red by their very nature.
Now, if their reality were established according to their own whims and according to their own inclinations, that would be mere intellectual arrogance; the ultimate truth is not like that.
Thus, even though I have not shown great regard for this independent composition consisting of fallacious reasoning,
I shall now reveal the essence of the ocean of the nectar of literary meaning.
By means of which even this twofold [characteristic], defined as reality and its manifestation,
will produce for those who know it a wondrous joy and aesthetic rapture.
At the beginning of a work,
it is the established custom to perform a salutation to one's chosen deity; therefore, he first undertakes that very act.
I pay homage to the Goddess, who is the dancer in the temple of the moon-like face of the Lord of Poets,
radiant with the beautiful gestures of the movement of her eloquent speech.
Thus:
"I worship the Goddess"—that is, I praise the deity. To the question "Which one? he says: "The dancer in the temple of the dance of the moon-like faces of the lords of poets."
The moon-like faces of those preeminent poets—the best among poets—are themselves a theater for dance (*lāsyamandira*). In that [theater], she is the dancer (*nartakī*).
Of what sort? Radiant with beautiful gestures (*abhinaya*) consisting of the movement of well-spoken verses (*sūkti*);
that is, radiant and shining with those very beautiful and delicate gestures, such as the *sāttvika* and others, which are the playful manifestations of sublime poetry.

The meaning of the sentence is: "I praise her," or "I bow to her"—she who, it is said, shines as she dances upon the lips of a true poet, like a dancer in a theater of graceful movement (*lāsya*), distinguished by the gestures of her own charms.

This is the intended purport here: I praise Sarasvatī, who is in the form of Speech, the presiding deity of whatever subject matter is being presented, such as this composition on poetic ornaments, she who captivates the hearts of those with refined minds.

Having thus paid homage, he now introduces the subject matter, the expression, and the purpose, which constitute the scope of what is to be said: "In order to establish the fixed domain of speech, the expression and so forth are stated at the outset, like a measuring line for a construction. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 1.6)
This is an intermediate verse:
To achieve a variety that produces supramundane wonder, this certain unprecedented ornament of poetry is now prescribed. (Vjiv 1.2)
An ornament is prescribed; the act of ornamenting is performed. Of what? Of poetry (kāvyam).
Poetry is the work of a poet (kavi); [it is] of that.
But surely there exist ancient ornaments; for what purpose [is this work written]? To this he says: "unprecedented" (*apūrvaḥ*), meaning it expresses meanings distinct from those.
That quality of being unprecedented can belong to both that which is superior to them and that which is inferior to them; thus he says: "some unique one" (*ko 'pi*).

It is extraordinary and possesses excellence. To the question "For what purpose is it?", he says: for the sake of achieving a variety that produces supramundane aesthetic refinement (*alaukikātmakāra*), that is, for the attainment of a manifold state of being that ordains an uncommon delight.
Although there are hundreds of poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṅkāra*), nevertheless, such a variety has not been achieved by any of them whatsoever.
The word *alaṅkāra* primarily denotes bracelets and the like, because they produce an excellence of beauty for the body;
it applies figuratively to similes (*upamā*) and so forth by virtue of their commonality in producing that [beauty],
and likewise to the poetic qualities (*guṇas*) which resemble them.

And likewise, in a treatise that expresses that [identity], there is a conventional usage of oneness between the word and its object because they share a common fate; for example: "The word 'cow' is the word 'cow', and the object 'cow' is the object 'cow'."
This is the meaning: "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) is the designation for the treatise; the collection of objects of knowledge such as simile (*upamā*) and so forth is the subject matter (*abhidheya*);
and the accomplishment of the aforementioned variety of forms is the purpose (*prayojana*).

Even though it has been established that this ornament possesses such a purpose, [the author] says that without a purpose for the poetry (*kāvya*) which is the object of that ornament, even its existence would be useless: "The composition of poetry, which is a means for accomplishing dharma and the other goals, presented through a refined sequence, brings delight to the hearts of the noble. (Vjiv 1.3)

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "the composition of poetry, such as the *sargabandha* (epic) and other forms, which causes delight to the heart and generates joy in the mind, comes into being.
To the question "Of whom? he says: "Of the noble-born (*abhijātānām*).
For the noble-born—such as princes and others—are indeed seekers of goals such as dharma, desirous of victory, and fearful of suffering.

Because their dispositions are delicate, even though poetry possesses that quality of being delightful, it follows that it is comparable to a toy or similar object; thus he states: "It is the means for accomplishing dharma and the rest.

It is the means (*upāya*) for the accomplishment—that is, the bringing about—of the fourfold aim (*caturvarga*), which is the goal (*upeya*) such as dharma and so forth, because it takes the form of instruction therein and is the cause for attaining it.

It is stated as follows: "What offense has been committed by other treatises, which are likewise devoted to the instruction on the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*)? [The answer is: Because it is 'expounded in a delicate sequence'—that is, being expounded, or told, in a delicate, beautiful, and heart-captivating sequence or arrangement—it serves as a means for attaining dharma and the other goals, since it inspires the noble-born by its capacity to delight them."

Furthermore, because the treatises present their methods in a rigorous manner, the instruction on dharma and other matters is difficult to comprehend; thus, even if such instruction exists regarding such subjects, it is utterly ineffective. Indeed, it is the princes who, having attained their own sovereignty, undertake the task of maintaining the order of the entire world.
Being independent due to their lack of commendable instruction, they are capable of initiating the total abolition of all appropriate worldly conventions;
it is for this very purpose that poets compose accounts of the deeds of kings from the past as examples for the sake of instructing them.
Thus, there certainly exists a preeminent purpose for the composition of poetry that transcends the [aims of] the technical sciences (śāstra).

Let alone the primary purpose, characterized by the attainment of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha), even another purpose—the maintenance of worldly affairs—such as the winning over of servants, friends, and masters, is not properly possible without this; thus he says:
Through the very mastery of excellent poetry, those engaged in worldly affairs attain a fresh sense of propriety regarding the beauty of social interactions.
"Vyavahāra" means worldly conduct; its "parispanda" (vibration) is its activity, characterized by a sequence of actions. Its "saundaryam" (beauty) is its loveliness.

That is obtained—meaning it is acquired—by those engaged in such conduct, that is, by practitioners, solely through the mastery of excellent poetry, that is, only through the thorough knowledge of beautiful poetry, and not from anything else.
Of what nature is that beauty? It is a novel propriety (*aucitya*).
That is to say, it is that in which there is a novel, fresh, and extraordinary propriety—the state of being appropriate.
This is what is meant: for when the conduct of great beings such as kings and others is described, all those things that constitute its constituent parts [must be depicted with similar novelty].

The chief minister and others, being bound by their proficiency in the specific duties and transactions appropriate to their respective offices, become instructors in the conduct of all practitioners.
Consequently, everyone who has exerted effort in some particular beautiful poem, having attained a preeminent beauty in the movement of its composition, becomes a partaker of praiseworthy fruit.

That human goal (*puruṣārtha*) characterized by the fourfold set (*caturvarga*), which is traditionally taught as the ultimate purpose of poetry through its being the cause for proficiency in the objects of acquisition, also culminates at that very moment, because the enjoyment thereof—which is its fruit—consists in producing delight arising from a different temporal state. Therefore, he speaks of another distinct purpose, one that is delightful through resonance with the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) and charming in the immediate present: [The verse follows: "O friend, this is not the time for you to go to the forest; rather, it is the time for you to enjoy the pleasures of love. For the moon has risen, and the night is filled with the fragrance of blooming jasmine. In this verse, the word "friend" (*sakhe*) is used to address a lover who is about to depart for the forest. By addressing him as "friend," the poet implies: "Since you are my friend, you should do what is beneficial for me. Thus, the departure for the forest is prohibited, and the enjoyment of love is enjoined. This is because the moon has arisen, and the night is fragrant with the scent of blooming jasmine. Here, the prohibition of going to the forest is the primary meaning, while the injunction to enjoy love is the secondary meaning. However, the latter is more powerful than the former, and thus the primary meaning is subordinated to the secondary. This is because the prohibition of going to the forest is merely a means to the end of enjoying love, whereas the injunction to enjoy love is the actual end itself. Furthermore, the prohibition of going to the forest is a general rule, while the injunction to enjoy love is a specific exception. Moreover, the prohibition of going to the forest is a duty toward others, whereas the injunction to enjoy love is a duty toward oneself. And finally, the prohibition of going to the forest is a duty toward the future, whereas the injunction to enjoy love is a duty toward the present. Since these reasons establish the superiority of the injunction over the prohibition, the latter is subordinated to the former. This is called *parivṛtti* (exchange), where the primary meaning is subordinated to the secondary. It is like a king who, having been invited by a friend, abandons his own kingdom and goes to his friend's house to enjoy the pleasures of love. In this case, the prohibition of going to the forest is like abandoning one's own kingdom, and the injunction to enjoy love is like going to the friend's house to enjoy the pleasures of love. Just as the king abandons his own kingdom to enjoy the pleasures of love at his friend's house, so too the primary meaning is abandoned to enjoy the pleasure of the secondary meaning. Therefore, this is called *parivṛtti*. It is like a king who, having been invited by a friend, abandons his own kingdom and goes to his friend's house to enjoy the pleasures of love. In this case, the prohibition of going to the forest is like abandoning one's own kingdom, and the injunction to enjoy love is like going to the friend's house to enjoy the pleasures of love. Just as the king abandons his own kingdom to enjoy the pleasures of love at his friend's house, so too the primary meaning is abandoned to enjoy the pleasure of the secondary meaning. Therefore, this is called *parivṛtti*. It is like a king who, having been invited by a friend, abandons his own kingdom and goes to his friend's house to enjoy the pleasures of love. In this case, the prohibition of going to the forest is like abandoning one's own kingdom, and the injunction to enjoy love is like going to the friend's house to enjoy the pleasures of love. Even transcending the tasting of the fruits of the four aims of human life,
those who know [this] experience an inner wonder through the nectar-like essence of poetry.
The meaning is that wonder is extended, astonishment is spread forth, and delight is produced again and again;
by what? By the nectar-like essence of poetry.
Poetry alone is nectar; its essence is the aesthetic flavor (rasa), which is its tasting, that is, its experience.
To the question "Where?", he replies: "Within the heart.
Of whom? "Of those who know it" (tadvidām).
"Those who know it" (*tadvidaḥ*) means those who understand it; "of them" (*teṣām*).
How so? Even having transcended the tasting of the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*);

that is, even having surpassed, having conquered, and having rendered as trivial as a mere touch (*paspaśaprāyam*), the experience—that is, the enjoyment—of the fruit of the four aims, such as dharma and the rest, which is renowned for its excellence.

This is the intended meaning here: that very savoring of the fruit of the four aims of human life, which is renowned as the purpose of all treatises by virtue of being the supreme human goal—even that cannot bear any comparison with even a mere fraction of the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) derived from chewing the nectar of this poetry.
For, due to defects such as being difficult to hear, difficult to recite, or difficult to comprehend, it causes unbearable suffering at the time of study.
It is also implied by the sense of this that the body of a treatise (*śāstrasandarbha*), which produces a charming wonder conceived for its own time, cannot in any way rival poetry (*kāvya*).
"The treatise is like pungent medicine, destroying the disease of ignorance;
poetry is like delightful nectar, removing the malady of lack of discernment. (VjivC 1.7)
Now, that by which poetry is produced— beautiful through the flow of aesthetic flavor both in the future and in the present— is being investigated.
These are two intermediate verses:
"The ornament is distinguished by being extracted from that which is to be ornamented;
yet reality is the state of poetry belonging to that which possesses the ornament, because [the ornament] is a means to that."
"Alaṅkṛti" means adornment (*alaṅkaraṇa*), derived from the analysis (*vigraha*) "that by which something is adorned. That [adornment] is examined and investigated;
and that which is to be adorned—that which is fit for adornment, namely the form of the expressive (*vācaka*) and the form of the expressed (*vācya*)—that too is examined.
The essential nature of these two is defined by means of their general and specific characteristics.
How so? By way of abstraction—that is, having extracted them and established each separately.
Since they are included within that composite form, they are distinguished from it;
for what reason? Because they are the means to it—"it" refers here to poetry (kāvya).

The means for that [poetic skill] is the means for that; the state of being such is "the state of being a means" (*tadupāyatā*). By virtue of this being the cause—since such a distinction (*viveka*) attains the status of being a means for proficiency in poetry—it is observed that even those things which do not exist as actual entities, yet fall within a composite whole, serve as causes for proficiency when they are extracted and analyzed.
For example, as in the case of the stem and suffix which are internal to a word, or the words which are internal to a sentence.

If it is argued that even though this analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*) is unreal, it is nevertheless employed as a means [to understanding], then what is the reality? He says: "The essence is the state of being poetry for that which possesses ornaments. This is the ultimate truth here: the state of being poetry—the status of being the poet’s work—belongs to the entire aggregate, including its ornaments, which exists as a whole with its parts set aside.
Thus it is established that it is the work adorned by those [figures] that possesses the nature of poetry (*kāvyatva*), and not that poetry is joined with figures;
for by stating "poetry is that which possesses figures," the essential nature of poetry has been indicated somewhat in a general way, but it has not been precisely determined.
He states what kind of entity possesses the designation of "poetry":
"Word and meaning, joined together and established within a composition characterized by the skillful operation of a poet, constitute poetry when they provide delight to those who know it. (Vjiv 1.7)
22. Word and meaning constitute poetry; that is, the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*), these two combined, are poetry.
To say "two are one" is a truly marvelous expression.

Therefore, as for the view held by some that poetry is merely the word itself, possessing a supreme beauty fashioned by the poet's skill, or the view of others that poetry is merely the signified which produces aesthetic charm through the variety of its composition— [The author proceeds to refute these views.]
Both positions are refuted because,
in each of the two cases, that quality of producing joy through its penetration exists in every single [particle], like oil in every sesame seed,
and not merely in one.
For example:

"Speak, O young woman with a face as beautiful as the moon that distills bliss, you who utter playful words! If you are going to the lover's house, then what is yours [to lose] for me? (Vajrāvalī 1.9)
Her wandering about with her jeweled girdle chiming softly and her lovely anklets tinkling incessantly causes groundless longing for her ruddy feet.

Due to the wretchedness of my poverty in poetic inspiration, this poet has uttered here merely a beauty of phonetic similarity (*varṇasāvarṇya*), but there is not even a grain of variety in the expressed meaning (*vācyavaicitrya*).
Indeed, it is as if some lover were to speak thus to a beloved woman whose loveliness is rippling with fresh youth: "If..."
"O young woman, you are going to the house of your lover; why then does your coming cause such groundless anxiety in me?"—this statement is excessively vulgar.
Furthermore, it is not without reason.
Since her departure was due to her disregard for him, the cause of his anxiety and fear regarding the distress of separation— stemming from his heart being devoted to her— is his own restlessness.
Alternatively, if it is meant to convey that he has done nothing wrong by wandering about,
this too is exceedingly vulgar.

Furthermore, the numerous vocatives found in hymns composed by sages—which are essentially forms of address—do not nourish even a trace of that delight experienced by those who know [the subject]; thus, such [instances] are trivial. Moreover, a mere statement of fact, devoid of any excellence in verbal beauty, does not deserve the designation of "poetry.
For example: [text follows].

Entities do not possess the nature of luminosity when in darkness, for if they did, they would not be as they are; yet how could this be so? This activity of the sun possesses the quality of a guru firmly initiated in the absence of the superimposition of qualities and the absence of delusion—what, then, is similar to that splendor?
For here, the poet has merely composed this object—which has appeared only as a flash of intuition—out of a passion born from a mind perfumed by the habituation to the language of dry logic.
Not even a trace of the aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) of the artful expression of meaning (*vācakavakratā*) is perceived;
because the very bed of logical argumentation constitutes the body of this verse.
And thus: the entities distinct from darkness are the subjects (*dharmin*);
"they do not have the nature of light" is the probandum (*sādhya*);
"because darkness is not such [i.e., does not have the nature of light]" is the reason (*hetu*).
In that case, why was an example not shown?
Because it is the logic of reasoning itself that appears in the mind.
Thus it is said:
For those who do not understand the example, both the presence [of the probandum] and the causal relationship [between the reason and the probandum] are made known;
however, for the learned, only the reason itself needs to be stated. (VjivC 1.12)
Thus:
the root *dadhāti* preceded by the prefix *vi-* (in the form *vidadhati*) functions in the sense of "doing.
However, that sense of "doing" here does not have a very clear syntactic connection.
They do not produce the nature of luminosity.

Even the term "nature of luminosity" (prakāśasvābhāvya) is indeed to be examined: that whose intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is luminosity is "that which has luminosity as its intrinsic nature" (prakāśasvabhāva).
When the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied in the sense of "the state of that," the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the first member would result.

Furthermore, in the case of "the state of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvasya bhāvaḥ*), namely *svābhāvya*, it is not appropriate to apply another abstract suffix to a word already ending in an abstract suffix.
Consequently, even the descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) "that which is both illumination and intrinsic nature" (*prakāśaścāsau svābhāvyaṃ ca*) is not correct.
Furthermore, in the third quarter, the excessive presence of compounds that fail to convey the intended meaning results in a defect that does not bring delight to those who know [the art].
In the expression "ravivyāpāra," the subordination within the compound of the word *ravi*— which was intended to be predominant— is not considered a flaw,
because an alternative reading, "raveḥ," is possible.
If it is asked, "But how can even a mere matter of fact, being devoid of poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*), produce delight for those who know [poetry]?"— this is not so;

because a matter of fact, though appearing as something unworked like a fragment of stone or resembling an uncut gem when first flashing forth in the poet's imagination, becomes manifest in the mind of the discerning poet precisely through the medium of another subject (*anyāpadeśa*) by means of an ornament characterized as *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), once it has ascended onto the crooked speech (*vakravākya*) composed by the skillful poet.
By virtue of its captivating brilliance, as if licked by the moon, it attains the state of bringing delight to those who know it.

And so, two sentences composed by two poets—one attentive and one inattentive—regarding the very same object, reveal this great difference: "Not favoring the glances of proud women, nor their faces clouded by warm tears... (35)
The moon, having risen very slowly with his beloved, seemed as if he were trembling with fear.
Gradually manifesting its digits— one, two, three, and so forth— in the sequence of a fresh lotus-root sprout,
the moon rises as if in concealment, fearing the sidelong glances of women whose eyes are inflamed by the fire of separation from their beloveds.
The distinction between these two is to be discerned by those with refined sensibilities (*sahṛdaya*); thus, it remains to be investigated by them alone.
Therefore, this is established: poetic nature (*kāvyatva*) belongs neither to the word alone as characterized by beauty, nor to the meaning alone.
Thus it has been said:
"Metaphor and other such ornaments have been described by many in various ways;
yet even the face of a beautiful woman does not shine when devoid of adornment. (VjivC 1.15)
Others declare that external ornaments consist of figures of speech (rūpaka) and the like;
they desire the refinement of words through the derivation of nominal and verbal suffixes to be their ornamentation.
Regarding this, they say: "Such is proficiency in words, not the analytical understanding of meaning;
however, for us, both are desired—namely, the distinction between verbal ornaments and the ornaments of the expressed meaning. (VjivC 1.17)
Therefore, it is established that poetry consists of both word and meaning joined together.

Having thus established that both possess the nature of poetry, [the author] says "joined" (*sahitau*) to address the possibility that the designation "poetry" might still apply even when one of the two is slightly deficient:
"joined" means existing in a state of union through their mutual association (*sāhitya*).
But surely, since the relationship between the signified and the signifier exists, there is no absence of concomitance (*sāhitya*) between these two in any way;
this is true.
However, it is a specific kind of concomitance that is intended here.
Of what nature is it?—It is the mutual ascent resulting from the rivalry between the wealth of *vakratā* (ingenuity), the various *guṇas* (excellences), and the *alaṅkāras* (ornaments).
By means of that, word and meaning, being endowed with all excellences equally, become united like two friends for the sake of each other's beauty. (VjivC 1.18)
Then the moon, its body dimmed by the first stirrings of dawn,
assumed the pale hue of the cheeks of women emaciated by love.

Here, the nourishment of the figure of speech (*arthālaṅkāra*)—achieved through the justification of the similarity between the whiteness of the moon, whose body has been dimmed by the movement of the dawn, and that of the cheek-slab of a love-languid woman—is what brings about an excellence of beauty.

Furthermore, the verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*), characterized by the artfulness of the arrangement of phonemes (*varṇavinyāsavakratā*) to be described hereafter, is also exceedingly charming. Indeed, there exists a wealth of the quality (*guṇa*) known as *lāvaṇya*, produced by the distinctiveness of the arrangement of phonemes.
And just as Śeṣa,
who bears the earth upon his head like a blue lotus,
surpasses all other men by his manliness, so too did he [the Buddha] excel all other men. // VjivC_1.20 //41 //
By Śeṣa, who playfully bears upon his head a blue lotus as if it were the earth itself,
the manly prowess of all other Śeṣas has been surpassed.

Here too, a certain poetic luster—delightful due to its capacity to convey meaning, charming through the presence of *yamaka* and *anuprāsa* composed with mere ease, and fashioned by the variety of expressed ornaments such as *aprastutapraśaṃsā* and *upamā*—gladdens the hearts of connoisseurs.

By the dual number used here, the duality of the *jāti* (genus) of the signified and the signifier is denoted. He says that if, however, the duality of the individual instances (*vyakti*) were denoted, then even two [words] situated within a single word would constitute poetry; thus he says: "situated in a composition" (*bandhe vyavasthitau*).

"Bandha" (structure) refers to the arrangement of words; "established therein" means they have taken their place through a specific disposition that is beautified by qualities such as *lāvaṇya* and by ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).

Regarding the term "conjoined" (*sahitau*), it is intended here that the conjunction between one word and another word, or between a meaning and another meaning, is characterized by mutual rivalry according to the appropriate principle of their respective classes;
otherwise, the capacity to produce delight for those who know [the art] would be lost.
How can you be resolved to make this world essence-less, to rob the three realms of their jewels, to leave the world without light, to leave kinsmen with death as their only refuge,
to render the God of Love devoid of pride, to make the creation of the eyes of living beings fruitless, and to turn the world into a withered wilderness? (VjivC 1.21)

In this regard, it is said that in a certain literary work, a particular Kāpālika, having resolved to kill a certain beloved woman, speaks as follows: "The cycle of existence (saṃsāra) has lost its essence;
the three worlds have had their entire treasure of jewels stolen; and the world of living beings is bereft of anything beautiful or worthy of being beheld."
"The creation of the eyes of all the world has become fruitless;
Kandarpa is stripped of the pride of conquering the three worlds; and by you, the world is being turned into a withered forest. Why have you resolved to perform such an improper act?"

In this verse, which is like a great aphorism (mahāvākya), other sentences resembling subordinate clauses have been composed; they are intent upon describing her wealth of beauty that captivates all the world, and being mutually competitive and exceedingly charming, they nourish a certain extraordinary poetic luster.
However, the phrase "relatives who are one's refuge in death" is not pleasing to those who know [poetry], as it does not merit even a sixteenth part of a comparison with these [other lines].

Furthermore, when many delightful expressions, which serve as a single syntactical unit, simultaneously enter the path of manifestation, the *pratibhā* (creative intuition) is further refined through effort in order to attain another [expression] corresponding to them for the sake of completing the meaning of the sentence.
In this very way, even another object that is a counterpart to the subject matter at hand becomes easily accessible—as in the phrase: “even the Creator, whose creative acts are marvelous.”
When no other object can serve as a substitute for the object that first flashed into the mind, poets bring forth a certain poetic luster by presenting something more delicate and unprecedented.
As it is said:
"The weighing of Mount Rudrādrī, the cutting of one's own throat-forest, the housing of Hari in a prison, and the seizing of the Puṣpaka chariot."

Having thus composed [the verse], since no other object corresponding to the meaning of the words previously established was possible, he introduced something entirely unprecedented with the phrase "he whose [verses] are such as these," by which even [these verses] were led to possess an indescribable charm. And just as:
The day was spent gazing at the moon of her face; likewise, the evening was passed in conversation with her, and the night too in the embrace of her limbs, as we took our delight in love.
Even now, my mind is filled with longing as I set out to see her once more, casting my eyes along the path. Why is this so?

Thus, even now, as I am intent upon beholding her in such a state, why is my mind so filled with longing? Even though the description of the object has reached its conclusion, he has arranged the matter in such a way— by saying "or rather, [a love] whose festival is not yet ended"—
that it is as if the very life of those who came before has been offered up.
Although the construction of the sentence-meaning in both of these cases is based primarily upon that [poetic suggestion],
nevertheless, it is the maturity of the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*) alone that stands as the primary factor.
An example of the absence of association between one word and another word is as follows:

Beauty adorned their bodies; the union with full and fresh youth adorned that beauty; in turn, the splendor of the fish-bannered god (Kāma) adorned that youth; and intoxication, which is adorned by union with a beloved, adorned that splendor. 51. VjivC_1.24.
When it ought to have been said, "The union with her beloved adorned her," the expression used—*madaḥ kīdṛśaḥ*, "of what kind was the intoxication?"—is flawed.

Because the compound *dayitasaṅgama-bhūṣā* ("the union with the beloved as an ornament"), which was intended to be the primary element, has been subsumed within the compound [of the sentence], it becomes subordinate; this lack of prominence fails to delight those who know such things.

Furthermore, since the figure of speech *Dīpaka* (Illuminator), which was employed to enhance the beauty of the poem, is nearly shattered at the point of its conclusion, the distaste caused by a breach of structural symmetry (*prakramabhaṅga*) cannot be avoided by those with sensitive hearts.
The variant reading "dayitasaṅgatirenam" is indeed easily understood.
In both of these examples, the absence of the company of one or the other has been explained primarily with respect to each individual case.
However, in ultimate reality, the absence of the company of either one results in the same consequence for the other as well.
And thus, even though an object manifests by its own nature when there is the presence of expressive words capable of denoting it, it remains as if dead;
likewise, a word that denotes a different meaning when the intended meaning suitable for the sentence is absent appears as a disease of the sentence—enough of this digression.
As for the subject at hand:

By what kind of composition? By one characterized by the operation of a poet (*kavivyāpāra*). That which is "crooked" (*vakra*) is that operation of the poet—distinguished by six types of crookedness—which differs from the conventional employment of words and meanings established in the sciences (*śāstra*) and other fields; it is that which "shines" (*śālate*), meaning it is praised, through the sequence of such activity.
Even though it may be marred by difficult conceptualization, he says [the following] because it possesses a distinction from the conventional: "producing delight like that [conventional]."

The word "that" (tat) refers to poetry (*kāvya*). Those who know that are "knowers of that" (*tadvidaḥ*), meaning those who understand it; [the term] produces joy—that is, bliss—for them. In this composition which brings such joy to the knowers of that, the two—*vakratā* (curvature/ingenuity) and the quality of bringing joy to the knowers of that—are established. He will provide examples for each of these types of *vakratā* and for the quality of bringing joy to the knowers of that as the occasion arises. Thus, having formulated the general definition of poetry, he begins the specific definitions.
In this regard, he first defines the essential nature of word and meaning:
"Although it is well known that the meaning is the signified and the word is the signifier, nevertheless, in this path of poetry, the ultimate reality of these two is as follows. (Vjiv 1.8)
Thus, such a thing is well-known and recognized: that which is expressive and communicative is "word" (śabda), and that which is expressed and denoted is "meaning" (artha).
Now, it may be objected that there also exist words that are merely indicative (dyotaka) or suggestive (vyañjaka).
Therefore, because they are not excluded [from the category], there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti);
for, by virtue of the commonality of producing the cognition of meaning, those two [the indicator and the suggested] are also indeed denoters through metaphorical usage.

Likewise, even in the case of the two meanings—the indicated and the suggested—they possess the status of being the "denoted" (vācya) through metaphorical usage, due to the commonality of being cognizable (pratyeyatva).

Therefore, although the status of being the signifier (*vācakatva*) and the signified (*vācyatva*) is well-established in common worldly usage as the definition of word and meaning, nevertheless, in this non-worldly path of poetry— the way of the poet’s craft— this [definition] to be described for these two is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), meaning it is some unprecedented truth.
To the question "Of what kind is it?", he says:
A word is that which expresses the single intended meaning even when other [words] are present;
its meaning is that which is beautiful through its own spontaneous vibration and brings delight to those with aesthetic sensitivity.
That sound which possesses the entire collection of factors appropriate to it is [the word] in poetry.
Of what nature is it? It is the sole designator of the intended meaning—that is, it is the one and only designator of that very meaning which the speaker desires to express.
How so? Even though others exist—
that is, even though many other words expressive of that [object] are present—
and likewise, even when there is a desire to speak of something in its general form.
Furthermore, a word that expresses its specific quality does not attain the status of a correct denoter [of the object].
For example:
"O Ocean, do not despise these many jewels because of the blows from the rocks tossed by the waves."
Was even Puruṣottama not made to stretch out his hand in supplication before you because of the Kaustubha gem? (57)
Here, the introduction began with a statement regarding the excellence of gems in general;

however, by using the word "kaustubhena" (by the Kaustubha), which denotes a specific gem, it concludes with a statement regarding the excellence of that particular [gem]. This discrepancy between the opening and the conclusion does not bring about any excellence of beauty. Nor can it be argued that whatever weight of a multitude of virtues exists in a particular instance must necessarily exist in the general category as well.
For there is a vast difference between horses, elephants, and iron; between wood, stone, and cloth; and between women, men, and water. (1.26)
Therefore, in such a context, only a word expressing the general sense attains the state of captivating the hearts of connoisseurs.
Accordingly, in this present case, an alternative reading is easily available: “Was he not indeed created by You alone?
And where it is intended to represent an object through its specific nature, poets employ only a designation that expresses that specific quality.
Just as both have now fallen into a state of lamentability through their longing for union with the Skull-Bearer (Kapālin)—
both that radiant digit of the Moon and this very world, which is the moonlight for the eyes of all beings. (Vajrāvalī 1.27)

Here, although there exist thousands of words capable of denoting the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the word "Kapālī" (the Skull-bearer)—which denotes the objective determinant (*ālambana-vibhāva*) for the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsa-rasa*)—is employed as an object of loathing, thereby producing an indescribable beauty of expression (*vācakavakratā*). Furthermore, the pair "now" (*saṃprati*) and "two" (*dvayam*) is exceedingly charming: for it is that very same [woman] who was previously singular, yet has now become pitiable due to being corrupted by her evil addiction.
Now, however, you are being ridiculed for having undertaken what is like an aid to her such wicked resolve.
Even the word "supplication" is exceedingly charming, because a union with her occurring by chance— like the "crow and the palm fruit"— is not something to be spoken of with reproach.
Furthermore, a mere prayer in this context would result in the stain of vulgarity.
Moreover, the pair "she" and "you" is employed with the intent of demonstrating the excellence of their mutual beauty, which is experienced as being in intense competition with one another.

By means of the possessive suffix *matup* in the words "kalāvataḥ" (of the skilled one) and "kāntimatī" (the lovely one), the praise of both is perceived; thus, no single meaning among these can be expressed by any other word.

Alternatively, the defining characteristic of denotation (*abhidhā*) is precisely its capacity to express the specific quality intended by the poet. For, when objects of experience— vibrating with some movement evoked at that moment within the creative intuition (*pratibhā*),

or having their inherent natures veiled by some excellence appropriate to the context at hand— enter the domain of what is to be expressed as being governed by the speaker’s intention, they are then denoted by a denotative function capable of conveying such a specific quality, thereby producing a flash of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) in the mind.
They fall into that state;
for instance, just as the lion’s fury directed toward an elephant, an insect, or a fragment of a cloud is merely a trace of pride inherent to his very birth, so it is with everyone.
Where can the lion of Amṛtāṇḍa display his excellence of wonder, he who remained unperturbed even when bound by the vast ocean-like mass of the elephants of hope? VjivC_1.28 //

Here, there is a disparagement of elephants by means of the designation "insects," a disregard for the clouds by the use of the word "fragments," and a contempt for "everything" in the sense that it consists mostly of something quite trivial.

Furthermore, the pride [of the poet] regarding his birth is indicated by the word *mātra* (mere), and the insignificance of his boastfulness is conveyed by the expression of the word *leśa* (a trace); thus, these words signify that they express a single intended meaning.
And the term *ghaṭābandha* (the binding of pots) is employed for the purpose of demonstrating the greatness relevant to the context, thereby serving as its basis.
Furthermore, for one who desires a specific designation, there arises a loss of luster because the nature of the object itself is devoid of those specific qualities intended to convey it.
Thus,
where this entire creation is as if nameless and uncarved, even the conception of a rival to its excellence reaches the ultimate limit of contempt.
For that jewel whose wealth surpasses the reach of the desires of all living beings, it is only fitting that its nature as a stone should be reduced to a mere semblance among stones.
Here, the word "ābhāsa" (appearance) itself is understood as signifying the state of being distinguished from [the actual] gems and so forth.
There is an alternative reading: "In stones that have been turned into gems by mere reflection, it is only fitting that they remain stones.
This will become manifest word by word on the occasion of defining the nature of the varieties of *vācakavakratā* (verbal artfulness); therefore, enough of this digression.

And what kind of meaning (*artha*) is characterized as the denoted? It is that which, in poetry, brings delight to those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*). Those with aesthetic sensitivity are those who know the meaning of poetry; it is that which produces for them delight, which is to say, bliss. By means of its own vibration—that is, by its own innate nature—it is beautiful and delicate.
This is what is meant: although a word-meaning may potentially be inlaid with various kinds of attributes, nevertheless, it is designated by way of such an attribute [as this one].
It is capable of bestowing delight upon the hearts of those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).

And that capacity for such delight is conceivable through either some inherent greatness of its own nature or its attainment of the state of being an integral part of the nourishment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
For example:

Victorious is that Boar, whose desires were thwarted by his own sovereign power: he did not find relief for the itching of his shoulders on mountain peaks crushed by his tusks; he did not obtain a plunge for his limbs in the oceans where the meager water trickled from the hollows of his hooves; nor did he find pleasure in wallowing in the mud of the underworld, since the earth was raised up by him using only his snout.

And here, such a power of the movement of objects is depicted, which, by obstructing other movements that would naturally occur, heightens the greatness of its own nature and thereby attains the quality of delighting the hearts of sensitive readers.
As for example:
The sage, who had gone out to gather kusha grass and fuel, followed the sound of her weeping and approached her;

his grief, born from seeing a bird pierced by a Niṣāda, took the form of a verse: "Alas, O bird! You have attained immortality through your death, for you have seen that which is difficult to see—the one who is the refuge of all beings. (Vajrācārya-vijaya 1.31)

In this context, while it would have been sufficient merely to state the synonymous term "the sage Vālmīki," the poet intended to convey that the internal movement of the mind of one who is supremely compassionate— whose sorrow arose from the mere sight of a bird pierced by a Niṣāda and which took the form of a verse (*śloka*)— is what delights the hearts of the sensitive (*sahṛdaya*), as it serves to nourish the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇarasa*) through his own state of being rendered helpless upon seeing the condition of Janaka’s daughter.
And know me, O lady whose husband lives, to be the cloud, the dear friend of your lord; I have come to your side by his command, which is held within my heart— I who,
with deep and tender sounds, urge on the crowds of weary travelers on the road who long for their wives to loosen their braided hair.

Here, first of all, the meaning of the word *māntraṇa* (addressing) is based on an activity that provides reassurance; by saying "know me as the friend of my lord," he proclaims his own worthiness of being accepted.
And that [friendship] is not ordinary;
by the word *priya* (beloved), he indicates his status as a vessel of confidence.
Having thus consoled her and turned her face upward, he introduces the subject at hand: that his arrival in your presence was due to her message.
By the phrase "placed in my heart," he illuminates the attentiveness required by their friendship.
To the objection—"Why was someone else, whose intellect is so skilled in such affairs, not appointed?"—he replies: "It is some inexplicable skill of mine alone that unfolds here."
The expression "water-carrier" (ambuvāha) indicates that it is designated as such because of its action upon the self;
it means that which hastens the multitudes of those who have set out on a journey, causing them to become filled with haste.
Of what kind [of people]? Of those who are weary, even though they are incapable of haste.
The word "multitudes" (*vṛndāni*) indicates that they have practiced performing it due to their great number.
By what means? By deep and melodious sounds.
The meaning is: by means of words charming with sweetness, that is, by employing the persuasive speech of a clever messenger.
Where? On the path, on the way.
[He says: "I am doing this merely by chance, somehow or other; why then should I not, through the impulse of affection for my friend, apply myself with effort and a sense of zeal?"
What kind of groups? "Eager for the release of the women's braids. By the word *abalā* (women), here is meant their inability to endure the distress of separation from their beloved;
thus, "eager for the release of their braids" indicates that their mental states are intensely attached to them.

Thus, the meaning of the sentence here is this: "I have always taken a vow toward the benevolence of bringing about the happiness of union for any lover whose mental state is mutually enamored and who is devoid of the separation ordained by fate. In this regard, that movement of the literal meaning (*padārtha*) which has been composed by the poet is, in the ultimate sense, the very lifeblood of the *Meghadūta* composition; therefore, it is exceedingly pleasing to the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
But it was not as it would later be, when Sītā— tender as a *śirīṣa* flower— having gone three or four steps with speed even to the outskirts of the city,
repeatedly asking, "How much further must we go today?", brought about the first descent of Rāma’s tears.
In this case, the physical movement characterized by the repeated utterance at every moment, "How much must be traveled today?", does not reveal the greatness of her inherent nature,
nor does it serve as a constituent part for the nourishment of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

For it is impossible for connoisseurs to conceive that, although such a matter was flashing in the heart of Sītā— who had resolved to go due to some innate propriety— this would actually emerge in speech simply because of her delicacy.
It is possible;
yet, even if it were recited at every moment, it would not achieve a perfect correspondence with the first appearance of Rāghava’s tears,
since that [appearance] occurs from hearing it just once.
And although this [definition] is exceedingly beautiful, it has been rendered defective by the poet due to a slight lapse in attention.
Therefore, the reading should be "avaśam" (involuntarily) in this place.
Thus, such a specific definition of word and meaning alone should be adopted.
Therefore, categories such as *neyārtha* (of indirect meaning) and *apārtha* (meaningless), having been already set aside, need not be mentioned separately.

Having thus stated that the nature of word and meaning consists of something other than their well-known conventional forms, he says that it is not merely that much which is useful for poetry, but rather that which is distinguished by further varieties of charm (*vaicitrya*).
These two are indeed to be adorned by absence;
yet their further adornment is called *vakrokti*—an expression characterized by the graceful artistry of wit.
Both of these—the word and the meaning—are the objects of ornamentation (*alaṅkārya*), and they are to be joined with some ornament that produces an excellence of beauty.
What is that ornament for them? It is stated: "The ornamentation of those two.
Even though those two are characterized by the number two, their ornamentation is, moreover, only one.
That by which even both [the speaker and the listener] are adorned—what is it? It is *vakrokti* itself. *Vakrokti* is a striking mode of expression that deviates from conventional designations.
Of what nature is it? It is an expression characterized by the artistry of wit (*vaidagdhyabhaṅgībhaṇiti*).
Wit (*vaidagdhya*) is the state of being clever, the skill in the work of a poet; its *bhaṅgī* is its distinctive charm (*vicchitti*).
An expression (*bhaṇiti*) produced through that charm is a diverse mode of signification, which is called *vakrokti* (oblique or figurative speech).
This is the intended meaning here: that word and meaning, which exist separately, are not joined by any distinct ornament;
rather, their mere expression through the application of the variety of *vakratā* (poetic deviation) constitutes their ornament, because that alone produces an excellence of beauty.
And this will be illustrated precisely at the occasion of explaining *vakratā* (curvature/obliquity).

Now, one might ask: why is this proposition asserted—which contradicts established consensus—that *vakrokti* alone is the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) and nothing else? For the ancients have handed down another ornament characterized as *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), which is exceedingly charming; unable to tolerate this, [the author] speaks in order to refute that very point: [The text continues: "But what is this being proposed, which contradicts well-known facts, namely that *vakrokti* alone is the ornament and no other? Since the ancients have taught another ornament characterized by *svabhāvokti*, and that is extremely beautiful... Thus, unable to endure [this], he says in order to refute it:
For those for whom natural description (*svabhāvokti*) is the ornament created by ornaments, what else remains [for them] once it has become the object to be ornamented? (Vjiv 1.11)
Those authors of ornaments, for whom the *svabhāvokti* (description of intrinsic nature) is the ornament— that is,
the expression or verbalization of the very movement of the intrinsic nature characterized by the properties of things— appear to consider that alone to be the adornment;
they are of such delicate minds that they are averse to the effort of discrimination.
For what is the meaning of "expression of intrinsic nature" (svabhāvokti)?

If the intrinsic nature itself, when being expressed, constitutes the ornament, then what other entity exists—distinct from that—which is like the body of poetry, such that it could stand as the object to be adorned by those ornaments?
The meaning is that there is nothing [else].
But was it not previously established that poetry belongs to the indivisible sentence itself when it possesses poetic ornaments? Why, then, is this being stated now?

True; however, it has already been said that even though such a division is unreal, it can be constructed by means of an analytical cognition (*apoddhāra-buddhi*), according to the principle of phonemes and words, and according to the principle of sentences and word-meanings.
To analyze this very point by way of another method, he says:
"It is not even logical to speak of [an entity] as distinct from its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because that which is devoid of it would result in being a mere non-entity (nirupākhyam). (Vjiv 1.12)
Apart from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), without its own activity (*parispanda*), it is neither logical nor possible to speak of or designate something as "without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*).
A real entity (*vastu*) is characterized by being expressible.
Why? Because that which is devoid of it—devoid of and abandoned by that intrinsic nature—would result in being a mere non-entity (*nirupākhya*).
That which has emerged from designation (upākhyā) is without designation (nirupākhyam). "Designation" is a word;
that which has become its non-domain is rendered simply unfit for verbal expression.

Because the etymological derivation of the word *svabhāva* is as follows: that from which both the designation (*abhidhāna*) and the cognition (*pratyaya*) arise is a *bhāva*; the *bhāva* of one's own self (*ātman*) is *svabhāva*.
Therefore, that very [self-nature] is the basis for the manifestation and description of any given entity whatsoever.
An object devoid of that [intrinsic nature], being a mere mental construction like the horn of a hare, falls outside the range of verbal cognition;

for only that which is endowed with intrinsic nature can, in every respect, enter the path of denotation. Consequently, even the sentences of common carters would possess poetic ornamentation by virtue of their being endowed with *svabhāvokti* (description of intrinsic nature).
He analyzes this very point by means of another argument:
"If the body is the ornament, what else does it adorn? The self itself never ascends upon its own aggregate. (Vjiv 1.13)
When any object being described is the very essence of that which is to be described by virtue of its nature as the subject of description,

if that [essence] itself is the ornament (*alaṅkāra*), then what else exists apart from it that could ornament or beautify it? If it is argued that "it ornaments its own self," that is incorrect, because it is logically untenable.
The meaning is that the self itself never ascends onto its own aggregate (skandha), nor does the body itself ever ascend onto its own body,
because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.

Moreover, even granting [your position], we say: if the ornamentation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is established by means of another ornament, then the cognition of the difference between those two must be either manifest or unmanifest. (Vjiv 1.14)
When [the figures] are distinct everywhere, there is commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭi*); when they are not distinct, there is confusion (*saṃkara*).
Consequently, no scope remains for other poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).

When the inherent nature is the ornament and the movement is the embellishment, and when another ornament or another embellishment is prescribed— that is, when it has been performed— then, that being the case, two possible courses arise.

What is this? It is the awareness of the distinction—the manifestation of difference—between those two other figures of speech, *svabhāvokti* and *alaṅkāra*, which is sometimes manifest and very clear, and sometimes unmanifest or indistinct.

When that [distinction] is manifest and clear, then in every case, in all poetic utterances, only the figure of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) would obtain. When that is not manifest and not clear, then in every case only the figure of *saṃkara* (blending) would obtain.
To the question "What would be the fault in that?", he says: "And no scope remains for other ornaments.
The meaning is that no domain or range whatsoever remains for other ornaments such as simile (upamā) and the like; it follows that they would simply become devoid of a subject matter.
Consequently, there would follow the absurdity that the formulation of their definitions is useless.

Furthermore, if those two— *saṃsṛṣṭi* and *saṃkara*— are postulated as their respective objects, that too is of no consequence, because those very authors of the *alaṅkāra* treatises have not accepted that point.
Enough with this futile composition, which is like chewing on empty space;
let us return to the subject at hand.

In every respect, when any kind of category of objects enters the path of description as the domain of a poet’s activity, its very nature—which brings delight to the connoisseurs—is what ought to be described as the body of poetry.
It proceeds [as such], and it alone should be joined, as appropriate, with some ornament that produces an excellence of beauty.
This is what was stated: "The meaning is beautiful through its own spontaneous movement, causing delight to those with aesthetic sensitivity" (1.9).
And [it says], "Both of these are to be adorned" (1/10).
Having thus stated the ultimate nature of word and meaning, the single term "word and meaning" (śabdārthau) in the definition of poetry (1/7) has been explained.
Now, in order to explain the term "conjoined" (*sahitau*) from [verse] 1.7, their conjunction is considered as follows:
Word and meaning always manifest in perception only when conjoined.
"These two together"—thus, those very same [two] are prescribed first by means of a boundary.
Word and meaning—namely, the signifier and the signified—are always and at all times perceived as conjoined and inseparable; they manifest together in cognition.
Therefore, what new thing is being enjoined by stating that "those two alone are conjoined and inseparable"? Nothing new is being produced;
the meaning is that what is already established is being affirmed.
Thus, since the coexistence of word and meaning is established by their very nature, what conscious person would again weary themselves with the useless task of asserting it?
This is true;
however, what is called "coexistence" in reality is not based on an eternal relationship characterized as that of the signified and the signifier.

Because if this were designated by the word "sāhitya" (poetics), then all disconnected sentences such as those beginning with *gaṅ kuṭa*—which are composed through forced constructions—and even the sentences of common carters would be designated by the term "sāhitya.

Consequently, there would be no distinction [of the field] as a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*) called "sāhitya" that is separate from grammar (*pada*), logic (*vākya*), and epistemology (*pramāṇa*).
Now, one might object: "But surely, that which is called 'sāhitya' and is distinct from words and so forth is also well-known."
Even if this were stated again, how would there not be the consequence of redundancy?
For this very reason it is said: that which is called "Sāhitya" (literature) is well-known by the mere word *sāhitya* throughout this boundless path of literary convention;

yet, even to this day, no discerning scholar has entered even slightly into the domain of inquiry as to what the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of this is, which has reached the pinnacle of excellence in the craftsmanship of the poet's work.

Therefore, today, this [work]— which is brought within the range of the six-legged bees that are connoisseurs, because it possesses an inner fragrance so enchanting as to be beautiful like a mass of drops of nectar from the lotus-heart of Sarasvatī— is being presented through the words of true poets.
There is a certain indescribable excellence in the beauty of these two when combined in literary composition (*sāhitya*).
The state that is captivating because it is neither deficient nor excessive.
The state of being together is *sāhitya*.

It is the particular, extraordinary mode of arrangement of these two—word and meaning—which, being a cause of a certain supramundane aesthetic wonder (*cetanacamatkāra*), exists in a truly marvelous way.
Of what sort is it? It is captivating because it is neither deficient nor excessive.
"Delightful due to mutual rivalry" means that in this [pair], there is no deficiency or inferiority in either one, nor is there any excess or superiority.
Now, one might object that such equality is possible even for two things that have been impaired; to this he says: "with respect to their possession of splendor."
"Śobhā" is said to be beauty;
he who shines or is distinguished by that is "śobhāśālī," and his state is "śobhāśālitā."

Regarding her who is praised for her beauty, "pratītyartha" means that very quality of being a source of delight for those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*). That state of existing in mutual rivalry toward her— a condition characterized by reciprocal equality— is called *sāhitya*.

And here, what is intended by "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) is the coexistence of the signifier with another signifier, or of the signified with another signified, because it has already been established (in 1/7) that the definition of poetry is fully realized within a single sentence.
Now, if it is asked: "Why is there no conjunction of the signifier with another signified, or of the signified with another signifier?"—it is not so.
Because there is no purpose in following either the regular or the inverted order, and because [the sequence] would otherwise lack coherence,

therefore, that particular excellence of the arrangement of words and meanings— which, according to their respective natures, arises from a collection of its own constituent factors and causes delight to those with aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya) by manifesting through mutual rivalry— is alone entitled to the designation of "literature" (sāhitya).
The arrangement of ornaments, which is fortunate in its conformity with the path, arises from qualities such as sweetness and is endowed with an excellence of artful curvature.
In this work, the nourishment of the aesthetic flavors (rasas), which is captivating through its propriety of expression,
exists in both [the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and the *Vakroktijīvita*] according to their respective natures, as if in competition with one another.
That certain state of being, which is the sole basis for the delight of those who know it and the essence of the movement from word to sentence, is called *sāhitya*.
And each of these four—grammar, logic, epistemology, and poetics—is useful for every sentence.

Thus, the function characterized by grammatical refinement (*pada-saṃskāra*) is as follows: "This very word, consisting of the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga, has such-and-such a form; and it is the signifier of this meaning, which is characterized either by the five types of nominal stem meanings or by the six types of verbal root meanings."

The utility of the investigation of sentences (vākya-vicāra) consists in this: that the intended meaning of a sentence is based upon the connection characterized by the mutual syntactic relation (parasparānvaya) of its constituent words. The purpose of the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa) is what is called "being endowed with reasoning" (yukti-yuktatva), namely, that this [sentence-meaning] is established by means of valid cognition such as perception (pratyakṣa) and so forth.

The utility of literary aesthetics (sāhitya) is that this very [meaning], through the power of its stylistic movement (parispanda), attains the state of captivating the hearts of the sensitive (sahṛdaya).

Although each of these possesses predominance within its own respective domain while the others remain subordinate, nevertheless, this very poetic operation characterized as *sāhitya*— which serves as the life-breath of the entire movement of the sentence— is in reality superior to all else. For even when this [poetic operation] is not primary, if it begins to impart refinement through its mere fragrance within another composition of sentences, that [other work] is devoid of beauty simply by being bereft of its perfuming influence.
It concludes [there].
Therefore, a falling away from its status as something to be adopted occurs;
and thus, there follows the consequence that its own activity is rendered purposeless.

It has already been established that this work possesses a purpose beyond that of ordinary treatises and yields a fruit superior to the four aims of human life (caturvarga) which are the subjects of such treatises (VjivC 1.3, 5).
Even when its meaning is not fully scrutinized, it brings delight to the hearts of those who know it through the excellence of its poetic beauty, just like a song. (VjivC 1.37)

In the accomplishment of understanding the expressed meaning, that which constitutes the very life of the words and sentences bestows upon the virtuous some indescribable internal experience, like the taste of a medicinal elixir.
Just as the body [is meaningless] without life, and life [is meaningless] without its throbbing,
so too does the poetry of the wise become lifeless without it.
Since whatever good fortune exists is accessible only to those who know that [reality], Sarasvatī now approaches them; this shall be investigated.
These are the intermediate verses.
Having thus explained that [the two] are combined, he now explains the "curvature" (*vakratva*) of the poet's operation (*kavivyāpāra*).
There are six possible types of this curvature of the poet's operation.
Each of these has many subdivisions, which are beautiful in their distinct arrangements.

The activity of poets is "poetic activity" (kavivyāpāra), characterized by the composition of poetry; its "crookedness" (vakratva) is its state of being crooked—a distinctiveness that deviates from established conventions. Its types or subdivisions are six;
the meaning is that, primarily, there are exactly that many.
Each of these has many varieties and specific subdivisions. Of what kind? "Adorned with artistic grace," meaning they shine with various modes of stylistic diversity;
the connection is that these "come into being."
He demonstrates that very point:
"The crookedness of the arrangement of phonemes and the crookedness of the first half of a word;
there is also another form of crookedness which rests upon the suffix. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 1.19)

The "arrangement of phonemes" (*varṇavinyāsa*) refers to the specific placement of letters; its "curvature" (*vakratva*) or "crookedness" (*vakrabhāva*) is the composition of a work with a distinctiveness that deviates from established conventions. It is an excellence of verbal beauty produced by a particular arrangement, which brings delight to those who know it. For example: "First having the hue of dawn-red, then the luster of gold, and thereafter the glow of the cheek of a slender woman fainting from separation..."
Then, at the onset of night, the moon—the destroyer of darkness, possessing the luster of the bulbous root of a fresh lotus stalk—spreads its light.
Here, the excellence of verbal beauty produced solely by the artifice of arranging syllables is brought forth most clearly.
This very artifice of arranging syllables is well known among the ancients as *anuprāsa* (alliteration).
An investigation into its various divisions and essential nature will be undertaken in the section on its specific characteristics (2.1).

*Padapūrvārdhavakratā* (the curvature of the first half of a word): the curvature, the state of being crooked, or the variety of arrangement belonging to the first half of a word—whether it be a nominal base (*subanta*) or a verbal root (*tiṅanta*), characterized as either a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or a verbal root (*dhātu*).
In this regard, many varieties are possible.

Where there is a composition consisting of a conventional word (*rūḍhiśabda*) itself, which is appropriate to the context and contains the superimposition of another well-known attribute of the expressed meaning, that is the first variety of *padapūrvārdhavakratā*.
Just as Rāma was, so am I; I endure everything.

The second [type of *parikara*] is that wherein there is a composition based upon the superimposition of a supramundane excellence onto a quality already well-known as the expressed meaning (*vācya*) of a conventional term.
For example: "He is that Rāma who has attained supreme renown in the worlds through the virtues of his prowess; it is only due to the reversal of our own fortune that Your Majesty does not know him.
This wind, as if a bard, sings his glories with its seven notes, which are emitted from the hollows of the vast palm trees turned into a single row by the strike of his single arrow. (Vajrāvalī 1.43)
Here, the word "Rāma," employed for the purpose of superimposing extraordinary qualities such as superhuman valor, manifests a form of poetic curvature (*vakratā*).

This is another variety of curvature belonging to the first half of a word, called "curvature of the synonym" (*paryāya-vakratva*): where a thing has multiple synonymous designations, a particular synonym is employed because it accords with the context of the subject at hand, as follows:

May the first form of the enemy of Smara protect you—his left eye like collyrium, his chest with swelling, firm breasts, his waist suddenly slender, and the region of his hips possessing vast curves; being gazed upon repeatedly by the Gaṇas, who were struck with immediate wonder as he merged with his beloved.
In this context, the synonym “smararipoḥ” (of the enemy of Smara) unfolds a certain poetic ingenuity (*vakratā*).
For, since a physical union with the beloved is in no way conceivable for the enemy of Kāma, the immediate astonishment of the Gaṇas is rendered plausible.
Furthermore, because that [union] becomes a source of wonder through repeated contemplation, it is the very life-force of the word “first” (*prathama*).
And this "crookedness by way of synonyms" is also observed through the inclusion of another attribute that is not inherent in the literal meaning, as for example:
"O King of Aṅga, O General, O favorite of the king, protect Duḥśāsana from Bhīma! VjivC_1.45 //

Here, the three synonyms are ridiculed by implying their inherent incapacity to provide protection, characterized by the impossibility of their being fit vessels for such rescue—expressed as "protect him.

A different variety of figurative deviation (*upacāra-vakratva*) exists within the deviation of the first half of a verse-line, wherein an immaterial entity is expressed through a word denoting a material substance by means of metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*).
For example: "Even a mere atom of humiliation, when causeless, exhausts the mind of the high-minded."

For example: "His fame is to be gathered by the hand. Here, the word *kaṇikā* (a small particle) primarily denotes a small portion of a material object; however, through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the general quality of "smallness" (*stokatva-sāmānya*), it is employed with the intent of denoting even a non-material slight (*nikāra*). Because it produces delight for those who understand it, it nourishes *vakratā* (poetic curvature).

The expression "to be gathered by the hands" (*hastāvaceya*)— applied through the metaphorical transfer of the common property of being a collection of material objects such as flowers to fame, which is itself immaterial— brings about a striking poetic curvature (*vakratva*). It is well-established in the tradition of poets that a word denoting a liquid substance, based on qualities such as rippling, is employed as a denoter of even a solidified mass by relying on a mere semblance of similarity.
Just as on the slope of her breasts, rippled by the trembling of her breath.
In some instances, even that which is formless is employed as a denotative term to signify an object in a liquid state;
for example:

"These arms of his, eager to dispel the itching caused by the heat of their valor, might once again become occupied with the battle of the infant hosts of the gods long forgotten. (Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī 1.47)
In these two examples, the words "taraṅgiṇī" (river) and "vipruṣam" (drop) possess an indescribable curvature (*vakratā*).

This is what is called the "curvature of the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇavakratva*), a variety of the curvature of the first half of a word; it occurs where the very power of the qualifier brings forth that curvature characterized by delighting those who know such things, as for example: [Example omitted in source] In this case, the curvature—defined as the capacity to produce aesthetic rapture in connoisseurs—is manifested solely through the greatness of the qualifying attribute.
A burning fever consumes her like water poured into a small vessel; her tears flow in abundance; her sighs are observed by the flickering flames of the lamps; her body is submerged in pallor.
What more shall I say? Throughout the entire night, she remains at her window, her moonlight obscured by the parasol of her hand as she gazes toward the path you have taken.
In this case, no variety has been manifested in the burning, the tears, the sighs, or the body;
yet, through the power of each individual qualifier, a certain degree of poetic curvature (*vakratā*) is perceived.
As for example:
Because of her shame, with her face cast down in the presence of her elders and her jar-like breasts trembling, she restrained her inner resentment;
what indeed did she not say "Stay," when she cast aside her tears and fixed upon me that third part of her eye which steals the gaze of a startled doe?

In this context, the adverbial phrase "cakitahariṇīhārī" (stealing the glance of a startled doe) brings about an indescribable power of enchantment in the side-long glance of the eye— a glance made lovely by its timidity due to the presence of elders— by means of its similarity to the gaze of a startled doe.
This is another variety of the curvature of the first half of a word-line, namely what is called "curvature through concealment" (*saṃvṛtivakratva*), wherein...

The true nature of an object, which— due to its conformity with the context— is joined with some degree of deficiency or excellence and cannot be directly expressed in its manifest clarity, is denoted by a word that functions through the power of conventional usage (*saṃvṛti*).
For example:
Thus, this man, maintaining his vows out of hypocrisy, is intent on doing something [deceitful] toward his beloved.

In this context, Vatsarāja— his heart distressed by the calamity that befell Vāsavadattā and yet desiring to marry Padmāvatī out of a longing to recover her— recognizes that very act as something not to be done; he thus proclaims the unspeakability of that matter, which is like a great banner of infamy,
by means of the pronoun *kimapi*, a term capable of concealment.

Even now, those sweet syllables of hers— neither meaningful nor meaningless, uttered by that fair-limbed woman whose eyes were half-closed in sleep and who was languid with intoxication— resound in my heart in some inexplicable way.

Here, by the phrase "something [unnameable]," it is established that the aesthetic wonder (*cittacamatkṛti*) produced by hearing that [sound] is indefinable, characterized as being accessible solely to direct experience.
By the word "those," it is indicated that they are remembered as being qualified by such an experience.
Furthermore, by the phrase "nor even meaningful," it is revealed that, due to being self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*), they are not objects of verbal designation.
And as for those [words] which are not meaningless, their lack of purpose is precluded because they produce a non-worldly charm (*alaukika-camatkāra*).
In all three of these cases, the "curvature" (*vakratva*) of the qualifier is perceived.

This other variety of the curvature of the first half of a word is possible, namely what is called the "curvature of the variety of stylistic modes" (*vṛtti-vicitrya-vakratva*)—wherein poets employ only certain varied stylistic modes, such as compounds (*samāsa*), and so forth.
An appropriation is made,
just as sprouts [arise] from a seedling in the middle.
And just as his body was submerged in paleness.
Or just as even a fragment of the moon, which brings forth the splendor of the flowing nectar of ambrosia,
does not fail to cause people’s minds to soar in rapture.

Furthermore, another variety of the curvature of the first half of a word, known as the "curvature of diversity of gender" (*liṅgavaicitryavakratva*), is observed—wherein words of different genders are placed in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) for the sake of aesthetic variety, as in:
"In this inert world, who indeed could have ears of such great magnitude? Surely it must be an elephant, the fit recipient of [this] sound. (VjivC 1.55)
And as in the verse, "Just as Maithilī was his wife" (VjivC 1.56),
there is another type of curvature through the variety of genders— where, even though multiple genders are possible, poets employ only the feminine gender out of a sense of delicacy.
"Thinking that 'the mere name "woman" is charming,'" as it were. For example:
"Behold this shore before you. // VjivC_1.57 //

Within the first half of a verse-line, there exists another variety of *vakratā* (poetic curvature) called the "curvature of the manifoldness of action" (*kriyāvaicitryavakratva*) pertaining to the verbal root (*dhātu*).
This is where poets compose linguistic applications that are made beautiful by the artful expression of cleverness, with the intent of demonstrating the manifoldness of action.
In that regard, the manifoldness of action is seen to be of many kinds, characterized by an extensive range of aesthetic distinctions (*vicchitti*).
Victorious is the third eye of Rudra, which was kissed by Pārvatī while his pair of eyes were covered by her sprout-like hands as she pulled away her garment during their amorous play.
Victorious is the third eye of Rudra, kissed by Pārvatī, while his pair of eyes were blocked by her lotus-stalk-like hands as she removed her garment during their amorous play.
Thus ends the shadow.

In this verse, although the purpose of concealment and the general quality of being an eye are the same for both, the meaning of the sentence is that the Blessed One’s third eye— which achieves the obstruction [of the world] by means of kissing the Goddess— triumphs, existing in a state of supreme excellence.
Here, a certain wondrous beauty, perceivable only by the hearts of sensitive connoisseurs, is clearly manifest in the verbal root *ji* (to conquer/triumph).
And may the nails of the Enemy of Mura— those lions at will, which eclipse the moon with their own pure luster— protect you, for they sever the suffering of those who have sought refuge in him.

In this instance, a certain unprecedented variety of action characterized by the cutting away of the distress of those who have sought refuge is depicted, which is distinct from the act of cutting [objects] well-known to all the world, such as nails.
And just as it is said:
"May that arrow-fire of Śambhu burn away your sin. (VjivC 1.60)
And here, as before, there is the perception of a variety of actions;
for example:
