Now, propriety (*aucitya*) is a poetic quality (*guṇa*).

Of what nature is it? It is that by which the greatness or excellence of the essential nature of an object is nourished—that is, brought to full development—through a manner that is straightforward and very clear.
Since the word "manner" (*prakāra*) has been introduced [in the definition], it is the variety of expression (*abhidhāvaicitrya*) that is denoted here by the term "manner."
Of what kind? It is that whose life—its ultimate reality—is a fitting narrative and noble expression;
it is so described because the arrangement of ornaments brings about aesthetic charm only when it is in harmony with this very [life].
For example:
With rosaries held in the palms of their hands, their fingers slightly trembling with rising trepidation,
and their beautiful matted locks arranged with care, they appeared like another meeting of two Īśvaras.
Or else, let this army of Indra encamp on the opposite shore of the mountain, like a settlement at the foot of a hill;
for surely your elephants, difficult to restrain, will not tolerate the scent of the ichor from the divine elephant Airāvata in their vicinity.
And furthermore,
O Nāgarāja, when you wrap your coils many times tightly around the slopes of Mount Mandara,
what excessive burden is there for you, who have mastered the practice of the cross-legged posture through the playful union with the unbearable bull-vehicle?

In the two preceding examples here, the nourishment of that quality occurs solely through the excellence of the ornament (*bhūṣaṇaguṇa*), whereas in the other case, it occurs through the expression of natural nobility (*svabhāvaudārya*).
He now reveals the true nature of propriety (*aucitya*) itself by means of a different perspective:
Where the expressed meaning of the speaker or the knower is concealed by the speaker’s own nature through an excellence of beauty, that too is called propriety (aucitya). Vjiv 1.54.

In whatever case, when the object to be expressed— the thing denoted— by the speaker, the designator, the knower, or the experiencer, is concealed or veiled by the speaker’s own nature or movement through an excellence of beauty that is captivating in its loveliness, that too is called propriety (*aucitya*).
For example:
O lord of men, standing there with only your body remaining, you shine with the splendor bestowed by sacred fords;
you appear like a stalk of wild rice left behind, its yield of grain gathered by forest-dwellers.

In this context, while describing such an activity of a great king as something worthy of praise, the application of poetic ornaments by the sage, in accordance with the worldly conventions established by his own experience, brings about a nourishment of propriety (*aucitya*).
Here, by the very nature of the speaker, the activity of the expressed subject is perceived as being largely concealed (*saṃvṛta*),
just as in the case of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
With her clusters of blossoms being drunk by bees and her young shoots trembling, the Ashoka branch was seen by the women imitating the forceful biting of lips and the shaking of hands.
In this context, it is appropriate for young women to experience such delight in its beauty according to the impressions of their own personal experience;
as in the verse:
"O dear friend, the lotus-beds in the pond are seen by those who have gone to bathe."
They do not hold it in their hands, they say "no," yet they give way to turn back.
The groves on the banks of the pond are seen by those who have gone there to bathe;
they cannot grasp them with their hands, they cannot enjoy anything there, and furthermore, they do not yield [their fruits].
This is the "shadow" (chāyā).

Here, by means of the nature of a certain subject who is beautiful through the vibration of her extraordinary innocence, the expressed meaning is veiled, which brings about the nourishment of propriety (*aucitya*).
Having thus explained propriety, he now explains beauty (*saubhāgya*):
Thus, within this category of what is to be adopted, that quality by which the poet’s creative intuition (pratibhā) exerts itself correctly is called "grace" (saubhāgya). Vjiv 1.55.

In this manner, regarding this collection of things to be adopted— the aggregate of goals such as fame and so forth— for the sake of which, and for what purpose, the poet’s *pratibhā* (creative intuition) or power exerts itself and resolves with full attentiveness, the excellence (*guṇa*) belonging to that subject matter— which is designated as poetry— is called and spoken of as "grace" (*saubhāgya*).
And that [attainment] is not accomplished by the mere intensity of manifestation, but rather must be produced by the complete assembly of all the requisite conditions; thus he says:
"It is to be accomplished by the activity of all perfections for those whose nature is full of aesthetic flavor (*sarasātman*)."
It produces extraordinary wonder and is the sole lifeblood of poetry.

That which is to be accomplished through the dynamic manifestation (*parispanda*) of the perfection that constitutes the pinnacle of faultlessness—the perfection of the entire mass of things worthy of being adopted, which is itself produced by the movement of all prosperity—and furthermore, what is it like? It is that which produces extraordinary wonder for those whose souls are moist with feeling, bestowing a supermundane joy.
In short, this is the sole life-force of poetry; the meaning is that it is the supreme, ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of poetry.

This is that city of the lord of the Niṣādas in the *Raghuvamśa*, where, having cast off my crest-jewel, I bound my hair in matted locks; there Sumantra wept, saying, "O Kaikeyī, your desires have borne fruit!"

In this context, for the Lord of the Raghus— who is being described as possessing the priceless attributes of a Great Man— to be reminded of such a trivial matter as "O Kaikeyī, your desires have borne fruit," and for that to be expressed,
brings about extreme impropriety.
Even in a literary composition, if there is a lack of propriety in even a single part of the work, it results in a state akin to a burnt cloth that has been damaged by a fire in one spot.
As it says in the *Raghuvamśa*, during the occasion of the dialogue between Dilīpa and Siṃha:
"You fear your guru, who is like a fire because of his fierce anger over the offense of a single cow;
yet even you can appease his wrath by offering him crores of cows with udders as large as jars. (VjivC 1.123)
Thus, it was indeed appropriate for the lion to speak in this manner,
as he was speaking with the intent of mocking the king;
for this king, however, being intent on preserving his own glory, his life appears to him as light as a blade of grass.
Regarding this, as a rebuttal to that preliminary objection:
"How indeed could the great seer be propitiated by anything other than the gifting of milch cows?
Know this cow to be no less than Surabhi herself; it was only by the power of Rudra that you struck her."

If the capacity to provide a corresponding object for other cows were ever possible, then this indifference toward preserving our lives—both that of the sage and mine—would be justified; however, since this is the ultimate conclusion of the intent, this statement is utterly improper.

And as in the *Kumārasambhava*, when the Lord of the Gods was addressed by Manmatha on the occasion of his desire to conquer the enemy named Tāraka, whose prowess was intent upon overwhelming the three worlds:
You desire that woman of shapely hips— who was once the devoted wife of another, whose character was defined by the hardships of her vows, and who entered your fickle mind through her beauty—

Thus, this devotion to the practice of impropriety—described as being intent on following such inclinations even though he was established in the sovereignty of heaven—brings about a lack of decorum.

And this is considered in light of this very poet’s innate delicacy, which is the beauty of the vibration of his well-spoken verses; it is not, however, [the case] for others who merely boast of their skill in the composition of artificial poetry.

Moreover, *saubhāgya*— the singular life-force of poetry, perceivable by the hearts of the sensitive, which produces a transcendental charm, beautiful through the tasting of various blended sentiments, and manifesting as a distinct quality of poetry by pervading all its constituent parts— is something that shines forth as a separate excellence of poetry, possessing manifold lovely causes within each word, sentence, context, and composition; but enough of this digression.
Now, having concluded this, he introduces another topic:
This triad of paths has been traversed many times by certain seekers eager to attain what is to be reached; having reached some region therein, they have attained renown.
All poets, charming in their free movement, shall now follow it. In that regard, a certain particular sequence of steps consisting of beautiful and excellent words is being described.

This triad of paths, beginning with the delicate (*sukumāra*) and so forth, has been traversed through repeated practice many times by certain great poets alone— not by ordinary people— and by those who were eager to attain [their goals] and yearned for what was to be reached.

In whichever of these three paths they have attained renown by reaching a certain stage— having reached a supramundane level and gained recognition— now all poets shall go by that path which is charming with its free roaming, delightful for wandering at will; it is a certain extraordinary path, made beautiful and excellent by the virtuous, characterized by a graceful succession of well-placed steps.
The systematic arrangement of the sequence for the assignment of fortunate verbal roots and suffixes is being told;
words such as *mārga*, *svaira-vihāra*, *pada*, and so forth are to be explained by virtue of their distinction through the shadow of paronomasia (*śleṣacchāyā*).
Thus ends the first chapter (*unmeṣa*) in the *Vakroktijīvita*, a treatise on poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṅkāra*), composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Kuntaka.

In the second unmeṣa of the *Vakroktijīvita*, it is stated that once a general definition has been established, a specific definition must be formulated. Having thus provided the general definition of poetry as "word and meaning joined together" (*śabdārthau sahitau*) and so forth (1.7), the specific definition of the "joining" (*sāhitya*) of word and meaning— which constitute its constituent parts— was already set forth in the first unmeṣa.

Now he begins the specific definition of the curvature of syllable arrangement (*varṇavinyāsavakratva*), which was mentioned first: When one, two, or many syllables are repeated again and again with little interval between them, that is said to be the threefold curvature of syllable arrangement (*varṇavinyāsavakratā*). (Vjiv 2.1)

In this context, the term *varṇa* refers to the artistic arrangement of phonemes (*vyañjana-vinyāsa-vicchitti*). It is said to be threefold, described in three ways. What, then, are those three ways? It is stated: one is [a single] phoneme alone;
sometimes two or many phonemes are joined together, being repeated again and again.
Of what kind? "With very little interval" (*svalpāntarāḥ*).
Those for whom the *antara*—that is, the separation or distance—is extremely small (*sutaram alpaṃ*) or slight (*stokam*), are so described.
These alone are called the three types.

Here, by means of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) "again and again," the restriction is intended to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), not to exclude connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).
Therefore, they are indeed bound again and again.
But it is not the case that they are bound again and again.
In this regard, an example of the connection with a single consonant (*ekavyañjananibandha*) is as follows:
"A braid of hair adorned with a few scattered flowers; a smile that is the very pinnacle of beauty; a cleverly sweet arrangement of words; and a soft, fifth-note (*pañcama*) melody in the throat."
With eyes whose pupils were languid with playfulness, moving with the grace of amorous charm—such was the indescribable gait of that fawn-eyed woman, refined by the impact of the arrows of Love.
An illustration for one, two, and many [subjects] is as follows:

"The winds of the ocean, which break the rows of cardamom creepers, cause the clusters of plantains to tremble, and scatter the betel-nut trees, rose-apples, and citron trees; where the *tāla*, *tālī*, and *sarala* trees dance with swaying grace, and the waves surge with playful force, shattering the inertia of the marshes along the banks—these winds have removed the exhaustion of the women of his army caused by their incessant practice of lovemaking. (Vajrāvalī 2.2)
He distinguishes this very same curvature by means of another poetic figure (vicchitti):

"The stops (sparśas) joined with the final letters of their respective classes, the doubled consonants, the *ta*, *la*, and nasals (*nādi*), and the remaining consonants when conjoined with the *ra*-group—these shine with the appropriateness of the context at hand. (Vjiv 2.2)
This other type of "curvature of phoneme arrangement" (*varṇavinyāsavakratā*) is said to be threefold, in three ways; this is connected with the word "and" (*ca*).

What, then, are its three modes? He says: "The stops (*sparśa*) joined with the finals of the classes. The "classes" (*varga*) are the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*; those which have a conjunction (*yoga*), that is, a union (*saṃyoga*), with the finals of those classes, such as *ṅa* and so forth, are described in that manner.
Being bound again and again— this is the first type.

The consonants *ta*, *la*, *na*, and so forth— beginning with the letters *ta*, *la*, and *na*— when doubled, uttered twice, and thus made twofold, being bound again and again— this is the second type.

The remaining letters, distinct from those [already mentioned], which are designated as consonants (*vyañjana*), when joined with the letter *ra* and so forth, and being repeated again and again—this is the third [type]. They are all connected by the qualities of having "very slight intervals" and being "separated by limited distances.
And what are they like? They are "those that enhance the beauty of the context under discussion."

That which is "present" is the subject matter currently being described; those things that "shine by virtue of its propriety"—meaning by virtue of its fitness (*ucitabhāva*)—are what have been so described.

However, they are not merely composed out of an obsession with phonetic similarity (*varṇasāvarṇya*), for such [mere similarity] causes the fading of the propriety of the subject matter. Because they shine through the propriety of the subject matter, in certain instances where a harsh sentiment (*paruṣarasa*) is introduced, he permits exactly such [words].
Now, an example of the first enclosure (prākāra) is as follows:

and who, trembling, clung to his neck with the weight of her full breasts.

Thus is the shadow (*chāyā*). Having thus explained this curvature of the arrangement of phonemes (*varṇa*), he concludes that very point: "In accordance with the shadow of the phonemes, it follows the path of the qualities (*guṇa*)."
"That very [nature] is described by the ancients as being endowed with a variety of modes of existence."

That which follows—that is, the pursuit through entering into the very nature of what is to be attained—the shadow or luster of phonemes and syllables by means of the causal perfection of qualities such as being pleasant to hear;
and that which conforms to the paths of quality (guṇa-mārga) beginning with the "delicate" (sukumāra) and so forth, is described as such.
In this context, the qualities are presented first because of their internal beauty.
Since it is appropriate to follow the paths by means of their qualities alone,
this is the meaning here: even if this curvature of the arrangement of phonemes follows only the shadow of the consonants,
nevertheless, it must be so fashioned that it brings about an entry into the essential nature of the paths— which are distinguished by specific qualities— by way of conforming to those qualities.
And for that very reason, its extensive varieties, which are based upon it, manifest themselves.
However, the ancient masters have declared that this [rhetorical figure] itself is endowed with the diversity of *vṛtti* (modes of expression) by virtue of its independence.

It has been described by the former scholars as being "endowed" (*yuktā*)—that is, possessed—of the "diversity" (*vaicitryam*), or manifold nature, of the *vṛttis* such as *upanāgarikā* and others, which is distinguished by differences in their own inherent numerical classifications.

This is the intended meaning here: since this [poetry] follows the modes such as the *sukumāra* (delicate) and others through its adherence to the synthesis of the essential nature of all the poetic qualities (*guṇas*), both its dependence and its manifoldness are necessarily present; therefore, [the claim that it possesses] independence and a limited number of modes is not very convincing.

If it is objected: "But why was this stated, since you yourself have already explained the limited modes—such as 'one,' 'two,' and so forth—as well as independence, by way of those very categories?"—this is not a fault.

For the authors of grammatical definitions (*lakṣaṇakāra*) first delineate the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of any given category that functions in dependence upon a composite whole as being independent, by means of an analytical abstraction (*apoddhārabuddhi*), for the sake of teaching others;
thereafter, its inclusion within the composite whole will follow. Enough of this digression.

That very ornament of the expressive word called "curvature through the arrangement of phonemes" (varṇavinyāsavakratā), which was previously enumerated as having the entire sentence as its scope because it lacks restriction to a specific position, produces a different kind of aesthetic charm when it is composed with a fixed location by being distinguished by a different mode; thus he says:
"Having identical phonemes, possessing a different meaning, clear, and sweet to the ear..."
That which is endowed with propriety and shines in its fixed initial position and so forth; Vjiv_2.6 //
A certain variety of this [verse], known as *yamaka* (rhyme), is observed;
however, because it lacks a different kind of beauty, it is not elaborated upon here.
Some particular mode of this aforementioned [consciousness] is observed;
some unprecedented distinction of it is discerned.
He asks, "What is this? and says: "It is called *yamaka*.
*Yamaka* is its established name. And what is it like? It consists of identical phonemes (*samānavarṇa*).
That in which the phonemes (*varṇa*) are equal, similar in form, and identical in sound is described as such.
Thus, whether separated or contiguous, that very arrangement of one, two, or many sounds that are identical in hearing is called *yamaka* (chiasmus).
Therefore, even though there is a single form existing in two arrangements, it has "another meaning," that is, a different denotation.

And what else is it like? It is *prasādi*, meaning endowed with the quality of clarity (*prasāda*), which conveys the meaning of the sentence instantaneously—that is, it is intelligible without difficulty. This very term is further specified as *śrutipeśalam*: *śruti* refers to the sense organ of hearing, and *peśalam* means pleasing or delightful to it.
It is composed of words that are not harsh.
Of what nature? Endowed with propriety (*aucitya*). Propriety is the excellence of the inherent nature of the object being described; it is joined with, that is, possessed of, that.
The meaning is that even when there is an addiction to the composition of *yamaka* (rhyme), its propriety (*aucitya*) remains unfaded.
He qualifies that very same [propriety] with another attribute: "that which shines by means of fixed positions beginning with the first.

Those things whose "first" is the "first" are so described; namely, the beginning, middle, and end. That which shines—that is, which radiates—by means of those very fixed positions, which are specific arrangements, is so described.
In this context, terms such as "first" (*ādyādi*) are relative words that must be qualified by terms such as "foot" (*pāda*).
Although that category exists as being endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, it is not elaborated upon extensively here in this treatise;
why? Because there is no other [distinct] beauty [to be gained].
The meaning is that no other distinct beauty or distinct shadow [of expression] is possible apart from the restriction of position.
Furthermore, nothing else whatsoever is observed as a different "life-force" (jīvita) apart from the variety of the arrangement of phonemes;
therefore, it is logical that this is simply a type of ornament (alaṅkāra) mentioned immediately above.
Examples of such *yamakas* that convey meaning are found here in the fourth canto of the *Śiśupālavadha*,
or in the description of spring in the *Raghuvamśa*.

Thus, having examined the poetic curvature (*vakrabhāva*) in the arrangement of phonemes as parts of words, the examination of the poetic curvature of the word itself— which consists of a collection of phonemes— is now reached.
In this regard, he begins to discuss how many varieties of the "crookedness" (vakratā) of the first half of a verse-line are possible:

"Where it is perceived that there is either an internalization of the superimposition of an impossible quality upon a conventional usage, or an internalization of the superimposition of an excellence of a real quality. (Vjiv 2.8)

With the desire to express a praiseworthy excellence that transcends the mundane, a certain strikingness of conventional usage (*rūḍhivaicitryavakratā*) is described for the expressed meaning (*vācya*). Vjiv_2.9.
Where it is understood that conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) consists in the superimposition of an improbable property,
this is called the "fixed application" (*niyatavṛttitā*) of a word; for conventional usage is so termed because it is a "growing" (*rohaṇa*).
And that [conventional usage] occurs in two ways: as functioning through a restricted generality and as functioning through a restricted particularity.

Therefore, by the term *rūḍhi* here, a word in which convention is predominant is denoted, because one observes the metaphorical treatment of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) as non-different.

In whatever domain (*viṣaya*) there is the superimposition (*adhyāropa*), the assignment (*samarpaṇa*), of some quality (*dharma*)—such as a movement—that is impossible (*asaṃbhāvya*), i.e., incapable of being conceived, for a conventional word (*rūḍhiśabda*); that which has such a superimposition as its internal intention (*garbha-abhiprāya*) is so described, and the state of being thus (*tattā*) is what is perceived, i.e., what is communicated.
This is the connection with the word "wherein" (*yatra*).
Alternatively, it means "having as its core the attribution of an excellence to the True Dharma.

It is the state (*tattva*) of that which is so described— that which has as its core (*garbha*), namely its essential nature, the attribution (*āropa*), that is, the conferral, of some unprecedented excellence, a marvelous form, or majesty (*mahiman*) upon the vibration (*parispanda*) of an existing entity (*saddharma*), which is both real (*sat*) and the Dharma (*dharma*).
And that [superiority] is perceived in whatever [object] it resides.
By what cause? By the desire to express a contemptuous surpassing and a praiseworthy excellence.

"Supramundane" (*lokottara*) means surpassing all; "contempt" (*tiraskāra*) means humiliation; and "praiseworthy excellence" (*ślāghyotkarṣa*) is preeminence that is desirable. The "desire to express" (*abhidhitsā*) these two is the wish to speak, the intention to utter them.
By that [convention].
Of what denotable object? Of that object which is the denotation—the signified meaning—of a conventional word (rūḍhi-śabda).
It is said that there exists a certain extraordinary (*alaukikī*) curvature of the variety of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
This "curvature" (*vakratā*), or state of being curved, belongs to the conventional word itself through such a variety—that is, through its manifold nature.

The intended meaning here is this: although for words that touch upon generalities and varieties, an embrace by a fixed particular—just as in the case of inference—is not possible at all by their very nature, [the poet achieves it].
Nevertheless, when led by this reasoning toward a specific, intended particularity by the poet, they attain a certain capacity to produce aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
As it is said:
"The qualities arise from the palm tree [only] when they are grasped by those who know how."
The lotuses, graced by the rays of the sun, cause other lotuses to fade.
Virtues arise only when they are perceived by those with sensitive hearts;
lotuses become truly lotuses only when graced by the rays of the sun.

Thus is the shadow [of the meaning]. This is the intended sense of the variety of verbal forms such as "is perceived" (*pratīyate*): that in such a case, words do not function by way of denotation (*vācakatva*), but rather merely by causing a cognition similar to that of other real entities. Although this is logically sound, it will not be elaborated upon here at great length.
Since the relationship between the suggested and the suggester has been thoroughly established here by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*, what is the point of repeating it?

Furthermore, that "beauty of deviation" (*vakratā*) arising from the variety of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) occurs in two ways: namely, where either the speaker himself or someone else, desiring to superimpose excellence or deficiency upon the conventional meaning itself, employs it.

Let the clouds, with their glossy dark luster coating the sky and swarms of cranes fluttering about, be as they will; let the winds be laden with spray, and let the sweet warbling of the peacocks—the friends of the clouds—be as joyous as they please.
I am Rāma, possessed of a heart hard as stone; I shall endure all. But how will Vaidehī fare? Alas, alas! O Queen, be steadfast.
In this context, by the word "Rāma," that very thing which cannot be conveyed by either of the two phrases— "firm" or "hard-hearted"— namely,

the capacity to endure the abundance of such various excitant factors (*uddīpana-vibhāvas*), characterized by a lack of shame and skill in preserving one's life even at a time when one is overwhelmed by the unbearable agony of separation from Janaka’s daughter— the son of the King— is established as the basis for the designation [of the name].
An extraordinary and unparalleled cruelty is perceived;
by the word "Vaidehī," a certain timidity—natural to her innate delicacy—is established, which conveys her inability to endure the sight of objects beautiful during the rainy season.
This is precisely that.
And [this] is the lifeblood of the word "but" (*tu*), which expresses a distinction from what precedes;
it consists in the superimposition of an excellence upon an existing property, as for example:
"Then, having laughed at Purandara, the son of the Indra of the earth, being free from fear, spoke again."
Take up your weapon if this is your resolve; for you shall certainly not achieve success without having conquered Raghu.

"By the word *raghu* here, in every instance, there is perceived a certain excellence of his own prowess—based on his capacity to thwart even the Lord of the Gods (Indra), despite the latter's unimpeded power—due to such a determination;
this very point is reinforced by the word *prahasya* ('laughing'). An example where another speaker is involved is as follows:"

His command is cherished by the crest-jewel of Śakra; the scriptures are his fresh eyes; devotion to the Lord of Beings, the wielder of the Pināka bow, is his lotus-feet; his residence is the divine city of Laṅkā;
and his birth is in the lineage of Brahmā. Oh, such a suitor is not easily found! Yet, were he not Rāvaṇa, where indeed could all these virtues be found together?

By the word "Rāvaṇa" here, there is understood a certain blemish (*aupahatya*)—the cause of unacceptability—which eclipses the entire perfection of all excellent qualities characterized by noble lineage, discernment, virtuous conduct, power, enjoyment, happiness, and prosperity; this blemish is distinct from the notorious misconduct of the ten-faced one well-known to the whole world.

In this very instance, the presence of an implied superimposition (*adhyāropa*) based on an excellence of qualities actually existing [in the subject] is as follows: "That Rāma has attained supreme renown in the worlds through his qualities of valor. (VjivC 2.30)

Here, by the word "Rāma," there is perceived an excellence of valor that surpasses the entire three worlds and serves as a source of wonder for the followers of Rāvaṇa. And this crookedness (*vakratā*) consisting in the variety of conventional usage (*rūḍhivaicitrya*) is divided into many types due to the abundance of implied attributes (*pratīyamāna-dharma*);
that [variety] should be inferred by oneself.
Just as the one who had mastered the Vedas, having failed to obtain wealth from Raghu for the sake of his teacher,
went to another donor— may this not become a new occasion for my censure.
“By the word ‘Raghu’ here, an excellence of magnanimity that surpasses the three worlds is understood.

In this kind of poetic curvature (*vakratā*), the ultimate truth is precisely this: that by setting aside mere generality, an extraordinary beauty characterized by the capacity to convey the specific intended meaning of the poet is made to shine forth.
One should not say that no relationship of general and particular is possible because proper names (*saṃjñā-śabda*) are restricted to fixed meanings.”
Since it is indeed possible for even those [synonyms]— whose denotative function is common to thousands of states— to be restricted to a specific, fixed condition as intended by a skilled poet,

according to the principles of musical intervals (*svara-śruti*) and the analogy of clinging silk (*lagna-aṃśuka*); having thus analyzed the crookedness (*vakratā*) of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), he now analyzes the crookedness of synonyms (*paryāya-vakratā*), which follows in the sequence of the discussion:
The most intimate among the objects of expression nourishes its excellence;
through contact with other beautiful shades, it is capable of adorning it. (Vjiv 2.10)

Furthermore, that which is described by means of its own qualification as being delicate with the excellence of its own radiance, containing within it the capacity to be a vessel for an inconceivable object; Vjiv_2.11 //
A synonym is a composition that captivates the mind through the refinement of ornaments;
by means of it, there arises a variety known as the supreme "curvature of synonyms" (paryāyavakratā).

That which is characterized by the previously mentioned attributes, occurring in the context of poetry, is a *paryāya* (synonym/turn); by reason of that, whatever variety (*vaicitrya*), whatever state of diversity (*vicitrabhāva*), or whatever specific strikingness (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) there may be, that is called a certain supreme or preeminent *paryāyavakratā* (the crookedness of synonymy).

A word in which the synonym is predominant is designated as a *paryāya*. And its very predominance as a synonym consists in this: that it sometimes functions as the expressive denoter (*vācaka*) for a particular intended object.

"Or sometimes another denoter. By that [statement], according to the principle previously stated, many types of synonyms have been mentioned; therefore, he asks how many types there are of it, and says: "that which is most similar to what is not the denotable object."
The "subject matter" (abhidheya) is the thing to be expressed; that which is its "innermost" (antaratama) is the most proximate.
This is because, even though other words may be synonyms, this particular term—due to its internal fitness (*antaraṅgatva*)—manifests the intended object in a way that no other word can.
For example: [text follows]
"You do not wish to bring a falsehood upon yourself; what regard have you for the arrows of ascetics?
For we possess other arrows against the mountain-king, which are the very strides of the wielder of the thunderbolt."

Here, although countless synonymous terms expressive of Mahendra are possible, the use of the word "vajriṇaḥ" (the wielder of the thunderbolt) nourishes the beauty of synonymic deviation (*paryāyavakratā*).

For, even though the Lord of the Gods possesses the thunderbolt ever at hand, the perception of the extraordinary nature of his arrows arises from the description of them as "parākramavasūni"—that is, as wealth consisting of valor.
Furthermore, the word "tapasvi" (the ascetic) is exceedingly charming.
For while respect or high esteem may occasionally arise toward the arrows of a great warrior, what cause for agitation can there be toward the arrows of ascetics, which are utterly ineffective?
Or as it is said:
"Who are you? You shall know me; remember, do you remember me? By good fortune have you come here to drive me mad? How indeed? What power do you have by force? Behold it!
Having said, "I shall see," he [Śiva] struck with his eye alone—blazing like fire—that one whose arms were entwined around the neck of his beloved; homage to that wielder of the trident!

Although thousands of synonyms for the Supreme Lord are possible here, the reason the term "to the trident-bearer" (*śūline*) was employed is this: what else could be said of that Blessed One other than an act of salutation?

For even though he was provoked by Smara—who had abandoned the conduct of modesty through such insolence—he did not, despite possessing a trident that is ever-present, take up a weapon appropriate for his anger, except for casting a glance toward his beloved.
By performing an act of wrath with a mere glance from his eye, the extraordinary majesty of the Blessed One is fully nourished;
for this very reason, the expression "let there be salutation to him" attains logical consistency.
This is another variety of the cause of the curvature of the first half of the verse—a factor that nourishes his excellence.
That which nourishes the excellence or superiority of the subject matter to be expressed is so described;

for even a thing that is naturally charming due to its innate delicacy, when its excellence is further nourished by that [poetic embellishment], attains an even greater capacity to captivate the hearts of those with aesthetic sensitivity.
For example:

O beautiful one, behold this moon, the crest-jewel of the wives of Caṇḍī’s husband; he is a kinsman of the Raghu kings, the initiating preceptor for the rites of the god of love, well-acquainted with the likeness of the faces of fair-limbed women, and possessing a brilliance as white as the freshly polished teeth of young Southern damsels.

In this regard, these synonyms—which manifest a certain excellence that causes delight in the hearts of connoisseurs even for the moon, though it is already endowed with the perfection of innate beauty—possess a curvature in the first half of the word. For instance, when Rāma, having slain Rāvaṇa and traveling by the Puṣpaka chariot, spoke these words with full confidence during his private conversations with Sītā: "O beautiful one, let the moon be looked upon," meaning, "O you who captivate with your loveliness, let the moon—the festival for the eyes of all people—be considered."
For such a sphere of inquiry is appropriate only for those of that kind;

and by the phrase "related to the Raghu kings," it is understood through the observation that "this is no stranger to us" that he is to be honored, whereby his greatness is perceived in another manner as well.
Furthermore, the learned manifest their own inclination toward bestowing excellence upon him.
And for this very reason, because the excellence of each individual synonym is manifested separately with respect to the subject at hand, there is no tautology even among many synonyms.
In the third quarter, there exists the artfulness of the adjectives (*viśeṣaṇavakratā*), not the artfulness of synonyms (*paryāyavakratva*).

This is another variety of figurative turn of phrase based on the curvature of the first half of a word—namely, that which is capable of adorning it; the meaning is that which has the power to embellish the object characterized by its denotation. Why? Because of the touch of another beautiful shadow (or aesthetic luster).

The meaning is that through contact with that which is delightful, charming, possessing various shades of shadow, various modes of artistic arrangement, and so forth—such as close proximity—the perception of a different splendor arises.
How? Even by means of its own qualification.
"By oneself alone," either by [the word] "self" itself or by another word serving as its own qualifier.
In that regard, an example of "by oneself" is as follows:

"In this inert world, who indeed could be a worthy recipient of a sound other than an elephant with ears of vast proportions?"—thinking thus, he suddenly crushed the bee; what more can be said of him than that he was truly an elephant? (VjivC 2.35)

Here, the word "mātaṅga" applies to the elephant alone in its primary context; yet, by means of a double entendre (*śliṣṭa-vṛtti*), it produces the cognition of the non-contextual object characterized as a *caṇḍāla*. Through the touch of the shadow of the figure of speech *rūpaka*, and because the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) based on similarity is possible according to the maxim of "the Vāhīka is a cow," it superimposes the identity of the non-contextual object upon the contextual object.
It nourishes the curvature of synonyms (paryāyavakratā),
because in such a context, the connection between the subject at hand and that which is not the subject is established either by means of the figure of speech *rūpaka* or sometimes by way of *upamā*,
such as "this is that very one" or "this is like that."
And this alone is the domain of *padadhvani* (word-suggestion), which consists of a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of the word;
and when there are many such instances, it is the domain of *vākyadhvani* (sentence-suggestion).
For example:
Concluding the pair of seasons known as the Flowering Time, the Great Time named Summer burst forth with the loud laughter of blossoming jasmine flowers, white as a smile.
"Just as in this great dissolution that has occurred, you alone remain now, O Śeṣa, to support the earth"— in this [verse],
although words such as *yuga* and so forth are employed with the intent of expressing the subject at hand, they bring about the cognition of an irrelevant matter.
Manifesting some particular poetic luster, they become the recipients of the designation "suggested figures of speech" (pratīyamānālaṅkāra).
By way of this qualification:

"When the women of the city beheld that clever man—white as very smooth milk, drenched in sweet and innocent grace—they surely reduced Madana to ashes; indeed, they knew him to be none other than the Lord Śiva himself. (VjivC 2.38)

Here, the qualifying word "wood" (kāṣṭha), while conveying the passionlessness of the God of Love in relation to the subject being described, produces a cognition of another unmentioned object— namely, the tree called Madana— which possesses a charming arrangement through a pun that touches upon a different beautiful luster; thus, by its contact with the shadow of the figure of speech *rūpaka*, it brings forth a certain form of *paryāyavakratā* (permutation-crookedness).
This is another variety of the cause for the curvature of the first half of a verse-line—one that is exquisite through the excellence of its own luster.
Its "own luster" (*svacchāyā*) is its beauty; it is "exquisite" (*peśala*), meaning heart-stealing, by virtue of the excellence—that is, the pre-eminence—of that tenderness.

This is the intended meaning here: although the object being described is established as manifesting other modes [of expression], nevertheless, it is only the perfection of the beauty of its movement that captivates the hearts of the connoisseurs.
He proceeds in such a manner as has been thus proclaimed by the venerable feet of the teacher, who is a wave of the ocean of those skilled in the play of the *tāṇḍava* dance.
The separation from Smaravatī has arisen for me through the rays of this uneven stalk of family life, like the god of love.
In this context, the poet has employed the expression "viṣamakāṇḍakuṭumba" as a synonym for the moon.
For it is said by someone whose heart is distressed by separation and who loathes the rising of the deer-marked moon:

that although this [expression] is not well-known, it is brought to the state of being most familiar through its unfading semantic connection; and because it was the very first to be inscribed [in his mind], it penetrates the aesthetic wonder of the conscious mind.

And this [beauty], being exquisite due to the excellence of its own radiance and owing to its status as innate loveliness, is described by poets—avoiding other synonymous terms—as possessing a uniqueness that distinguishes it from any new description.
For example, instead of saying "she with dark, curly hair," one says "she whose locks are curved like the waves of the Yamunā.

Or, for instance, in the phrase "familiar with the likeness of a fair-limbed woman's face," although there exist thousands of words denoting a woman (*vanitā*) and so forth, the use of the term *gaurāṅgī* (fair-limbed) is exceedingly charming.

This is another variety of the manner of figurative expression (*paryāyaprakāra*), which is designated as "curvature of the first half of a word" (*padapūrvārdhavakratā*): "That which is expressed, containing within it the capacity (*pātratva*) for an object that is conceivable (*saṃbhāvya*)—wherein the capacity, that is, the state of being a fit vessel (*bhājanatva*), for some conceivable or inconceivable movement (*parispanda*) of the subject being described constitutes the inner intention (*garbha*) of the expression; having made the expression such, that which is expressed or spoken. In other words, it refers to a statement where the speaker intends to convey the suitability of the subject for an action, whether that action is easily imaginable or otherwise impossible to conceive. This is achieved by employing a specific curvature in the first half of the word used.
Enough, O protector of the earth, with your exertion; even a weapon discharged here would be in vain. The force of the wind, though capable of uprooting trees, falters before a mountain of rock.

Here, in the address "O Protector of the Earth" (*mahīpāla*), there is composed an invocation pregnant with the sense of being a worthy recipient for that which is inconceivable even in a dream: namely, the inability—even on the part of a king possessing the prowess capable of protecting the entire earth—to protect the life of a single cow, the source of livelihood, which ought to be preserved through such efforts.
Or, as in another example:
If you have compassion for living beings, then at least let this one cow be safe until your end;
furthermore, O Lord of Creatures, you protect your subjects from constant calamities like a father.
In this matter, if you practice the renunciation of your own life for the sake of compassion toward living beings, that too is improper;
because, at your end, only this single cow would remain safe—thus all three [yourself, the cow, and the calf] would become objects of disregard.
But as long as you live, O Lord of Creatures, you constantly protect and guard from calamities and misfortunes all the subjects dwelling within the circle of the earth, the sustainer of all beings.
The phrase "like a father" conveys an extreme degree of disregard.
Thus, although this meaning of the sentence is very clearly coherent, another underlying intention (*tātparya*) is perceived here:
because it is impossible for anyone who holds the position of lord of subjects to ever fail to protect them.
That was stated precisely with the intention of qualifying him as a fit recipient;

for, since you live as one who is indifferent to the protection of the life of the sacrificial cow (*homadhenu*)— which is being devoured by every living creature before your very eyes— it is impossible, according to this logic, that the protection of your subjects could ever be even slightly expected of you.
Thus it is established by valid means of knowledge.
This has been stated:
"Once this stream has arrived by virtue of its being supported by valid means of knowledge, who can stop its flow? (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi 2.42).
Thus [it is said].

Here, the mutual opposition (*parasparapratiyogitva*) of the word-meanings (*padārtha*) brought within the range of denotation and cognition should be understood according to the logic of example and counter-example (*udāharaṇapratyudāharaṇa*).

This is another variety of *paryāya* which effects a curvature (*vakratā*) in the first half of the word, consisting of a composition captivating through the refinement of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
In this context, regarding the term *alaṅkāropasaṃskāra*, both a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) and a sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) should be understood;
by this, two meanings are expressed.

That composition or arrangement (*nibandhana*) is so described because its embellishment (*upasaṃskāra*)—the imparting of another beauty (*śobhāntarādhāna*)—by means of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the like, is captivating (*manohāri*) and pleasing to the heart (*hṛdayarañjaka*).

Having analyzed the compound as "the refinement (*upasaṃskāra*) of an ornament such as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), which is the imparting of another beauty," an example under the third type of compound (the instrumental-tatpuruṣa) is as follows: "He who was the playful palm-leaf fan in private; he who was the lamp without a wick during her playful rages; he who was the weapon that caused pain from his biting; and he who was the sole sprinkling for her lower lip."

May that moon—the flower upon the stalk of Shiva’s matted locks, which served as a mirror for the Goddess during her adornment, and as a pillow for her head while she rested—remove all calamity from you.

Here, the employment of the poetic figure *rūpaka* (metaphor), based on the figurative identification (*abhedopacāra*) due to the commonality of effects such as the palm-leaf fan and so forth, is composed for all the synonyms in order to produce an excellence of beauty.
An example under the view of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is as follows:
"O Goddess, by your lotus-face, which eclipses the splendor of the moon..."
Behold, the lotuses, suddenly overcome, lose their luster.
Here, the natural fading of the lotuses at the appropriate hour of evening— which occurs spontaneously— is presented by the hero,

who is engaged in fondling his beloved out of urbanity (*nāgarakatā*), as if they had been conquered by the loveliness of the commencement of his advances; thus, it is established through the figure of speech known as *pratīyamānotprekṣā* (implied poetic fancy).
And this alone is logically consistent;
for it is observed that every lotus whatsoever possesses the quality of eclipsing the beauty of the moon.

However, by your lotus-face—which itself eclipses the moon’s beauty—it follows by logical necessity that [other] lotuses have been utterly defeated and are, as it were, becoming lusterless. This constitutes the figure of speech known as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), characterized by what is implied.
An excellence of beauty is brought forth.

Having thus considered the crookedness of synonyms (*paryāyavakratā*), he now considers the crookedness of metaphorical transfer (*upacāravakratā*), which occurs at an appropriate moment in accordance with the sequence:
"where a common property (*sāmānya*) is metaphorically transferred from one thing to another that is far removed."
To speak of even a slight excess in your conduct would be impossible.

That poetic figure (alaṅkāra), such as metaphor (rūpaka) and the like, which is rooted in the striking depiction of rasa and primarily consists of figurative application (upacāra), is called a certain kind of "curvature" (vakratā). Vjiv_2.14 //

This certain unprecedented form of *vakratā* (curvature/obliquity) is being described; it is called *vakrabhāva* (the state of curvature). Of what nature is it? It is "predominantly figurative" (*upacārapradhānā*).
*Upacaraṇa* is figurative usage (*upacāra*), and that which has this very thing as its primary element is so described.

Of what nature is it? It is that in which—referring to a certain object being described as the subject at hand—some common property (*sāmānya*), that is, some shared attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*), is intended to be expressed by metaphorically attributing it from another distinct entity. Regarding which object being described? One that is "at a great distance" (*dūrāntara*). That is to say, it is so called because its interval (*antara*) or separation (*vyavadhāna*) is "far," meaning not small.
Now, an intervention [of something else] for the object being described is certainly not possible in terms of space, because that object is formless;
nor is it possible in terms of time, because time is the domain of action alone.

Although the object being described consists of both the nature of the action (*kriyā*) and the nature of the factors of action (*kāraka*), nevertheless, there should be no separation here by way of space or time;
for, as in the case of inference, words are only capable of making the universal (*sāmānyamātra*) of things their object, not the particular (*viśeṣa*).
How, then, is "extreme distance" established?
This is true;

however, although the term "dūrāntara" primarily refers to remoteness in terms of space and time—the absence of proximity—it is used figuratively to denote remoteness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*).
This is the remoteness of intrinsic nature (svabhāvaviprakarṣa) among entities, characterized by the superimposition of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa);
for example, corporeality with respect to incorporeality,
and fluidity with respect to solidity.
"Consciousness exists in relation to unconsciousness.
What kind of generality is that? It exists even in the slightest degree;
it exists even by a mere fraction.
For what purpose? To describe a certain unprecedented state of exalted conduct, to express a state of surpassing activity—as [in the verse]:
"The sky was smeared with the glossy, dark luster [of his body]. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 2.45)

In this regard, just as some who act with deliberate intent, desiring to produce an excellence of color and luster in something sentient, smear a certain object possessing form— such as a cloth— with a specific dyeing substance like indigo that possesses the capacity for adhesion and exists in a physical state;

in exactly the same way, the common property of being "so acted upon," though existing only in a slight degree, is figuratively expressed as "the sky (dyau) is smeared with a glossy, dark radiance" in order to describe a certain heightened state of manifestation.
The word "snigdha" (smooth/glossy) is also merely figurative.

Just as a material object perceivable by touch is called "snigdha" due to its connection with the quality of oiliness (*sneha*), so too is luster, though formless, called "snigdha" through metaphorical usage.

Or as women go at night toward their lovers' dwellings along the royal road, where the light is blocked by darkness thick enough to be pierced only by a needle— show them the path with a flash of lightning, smooth as gold on a touchstone; but do not be made resonant by the thundering release of rain, lest they become terrified.
Here, although darkness is formless, because it is so excessive and dense, the quality of being "pierceable by a needle"—which is appropriate for material things—is figuratively attributed to it.
Or, for example:
"The sky is filled with intoxicated clouds, and the forests have Arjuna trees drenched by torrents of rain."
The moon, free from ego, and the dark nights captivate the heart.
The sky filled with intoxicated clouds, the forests where the *arjuna* trees are drenched by torrents of rain,
the deer who are free from ego, and the dark nights— all these captivate the heart.
Thus ends the section on *chāyā*.
Here, the states of intoxication and lack of egoism are metaphorically attributed (*upacarita*) as common properties of consciousness.

This variety of figurative indirectness (*upacāravakratā*) occurs by the thousands in the tradition of great poets; therefore, it should be envisioned by the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) for themselves. And for this very reason, in this proximity of metaphorical attribution—
It is not a figurative usage (*vakratā-vyavahāra*), such as "the Vāhīka is an ox.

This is another characteristic of metaphorical deviation (*upacāra-vakratā*): that which is the root of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the like, which are full of aesthetic flavor (*sarasollekhā*).
That which has "rūpaka" as its root is so described;
that which has "rūpaka" as its beginning is so described.
What is it? It is "alaṅkṛti," meaning ornamentation; the sense is that it is the distinct variety of ornaments beginning with *rūpaka*.
Of what kind? "Possessing a fresh delineation" (*sarasollekhā*).
That which has a delineation (*ullekha*)—meaning a manifestation—that is "fresh" (*sarasa*), i.e., flavorful (*sāsvāda*) and characterized by aesthetic wonder (*sacamatkṛti*), is so described.
Here, there is a relationship of cause and effect between the two terms in apposition, as for example:
"King's beans are too heavy and must not be eaten. // VjivC_2.48 //

Since the poetic ornamentation beginning with metaphor (*rūpaka*), which is full of aesthetic flavor (*sarasollekhā*), has this as its root, the meaning is that the entire collection of ornaments such as metaphor has "the crookedness of figurative usage" (*upacāravakratā*) as its very life-force.
Now, one might ask: what is the distinction between this and the previously mentioned type of crookedness of figurative usage?

In the former case, because of the remoteness of their intrinsic natures (*svabhāvaviprakarṣāt*), one proceeds to superimpose merely those attributes [of the object] upon [the subject] by relying on a slight similarity in a general sense, in order to demonstrate its excellence.

In this case, however, because it is appropriate due to the proximity arising from a resemblance that is not remote, the actual identity itself is superimposed as the basis for the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*).
As, for example:
When there are these lotuses of fame that bloom at all times, these poisonous shoots of the forest-line of armies,
and these lords of serpents in the depths of majesty— among such attachments, who indeed is Murāri to you?

In this case, the superimposed identity—which is based on metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra) and whose proximity is produced by the resemblance between the time [of the eclipse] and the blue lotus—is what is attributed.

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), it is indicated that the life-force of a certain variety of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), characterized as an "indication of another" (*anyāpadeśa*), consists precisely in such metaphorical artfulness (*upacāravakratā*).
Thus, having placed some other entity in the mind as the primary object of perception, one establishes its connection with a corresponding similarity of characteristics.
Poets are generally seen to rely on this [device], bringing about the expression of one thing by means of another.
For example:
"The indescribable, supreme majesty of Hari’s power alone shines forth, generating wonder throughout the three worlds."
That which is the form of the moon wandering in the sky is your forest land; that which is the mass of rays pouring forth a flood of nectar is your mouthful of young grass.

In this context, relying upon the universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by transcendence (*lokottaratva*) which underlies both [types of figures], the nature of the intended subject—which primarily functions as something implied—is superimposed through the basis of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). Thus, although the life-force of these two figures consists equally in the curvature of metaphorical usage (*upacāravakratā*), the difference in their essential nature (*svarūpabheda*) is determined by whether it is expressed directly (*vācyatva*) in one case and implied (*pratīyamānatva*) in the other. This point will be further clarified during the detailed explanation of the specific definitions (*svalakṣaṇa*) of both.

Having thus distinguished the curvature of metaphorical expression (*upacāra-vakratā*), he now analyzes the curvature of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-vakratā*), which finds its opportunity immediately following it:
"When the aesthetic charm (*lāvaṇya*) shines forth due to the greatness of a qualifier—whether of an action, an agent, or an object—that is the curvature of the qualifier. (Vjiv 2.15)
That is called the "curvature of the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇavakratā*), which is defined as the aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) arising from the curvature of a qualifier.
Of what kind is it? It is that in which beauty (*lāvaṇya*) shines forth and loveliness (*rāmaṇīyaka*) breaks out—of what? Of either an action (*kriyā*) or a grammatical factor (*kāraka*).
Whether it be a thing characterized by action (*kriyā*) or one characterized by an agent (*kāraka*), why [is there a distinction]? It is because of the greatness of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
This is because each of these two has a qualifier—a distinguishing factor that is a distinct category of entity—which possesses excellence (*sātiśayatva*).
It consists in heightening the delicacy of the essential nature of the state (*bhāva*) and in nourishing the excellence of the shadow of the poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
For example:

"She, fainting from the burning sensation of fresh nail-marks produced by the sprinkling of perspiration, was half-concealed by the mass of lovely curls and earrings disheveled by her lover’s impetuous embrace."

Victorious is the gaze of the young woman at the end of the night—slightly shy from the lingering fragrance of the various sequences of lovemaking performed with the passion of desire, and clear yet slightly crimson from the intoxication of her slender body’s honeyed wine.
Or, for example,
here the slender maiden hears the sound of singing, her cheeks pressed against the hollow of her hands, her eyelashes closed by rising tears, and her mental faculties concentrated within her ears.
Or just as the quarters of the sky, bathed in pure and cool moonlight and enchanting with long-standing silence,
became the cause for either tranquility or the arousal of passion in the heart of some person.
An example of the curvature of adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇavakratva*) is as follows:
"The lord of elephants, with eyes closed, remembered the great festivals of dwelling in forests for his own pleasure. (Vajrāvalī 2.54)
In all these cases, the function of the qualifiers is to manifest the inherent beauty [of the subject].

As for the function of a qualifier to nourish an excellence of the shadow of a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*), it is as in the case of the moon, which is surpassed by the splendor [of its surroundings]. (VjivC 2.55)

This very quality called *viśeṣaṇavakratva* (the artfulness of epithets) is characterized as the life-breath of all excellent poetry, in accordance with the propriety of the subject at hand; for by means of this alone, aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is brought to the highest state of full development.
As, for example:
"With his hands held between his knees. // VjivC_2.56 //

That by which the extraordinary splendors are brought forth through its own majesty—the aesthetic essence (rasa), the nature [of the work], and the ornaments—is the defining characteristic of that [poetry]. VjivC_2.57.
(Thus) is the intermediate verse.

Having thus examined the ingenuity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇavakratā*), he now examines the ingenuity of concealment (*saṃvṛtivakratā*), which finds its proper occasion through the sequence [of the preceding discussion]: "Where a thing is concealed by means of certain pronouns and so forth, with the intention of expressing its manifold variety—that is called the ingenuity of concealment. (Vjiv 2.16)

The "crookedness of concealment" (saṃvṛti-vakratā) has been explained—it is said that such a thing as this is called "the crookedness of concealment. The compound [saṃvṛti-vakratā] means either "crookedness by way of concealment" or "that which is primarily characterized by concealment. It is that in which, or within which, a thing—the defining characteristic of an entity—is concealed or covered over.
By what cause? By the desire to express variety—that is, by the wish to denote a manifold state—by which the referent (padārtha) attains a manifold state; this is the meaning.
By what is it concealed? By certain [words], such as pronouns and the like.
"Every name" (*sarvanāma*) refers to those words that begin with such terms; the meaning is "by certain unprecedented designators.
In this regard, many possibilities arise:
where some object of extraordinary excellence can be expressed, yet because it is not directly denoted and is limited by its specific measure...

Thinking, "Let it not appear as something limited," [the poet] conceals it with a pronoun denoting a universal, and then leads it into the range of cognition through another sentence that expresses its effect or is intent upon expressing its excellence.
For example:
When his father was desirous of taking him as a son-in-law,
that most delicate youth performed a certain subtle deed by which he fixed his gaze upon Manmatha, whose cheeks rest upon the tip of the flower-bow.

In this context, it can be stated that Śantanu— whose inner heart was permeated by devotion to his guru through his inclination toward the conduct of the virtuous, whose mind was free from thirst for the enjoyment of various objects due to his possession of extraordinary and noble qualities,

and who performed the restraint of his own senses despite its being seemingly impossible— was brought within the range of perception by means of a subsequent sentence expressing another matter, which concealed [the true fact] under the general term "all" (sarva) in the latter half of the verse.
It also possesses a certain marvelous quality.

This is another variety [of suggestion], wherein an object of such excellence—being mounted upon the pinnacle of its own inherent power—is beyond the reach of words; thus, having concealed it by means of all [other] names, it is revealed by another sentence that denotes its effect or expresses its excellence.

When the Enemy of Madhu had thus departed for Dvāravatī, Rādhā, filled with longing, clung to a *vañjula* creeper on the banks of the Yamunā that was bent low by the trembling it had received from him;
she sang that song with a voice faltering, slow, and choked with heavy tears— a song by which even the aquatic creatures moving within the water cried out in distress.
In this instance, the matter concealed by a pronoun is revealed by another sentence expressing its effect, thereby attaining a state that captivates the hearts of sensitive readers.
Or, for example:
"Then, O Kṛṣṇa, Viśākhā wept with a voice choked with tears."
Just as no one, even in a hundred lifetimes, can ever become beloved to someone.
In that way, O Kṛṣṇa, Viśākhā wept with a voice choked by tears,
so that no one might become her beloved even in a hundred lifetimes.
This is *chāyā*.

Here, in the first half [of the verse], the concealed matter characterized by weeping is led to a certain state of delight for those who understand it through another sentence that expresses its excellence.

This is another variety here, wherein a matter that is exceedingly delicate is elevated to a certain height solely through the charm of concealment, without the mention of an excellence in its effect.
Just as a woman, while looking at her reflection in a mirror, sees her lover seated behind her,
what various actions of shame did she not perform upon beholding her own image?

This is another mode [of expression] wherein a reality that is to be personally experienced through one's own realization is concealed in order to demonstrate that it is not an object capable of being expressed by words; as it is said: "Those syllables resonate with something indeterminate within the heart. (Vajracchedikā 2.62)
Thus it has been explained previously.
This other mode is also possible, wherein a conventional expression (*saṃvṛti*) is employed to demonstrate that an object perceivable by another's experience lies beyond the range of the speaker.
Just as the god of love fixed his gaze upon something indescribable.

For here, Kāma—whose majesty of power was renowned throughout the three worlds, yet whose mind was despondent due to such an obstruction of his might—reflected upon something entirely suited to his own experience. There exists another further variety here: where an object, by its very nature or through the poet’s intention, or due to some particular affliction, is not fit to be mentioned as if it were a great sin, and is therefore concealed for the sake of presentation.
If that deer had not acted with such power against you— that which is so difficult to speak of—
then perhaps the Lord of the Host would not have swiftly struck him down with a sharpened feathered shaft.
Or rather, O friend, let this young boy be stopped; he wishes to speak further, as his upper lip is quivering.
Not only does he who speaks ill of the great incur sin, but he who merely listens to such speech also shares in that guilt.

In this case, the killing of Arjuna and the blasphemy against the Blessed One were not fit for mention; thus, by means of concealment, they were rendered charming. An example of what is spoiled by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is as follows:
"This man, who maintains his vows out of hypocrisy, is intent on doing something [evil] toward my beloved. (VjivC 2.66)
Thus, this has already been explained at the very beginning.

Having thus investigated the curvature of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-vakratā*), there is now a certain aspect of the curvature of conditions (*pratyaya-vakratā*) which, because it is contained within the middle of the words, finds its appropriate occasion right here; therefore, he undertakes its investigation:

The suffix, by its own power expanding the aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) of the propriety of the subject at hand, brings forth another form of poetic curvature (*vakratā*) within the middle of a word. (Vjiv 2.17)

A certain suffix, such as a *kṛt* suffix, occurring in the middle of a word, brings forth a different, unprecedented form of *vakratā* (poetic curvature) and intensifies the state of *vakrabhāva* (curvature).

What does it do? It causes to blossom—that is, it causes to fully manifest—the *vicchitti* (distinction) or embellishment of the *aucitya* (propriety), which is the fitness of the subject matter currently being described;
and by what means? By its own majesty, that is, by its own excellence.
Like clouds with flickering cranes.
Or as it is said: "The two eyes are like affectionate side-glances. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 2.68)

Here, the present-tense suffix *śatṛ*, by illuminating a contextual elegance (*aucitya*) that is beautiful in its momentary movement and free from any confusion regarding past or future, brings about a strikingness of expression (*pratyayavakratā*) that captivates the hearts of connoisseurs.
Now, he examines another variety of this [type].
Beautiful through the movement of scripture and other sources, the supreme [poetry] nourishes an indescribable curvature of word that produces a striking beauty of composition. (Vjiv 2.18)
The second type of secondary condition (pratyaya) binds a certain unprecedented poetic curvature of words (*śabdavakratā*) and effects a curvature of the expressive power (*vācakavakratā*).
Of what nature is it? It is beautiful through the movement of suffixes (*āgama*) and so forth. That which has suffixes such as *mum* as its beginning is described as such.
The movement of that [poetry], such as its traditional sources (*āgama*) and so forth, is its own playful manifestation; by means of that, it is beautiful and delicate.
Of what kind is this verbal ingenuity (*śabdavakratā*)? It is that which produces the luster of composition (*bandhacchāyā*), meaning it brings about the beauty of its structural arrangement.
For example:
I know that your friend’s heart is filled with affection for me; therefore, I imagine her to be in such a state during this first separation.
It is not that my self-conceit as a fortunate man makes me talkative; rather, O brother, everything that I have said will soon be evident to you.
And just as burning consumes a stream of water. // VjivC_2.70 //
And just as one drinks again and again from a leaf of the plantain tree that has been fashioned into a cup; VjivC_2.71.
Thus:

here, in words such as *subhagaṃmanya*, the suffixes—which produce a beautiful arrangement and cast a shadow [of aesthetic effect]—nurture the "curvature" (*vakratā*) of the expressive word, characterized by the movement of the *mum* suffixes and so forth.

Having thus examined the curvature of suffixes occurring within the middle of a word, which is appropriate to the context, he now examines the curvature of the *vṛtti* (verbal derivation) that arises immediately thereafter.

That in which the beauty of the primary types of compounds, beginning with the *avyayībhāva*, shines forth should be known as the "curvature of the variety of compound formations" (*vṛttivaicitryavakratā*). Vjiv_2.19.
That "curvature" (*vakratā*) consisting in the variety of stylistic modes (*vṛtti*) is to be known—that is, understood.

The variety of styles is their manifold nature; it is an excellence of delicacy relative to its own kind, and by means of that, there is curvature, which is the strikingness (*vicchitti*) of the state of being curved.
Of what sort is it? It is that wherein loveliness shines forth.
In which [type of compound] does beauty (*rāmaṇīyakam*) emerge? Of what? Of the *vṛtti*s. Which ones? Of those primarily consisting of *avyayībhāva*s.

The *avyayībhāva* compound is the primary [type] among those [compounds], and thus they are so described; these are the compounds, secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), nominal inflections (*sub*), and verbal formations (*dhātuvṛtti*) well-known to grammarians.
This is the meaning here: where the beauty of their own movement attains manifestation through being bound to a suitable background, as for example—
Failing to find manifestation outside for the time being, yet somehow throbbing within itself, intensely concentrated in its own being—
oh, the new nectar of the springtime bestows upon the creepers a lovely splendor, made beautiful by the vibration of the rising fragrance of the god of love.

Here, in the word *adhimadhu*, although the compound is formed according to the sense of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) and thus denotes a conventional term (*samaya*), it nevertheless generates the perception of a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*), thereby unfolding the aesthetic variety of the "nine flavors" (*navarasa*) through the shimmering shadow of paronomasia (*śleṣacchāyā*). Even when the same meaning is perceived in a different arrangement devoid of this specific usage, there is no such capacity to delight those who know [the art]. In words such as *udvṛtta*, *parimala*, *spanda*, and *subhaga*, the metaphorical curvature (*upacāravakratva*) is clearly manifested.
And how is it that they did not bring whiteness to their actions, spreading a new splendor of light as far as the city of the serpents from the world of the gods?
For by those very actions, the decoration consisting of nail-marks upon the rival beauties was brought to a pallor during their separation from their lovers.

In this context, there exists a certain poetic charm (*vakratva*) arising from the stylistic variety of usage (*vṛttivaicitrya*) between the words *pāṇḍutva*, *pāṇḍutā*, *pāṇḍubhāva*, and the word *pāṇḍima*.
For example:

"The moon [is eclipsed] by the washings of the splendor of the faces of Siṃhalī women—which shine with the nectar-streams of loveliness gushing forth like a fountain during their ceremonial sprinkling with fragrant powders."

By which, in the course of the great festivals of drinking, the mind-born god [Kāma] of Your Majesty—who desires to conquer the entire world up to the realm of the Lord of the Thirty-three—is made to appear as if under a single umbrella.
Here, a certain variety of curvature (*vakratā*) shines forth in both the function of verbal roots (*subdhātuvṛtti*) and the function of compounds (*samāsavṛtti*).
Having thus examined the curvature of function, he now examines the curvature of meaning (*bhāvavakratā*), which occurs in the first half of the word and finds its appropriate occasion:
"Even disregarding its state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*), it is expressed as if already established (*siddhatvena*)."
Wherever this existence might occur, there is the crookedness of the diversity of existents.
This "curvature" (*vakratā*) consisting of the variety of *bhāva* (emotional states) has been described; it exists.

*Bhāva* is the form of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*); its "variety" (*vaicitrya*) is a manifold state (*vicitrabhāva*), a loveliness that is distinct from the expression of other modes. By means of that, there is "curvature," which is a specific kind of aesthetic deviation (*vicchitti*).
Of what nature is it? It is that in which the *bhāva* is expressed—that is, spoken of—as being established, meaning as something fully accomplished.
Having done what? Having disregarded its status as a goal (*sādhyatā*)—that is, having set aside even its well-known state of being currently produced.

This is the intended meaning here: since the development of the subject matter at hand is weak because it is expressed as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and thus remains unperfected, its expression as something already established (*siddha*) brings about a sufficient nourishment of the relevant theme by virtue of its perfected state.
Just as the luster of her lower lip has been soiled by the exertion of sighing, and the glow of her cheeks has turned pale with the thinness of the kandalī flower, while her armlets act as bracelets;

moreover, by the pair of her lotus-eyes, which are streaming with excessive tears, the pupils have been reddened at the corners to such an extent that the God of Love appears as if his power were overflowing.
In this context, the expression of a state (*bhāva*) as something already established is exceedingly striking.
Having thus examined the ingenuity of state (*bhāvavakratā*), he now examines the ingenuity of gender (*liṅgavakratā*) residing within the nominal stem (*prātipadika*):
"In which [verse], through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), two different genders..."
A certain splendor arises from this; it is the curvature of the diversity of gender signs.
This aforementioned "curvature of the diversity of genders" (*liṅgavaicitryavakratā*)—which is a specific manifestation of the curvature of diverse states such as gender—is what occurs;

for there is no other verb [to connect it]. Of what nature is it? It is that in which, due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), two genders of distinct natures—that is, having different bases—reside in a single substance because they share the same substratum; thus, it is something unprecedented.
Beauty arises and splendor shines forth;
for instance,
by the very act of stringing it, many were made to abandon their heroic vows— that bow of the Lord, its shafts feathered, was strung by me with these arms.
That jewel among women, born from no womb, was obtained by me from him with ease; thus, these twenty eyes of mine have become like a grove of blossoming lotuses.
Or,
just as the fragrant unguent— the abode of all perfumes— was scattered upon his chest by the southern breeze, using the tender sprouts of the wish-fulfilling vine as its fan.
Having carefully fashioned a garland from seasonal flowers,
he placed upon the slope of his shoulder a lotus-hand that dripped drops of nectar, serving as a graceful ear-ornament for Śrī.

And this is another form of the crookedness of diversity of gender: where, although another gender exists, the feminine gender is employed for the sake of producing beauty, because the name itself is charming as "woman. (Vjiv 2.22)

In a case where another gender is possible, yet the feminine gender is employed—that is, it is used and fixed—even though the referent possesses multiple genders, the usage is made with reference to the feminine gender. For what purpose? For the sake of producing beauty, that is, for the attainment of aesthetic charm.
For what reason? Because the name itself—namely "woman"—is charming;
the designation "woman" alone is heart-captivating, as it is suitable for the purpose of aesthetic flavor (rasa) and so forth through its particular mode of expression.
For example:
"This riverbank, filled with the heat of summer, its pale waters broken by the wind that stirs the withered, trembling shoots of the creepers, suffers intensely;
yet it possesses a fame more radiant than the moon. Therefore, I think there will come some extraordinary cloud, blessed by its power to pervade the entire circle of the world. (Vajrāvalī 2.79)
Although the word *taṭa* possesses all three genders here, the feminine gender alone has been employed due to its delicacy (*saukumārya*).
By means of this distinct charm (*vicchitti*), a certain future conduct of the hero is subtly indicated; thus, because of its extreme loveliness, it possesses a state of poetic deviation (*vakratā*).
This indicates another variety of it:

"Where a specific mark is employed even though it is possible in something else, for the sake of distinction—that is another [type of indication], according to the propriety of what is to be expressed. (Vjiv 2.23)

And there exists another, distinct form of "curvature of gender" (*liṅgavakratā*) of the kind already described, wherein a specific [gender]—any one of the three genders—is employed or composed by the poet's intention.
How so? Even when it is possible [to use] another [gender].
Even though another grammatical gender is present, for what purpose? For the sake of interruption—that is, for the sake of beauty.
From what cause? In accordance with the propriety of the expressed meaning (*vācyaucitya*).
From the "following" (anusāra), which means the pursuit of the propriety (aucitya)—that is, the state of being appropriate—of the object being described;
