the meaning is: by following the propriety of the thing denoted. For example:

O timid one, these creepers, out of compassion, have shown me the path by which you were carried off by the *rākṣasa*; though unable to speak, they indicated it with their branches whose sprouts were bent down.

Here, while descending from the Puṣpaka chariot together with Sītā, Rāma himself expresses her distress caused by their separation: "The very fact that you were carried away by Rāvaṇa along that path, whose mind was so utterly dominated by haste—that very fact has resulted in the creepers there assuming such a form and turning upward due to being trampled;
thus they have become the cause for my inference of your path. This matter is presented by Rāma through a distinct poetic figure (*vicchitti*).

For example: "O timid one, O you whose inner heart is distressed by its natural delicacy—these creepers, whose forms are now visible before my eyes, are surely showing me that very path by which you were carried away by Rāvaṇa, the perpetrator of such cruel deeds.

Since it is impossible for these [creepers] to actually show the way because they are insentient, the poet intends the figure of speech to be *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), functioning through what is implied (*pratīyamāna-vṛtti*).

For instance— having considered your timidity, Rāvaṇa’s cruelty, and my own devotion to the effort of rescuing you, these [women], due to their naturally tender hearts arising from the feminine disposition and the greatness of their partiality toward their own proper object, have out of compassion alone shown me the way.
By what means? By means of branches with downward-hanging shoots;
for, being devoid of the organ of speech, they are unable to speak.
Indeed, it is most logical that those who, remaining silent, provide guidance on the path do so by means of their arms—their leaf-like shoots—turned toward [the travelers].
And likewise, there is another statement in this very context which should be sought:
"The does, indifferent to the tips of the *darbha* grass, informed me—who was unaware of your arrival—by casting their eyes with rows of lashes upward toward the southern quarter. (Vajrāvalī 2.81)
And the does awakened me—
me who was ignorant of your path, not knowing the way shown by the creepers.
Then they properly enlightened her, because she had become somewhat awakened in comparison to them.
And what were they like? By virtue of witnessing such a slaughter, they were so afflicted with grief that they had abandoned even their consumption of grass.
What were they doing? They were directing their eyes toward that direction. Of what kind were those eyes? Their rows of eyelashes were raised upward.
Thus, by virtue of being positioned in such a stance, they were announcing with the sign that the southern direction had been traversed through the atmosphere.

In this case, although other genders such as the masculine (as in *vṛkṣa* or *mṛga*) are possible for the tree, the deer, and so forth, it is the feminine gender alone that the poet intends, as it produces a striking charm (*camatkāra*) through its suitability to the nature of the object.
Therefore, it possesses a certain kind of poetic curvature (*vakratā*).

In this same way, one should understand the curvature of the first half of the word—characterized by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and occurring within an inflected form (*subanta*)—according to its specific possibility.

Now, having considered both types of words— those ending in nominal suffixes (*su-pada*) and those ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-pada*)— he examines the "curvature" (*vakratā*) of that preceding portion which constitutes the nature of the verbal root (*dhātu*).
And its curvature exists solely as a basis for the variety of action (*kriyāvaicitrya*).

Therefore, in order to determine the nature of the various types of action—of what kind and how many varieties are possible—he says: "The extreme internalization of the agent, the diversity of other agents, the diversity of its own qualifiers, and the charm of metaphorical expression. (Vjiv 2.24)

The conventional [truth] regarding action and so forth consists of five types; these are traditionally known as the modes of the artful curvature of the variety of activities, characterized by the propriety of the subject at hand. (Vjiv 2.25)

These varieties of the crookedness (*vakratva*) of the diversity of action (*kriyā*), which are the specific divisions of the crookedness of the diverse states of the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), are thus remembered; their nature is being described as it has been proclaimed.
How many? Five, distinguished by the number five. Of what kind? Charming through the propriety (*aucitya*) of the subject matter at hand.

The subject matter under discussion is that which is being described; its *aucitya* (propriety) refers to its state of being appropriate, and by means of that, [the expressions] are beautiful and charming.
Among these, the first type is what is called the "extreme internalness" (*atyantaraṅgatva*) of the agent.

This refers to the extreme proximity (*atyantamāntaratamatva*) of the agent—who, as an independent and primary factor (*kāraka*), is the accomplisher (*nirvartayitṛ*) of the action—toward that action.
May that supreme head of the Blessed Śeṣa, its neck raised as it bears the unbearable burden of the world resting upon its crest-jewel,
maintain its loftiness; for when even a slight inclination occurs of its own accord, so many worlds surely roll about in succession within that void, accompanied by a violent trembling.

In this instance, the act of "lifting up," characterized by the function of holding, attains an internal inclusion within the head of the Lord of Serpents due to the greatness of the propriety of the subject matter; no other such action does so. Thus, it brings about a "crookedness" (*vakratā*) consisting in the variety of actions.
Or, for example:
"May the kissing of the back of the wielder of the Pināka bow, when asked 'By whom have I been adorned?', protect you"—this serves as the answer.

In this context, since no other action whatsoever can produce such an extraordinary excellence of Gaurī’s beauty as described by the Blessed One— apart from the act of kissing— it brings about a state of *vakrabhāva* (poetic deviation) based on the variety of actions. And as follows:
Victory to the third eye of Rudra, which was kissed by Pārvatī!
Victorious is the third eye of Rudra, kissed by Pārvatī.
Thus is the shadow; or as it is said: "When the moon has waned, the god of love triumphs. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 2.85)
Victorious is the one whose banner bears the sea-monster, who has slackened his bow.
Thus ends the section on *chāyā*.
The variety of these two has already been explained.
This is another mode of the crookedness (*vakratā*) of the variety of action (*kriyā*): the variety of a different agent (*kartṛ*).
Another agent is distinct from that other agent; "variety" (*vaicitryam*) refers to diversity.
Because it is the subject under discussion and because it belongs to the same class as the agent, it is the agent alone [who possesses this variety].
And this is precisely its variety: that it brings about an action itself in a diverse form by depending upon another agent.
Just as there is nowhere a cessation of capacity in a single thing, for all entities possess degrees of perfection established by their own intrinsic nature:
Agastya drank the ocean in a single mouthful, even as it was being consumed by the submarine fire for an entire eon.

In this case, the drinking of the ocean with a single handful, manifesting a certain wondrousness of action due to the intensity of the submarine fire’s ascent to the very peak of its constant and effortless resolve, brings forth a form of crookedness;
or as it is said:
"The nails of the one who destroys the suffering of those who have sought refuge."
Or rather,
may that fire of Śambhu’s arrow burn away your misfortune.
The variety of these two has already been demonstrated previously.

This is another variety of the curvature of the diversity of action: namely, the diversity of its own qualifiers (*svaviśeṣaṇavaicitrya*). Since the action is primarily the subject under discussion, "its own" refers to the self; a "qualifier" is that which differentiates it. The "diversity" is the state of being manifold through that qualifier.
For example:

When the moon had risen, the women—whose eyes and minds were captivated by the conversation of their female messengers of exquisite beauty—performed their act of adornment, which caused their friends to laugh as they applied their ornaments in a reversed order. (Vajrāvalī 2.89)

Here, by the epithet "with her friends laughing at the misplaced ornaments," a certain delicacy (*saukumārya*) is revealed regarding the action characterized by the act of grasping and arranging the ornaments.

For, such an adornment (*prasādhana*) executed with such care, being presented as a suggestor (*vyañjaka*), primarily functions to manifest the beloved’s passion; and that passion, in turn, is further intensified by this very description.
Or, for example:
Attached to me, his three-quarters of an eye were like those of a startled doe.
Its variety has already been explained previously.
Moreover, this adverbial modifier brings forth the "curvature" (*vakratva*) of both the action and the agent;
for it is precisely the performance of a diverse action that constitutes the diversity of the agent.
This is another variety of the curvature of the diversity of action: the charm of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
Metaphorical usage is the superimposition of one property upon another by relying on a connection such as similarity; the charm resulting from that is its curvature.
For example:
As if her limbs were swimming in an ocean of stumbling, stainless beauty, her breasts and hips reveal their boldness;
and the flickering movements of her eyes clearly refute her former simplicity—oh, how deep is this young doe-eyed girl’s acquaintance with youth!
Here, because they appear to be floating by means of their throbbing, radiant vibrations within this ocean of pure, stumbling loveliness and this sea of overflowing, stainless beauty,

it is imagined that the limbs of young women— tremulous with youth— are attempting to reach the further shore; thus, the act of crossing is metaphorically attributed to them through a poetic identification based on a resemblance possible for sentient beings.
Since metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) itself predominantly constitutes the very life of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), it will be examined specifically in the section on poetic fancy.
Regarding the phrase "and the breasts and hips unveil the boldness of their breadth":
here, the breasts and hips act as the agents; they "unveil," that is, they reveal, the "boldness of breadth," which is the maturity of their largeness.

Just as some conscious person, having sealed a certain object to be protected and established a certain time, personally unseals and opens it at the appropriate moment for its use—so too, by virtue of the similarity in being caused by that [conscious agent], the "unsealing" (*unmudraṇa*) of the breasts and hips was mentioned above.
This is what is meant: that very same [object] which, during the stage of childhood, existed in a state of non-stability with its nature closed up as mere potentiality (*śakti-ātmanā*).
It bestows upon that expansiveness and boldness an extension and diffusion appropriate for the occasion of the first descent of youth:
"The restless movements of the eyes clearly refute her former straightforwardness"—
here, having overtly cast aside the clarity established in childhood, the surges of the eyes' playfulness impose a certain bewilderment suited to fresh youth.
Just as certain sentient beings, having set aside some established course of action regarding a particular object,

establish another movement that accords with their own intention, so too— on account of this similarity in agency— is the denial of straightforwardness attributed to the playful glances of Līlāvatī’s eyes; such a characterization is merely figurative.
Thus, since these three types of *vakratā* (poetic deviation) occur at every step through such figurative treatment (*upacāra*), they will be examined on another occasion.
This is another variety of the *vakratā* of the diversity of action (*kriyāvaicitryavakratā*): the concealment (*saṃvṛti*) of the object and other factors.
"Concealment" (*saṃvṛti*) refers to the covering or hiding of the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) beginning with the object (*karman*).
In accordance with the propriety of the subject at hand, there is a concealed expression (*samācchādyābhidhā*) for the sake of conveying an excellence;
and because it produces a variety of actions, it is designated as a "mode" (*prakāra*).
This occurs through the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the effect to the cause, as for example:
The beauty of lovely objects seems to offer something sweet within the corners of her eyes; it seems to whisper some unprecedented thing near her ear;
and it seems to scratch something deep within the heart of that woman with dark eyes, which is languid with passion.

In this context, because it is the sole object of that direct experience and thus inexpressible, the actions—accomplishing a certain extraordinary effect at every step—manifest a certain degree of curvature within themselves; here, too, there exists a charmingness of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
For [actions such as] offering (*arpaṇa*), speaking (*kathana*), and scratching (*ullekhana*) are based solely on metaphorical usage, since they are attributes belonging to conscious entities.
And as it is said:

"Cease for a moment your impetuous dancing; stay still while I adjust your crest-jewel upon your head so that it no longer wavers loosely"—when the beloved spoke thus with words sweet with affection and fixed the crescent moon upon his crest, there triumphs an indescribable pride in the blissful Śarva.

Here, by the use of the pronoun "some" (*ko 'pi*), the agent is concealed because [the subject] is beyond designation, being accessible only to direct experience; thus, the pride of Śarva is rendered extraordinary.
The phrase "is victorious" (*jayati*)—meaning he exists with supreme excellence—is based on the variety of the action.
In this way, the poetic curvature (*vakrabhāva*) of the first half of the verse is established.
Thus, this has been presented merely as a direction; the remainder is examined in the illustrative examples.
This is the summary verse.

Thus, having examined the "crookedness" (vakratā)— that is, the poetic or figurative treatment— of both nouns ending in case-suffixes (*suptiṅanta*) as well as nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and verbal roots (*dhātu*), which constitute the first half of the *pada*, according to their respective logical principles, he now examines the "crookedness" of the suffix-characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) that constitute the second half of those very same [words], each according to its own nature.

In this regard, the curvature of time is considered because it follows immediately after the curvature of the diversity of actions, since time possesses a sequential nature due to its function of delimiting action. Through the proximity of various forms of appropriateness (*aucitya*), time attains its beauty.
Wherever this goes, there occurs this crookedness of the diversity of time.
This is the nature of what has been introduced: there exists a "curvature" (*vakratā*) consisting in the variety of time.
Time is that which is well-known to grammarians and others as the present and so forth, denoted by suffixes such as *laṭ*, and which effects the emergence and concealment of things;
its "variety" is its manifold state, and its composition in such a manner constitutes "curvature"—that is, the aesthetic figure of curvature (*vakratva-vicchitti*).
Of what sort is it? It is that in which time—known as *samaya*—attains loveliness, reaches a state of great beauty.
By what cause? By the proximity of appropriateness (*aucitya*).
That is, by the internal intimacy of the appropriateness—the state of being fitting—of the subject matter under discussion, which is governed by the present context.
The meaning is: by way of producing an excellence [of that].
For example:
"Moving very slowly on all sides, without distinction between even and uneven [terrain]."
Difficult will they become to cross, surpassing even the reach of one's desires.
Becoming indistinguishable whether level or uneven, with a very slow movement in every direction,
the roads will before long become difficult to traverse even for one's desires.
Thus ends the shadow [of the verse].
Here, with a heart distressed by the agony of separation from his beloved, he— anticipating the greatness of the inference based on the probability of the coming time,
and unable to endure the sight of the beauty of her movements which manifests the power of the excitant emotion (uddīpana-vibhāva)— says something...

Having experienced a state of agitation due to fear, someone, overwhelmed by apprehension, says this: "Soon the paths will come into being that cannot even be traversed by the mind's desires. This verbal suffix denoting the future time reveals a certain extreme curvature of the ultimate goal.
Or, for example:

To whatever extent these new objects, making known to those with tender minds something never before experienced, strive to reach some indescribable state of supreme fortune; so long does a certain adverse effort of the Unborn One expand. But when the intoxication of honey has become sufficient, we tremble as to what this [effort] might do.

In this context, the notions "I am weary," "I yawn," and "I tremble"—each expressing its own specific time—proclaim a certain poetic curvature (*vakratā*) of the words that exceeds even the highest limit of expression.

And so it is: through the manifestation of a multitude of beautiful objects arising from the delicacy of the spring season that has descended earliest, and through the intensification of the natural splendor of the God of Love (*makaraketu*), there arises an incomparable power slightly awakened by the influence of Madhava; this [power] brings about the distress of tender hearts.
A certain agitation is manifesting itself;
therefore, by this inference, it further attains full development:

"In the midst of the splendor and playfulness of the spring season, there has arisen an occasion for a fitting desire to conquer, born from the excellence of innate delicacy that is habituated to crushing the pride of proud women."

"What will he do?"—thus they speculate, their inner hearts trembling in fear at the falling shower of his flower-arrows; with agitated minds we tremble in some inexplicable way. These are the words of a certain sensitive-hearted man, whose mind is distressed by separation from his beloved.
Having thus examined the crookedness of time (*kālavakratā*), he now examines the crookedness of grammatical factors (*kārakavakratā*), which occurs at an appropriate moment in the sequence:
"Where the general category of a grammatical factor is primarily established through the superimposition of its true nature, by means of expressing it as both primary and subordinate. (Vjiv 2.27)
In order to nourish a certain charm of figurative expression, the transposition of the grammatical factors (kārakas) is called the "crookedness of kārakas" (kārakavakratā). Vjiv 2.28.
Thus has been stated the "curvature of the grammatical factors" (*kārakavakratā*); that aesthetic deviation known as *kārakavakratva* has been described.

Of what nature is it? It is that in which there is a reversal of the grammatical factors (*kāraka*), a shifting of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and the mutual exchange of the subordinate and the primary roles.

How so? That which is a general category of *kāraka*, such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, when considered in relation to the primary [agent], is bound by its predominance and employed in its primary sense.
By what reasoning? Through the superimposition of that [primary status].
The word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the primary [agent].

Its state is its *tattva* (essential nature); [the term "metaphorical"] is used because of the superimposition of that [primary state] through the expression of the state of being a quality (*guṇabhāva*).
The meaning is: because of the expression of the primary thing's state as a quality, it is formulated as something non-primary.
For what purpose? To nourish a certain charm consisting of figurative speech (*bhaṅgībhaṇiti*).

In order to manifest a certain unprecedented charm of expression (*vicchitti*), there occurs a transposition of grammatical factors (*kāraka-viparyāsa*) which produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), wherein even an insentient object is granted the independence characteristic of a sentient being, or where agency is superimposed upon a non-primary instrument or other factor—as for example: [Example: "The moon, having become the face of the night-lotus, has become the eye of the world. (niśā-nīlotpalasya mukhaṃ bhūtvā jagato locanam abhūt) In this way, by attributing the sovereignty of a conscious agent to that which is insentient, or by metaphorically assigning the role of the agent to a non-primary instrument and so forth, a striking poetic effect is achieved.

The Ikṣvākus, well-trained, have never learned to make a request characterized by wretchedness and supplication; nor has a hand joined in salutation, accompanied by servility, ever been placed upon the head of one born in the lineage of Raghu.
All that has been done accordingly, yet the ocean has offered no obstruction. Now, why does my hand run toward the bow to seize it by force? What more is there to say?

In this case, where one ought to say "I wish to grasp the bow with my hand," the superimposition of agency upon the hand— which is actually the instrument— attains a certain curvature of the *kāraka* (grammatical factor).
This is as in examples such as "the pair of breasts" (*stanadvandvam*), and so forth.
Or rather, as if with the tips of their ten left hands— delicate in their placement and yet mutually threatening— they simultaneously cast down and grasp the bow; meanwhile,
in this narrow space for stringing the bow, a certain frantic scramble for "first place" occurs in the sky among those skilled in serving me with their right hands.
In this case, as before, the "curvature of the grammatical factor" (*kāraka-vakratva*) is based on the superimposition of agency;
for example,
in the phrase *baddhasparddha*.
Having thus examined the crookedness of the agent (*kāraka-vakratā*), he examines the crookedness of number (*saṃkhyā-vakratā*) arranged in its proper sequence,
because number serves to define that [agent]—
those who are dependent on the desire to express the variety of poetic artifice employ it.
Where there is a perversion of number, they know that to be the crookedness of number.
Where poets, dependent on their desire to express the variety of poetic figures and under the influence of their wish to describe various states resulting from their own actions,

effect a reversal of number or a transposition of gender— those who know such things recognize that as *saṃkhyāvakratā* (curvature of number) and understand it as *vacanavakratva* (curvature of gender).

Therefore, this is the meaning here: where a different number is employed instead of the singular or dual that ought to be used for the sake of stylistic variety; or where grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established between two words of different numbers. For example:
On your cheek, the decorative leaf-pattern has been crushed by the pressing of your palm; this nectar-like essence of your lower lip has been drunk away by your sighs;
repeatedly clinging to your throat, your tears cause your breast-slope to tremble. O you who are indifferent to my pleas, it is resentment that has become dear to you, not I.
In this context, although one should have said "not I," the plural form "not we" is employed to convey a sense of detachment and to demonstrate that [the ego] is not an intimate part [of the self].
Or, for example:
O bee, we have been ruined by our search for the truth; you, indeed, are truly fortunate!
Here too, as before, there is a perception of neutrality;
or, for example:
"The eyes are groves of blooming blue lotuses, and the hands are beds of lotuses."
In this case, a reversal of number characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the dual and the plural brings about a captivating effect for the hearts of connoisseurs.
For example:
"The scriptures are a new eye. (Vajravidāraṇā-dhāraṇī 2.104)
Here, as before, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the singular and plural numbers serves to produce a striking poetic effect (*vaicitrya*).

Having thus examined the "crookedness" (*vakratā*) of number, he now examines the "crookedness" of person (*puruṣavakratā*), which—since persons are the subject of that [number]—has its opportunity presented by the sequence [of the discussion]:
"The state of being the self (*pratyaktā*) and the state of being the other (*parabhāva*) are applied in reverse order."
Wherever this occurs for the sake of diversion, it should be known as "human crookedness."

In which [instance], one's own nature (*nijātmabhāva*) and the nature of another (*parabhāva*), as well as their difference (*anyatva*)—both of these—are joined through reversal (*viparyāsa*), that is, by being inverted and fixed;
for what purpose? For the sake of *vicchitti*, that is, for the sake of variety (*vaicitrya*).
This very thing, whose nature has been described, is to be known—that is, it must be understood—as *puruṣavakratā*, the variety of a person’s ingenuity (*puruṣavakratva-vicchitti*).
This is the meaning here: when another [suffix] belonging to the second or third person is to be employed for the sake of stylistic variety, sometimes the first person is used instead;
and because these share the same grammatical status (*ekayogakṣema*) as the person-ending, this results in the transposition of the verbal suffix and the nominal stem alone.
For example: [text follows].
I am well aware that our Kauśāmbī has been treated with contempt and seized by wretched enemies, as well as the negligence of my husband who hates statesmanship;
yet my mind, always distressed by the separation from those dear to women, does not dare to speak further on this matter—may the Queen herself understand it.

In this context, regarding the phrase "let the Queen know for herself," where the second person pronoun *yuṣmad* ought to have been employed, the use of the nominal stem alone conveys the speaker’s perception that the matter is beyond the Queen’s power to accomplish; from this indifference, there arises an independence characterized by a personal deliberation on what is beneficial or harmful, leading to the realization of her duty for herself.
This brings about a certain curvature (*vakrabhāva*) of the sentence, for it is precisely this that flashes forth as the very life-force of the utterance.

Having thus considered the *vakratā* (poetic deviation) pertaining to persons, he now considers the *vakratā* regarding the appropriate occasion for the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada*, since these depend upon the person. The usage of verbal roots based on fixed persons according to their grammatical characteristics is well known among the ancient masters as being denoted by the term "upagraha" (voice/mode). Therefore, he employs the very designation of that term in his discourse: [The verse follows: "The *ātmanepada* occurs when there is the desire for one's own benefit, or when there is the intent toward another, or when there is the state of being a servant; likewise, it occurs when there is the attainment of a desired object, or when there is the state of being a messenger, or when there is the state of being a witness. [Commentary: In this regard, the *ātmanepada* is prescribed when there is the desire for one's own benefit (*svārthecchā*). For example: *yācate* ("he begs"), *juhoti* ("he offers oblations"). Or, when there is the intent toward another (*parārthecchā*): *kathayati* ("he tells"), *pāṭhayati* ("he causes to read"). Or, when there is the state of being a servant (*bhṛtyabhāva*): *sevate* ("he serves"), *paricarati* ("he attends upon"). Likewise, when there is the attainment of a desired object (*iṣṭaprāpti*): *labhate* ("he obtains"), *vindate* ("he finds"). Or, when there is the state of being a messenger (*dūtībhāva*): *anuvyāharati* ("he speaks after"). Or, when there is the state of being a witness (*sākṣibhāva*): *paśyate* ("he sees [as a witness]"). Furthermore, the *ātmanepada* is also prescribed in the following cases: when there is the state of being a messenger (*dūtībhāva*), when there is the state of being a witness (*sākṣibhāva*), when there is the state of being a servant (*bhṛtyabhāva*), when there is the attainment of a desired object (*iṣṭaprāpti*), when there is the intent toward another (*parārthecchā*), when there is the desire for one's own benefit (*svārthecchā*), and when there is the state of being a witness (*sākṣibhāva*). In this context, the *ātmanepada* is used when there is the state of being a messenger, the state of being a witness, the state of being a servant, the attainment of a desired object, the intent toward another, the desire for one's own benefit, and the state of being a witness. Thus, the *ātmanepada* is established through these various conditions. [The verse continues: "When there is the state of being a messenger, when there is the state of being a witness, when there is the state of being a servant, when there is the attainment of a desired object, when there is the intent toward another, when there is the desire for one's own benefit, and when there is the state of being a witness—then the *ātmanepada* is employed. In this matter, the *ātmanepada* is used when there is the state of being a messenger, the state of being a witness, the state of being a servant, the attainment of a desired object, the intent toward another, the desire for one's own benefit, and the state of being a witness. Thus, the *ātmanepada* is determined by these specific circumstances. Nevertheless, apart from the establishment of the excellence under discussion, there is nothing new here.
Thus, having first described the poetic curvature (*vakratā*) of the denotative expression and the denoted meaning here, he now begins to describe the curvature of the sentence:

"The excellence of the path consisting of curved words, meanings, qualities, and ornaments—this is the distinct curvature of the sentence, which has such a mode of expression as its very life. (Vjiv 3.3)
The distinct beauty of the color, luster, and arrangement of the pleasing fruits is like some indescribable artistic skill of a creator who captivates the mind, as if in a painting.

The "other" crookedness (*vakratva*) of a sentence—that is, of a collection of words whose function consists in mutual syntactic connection—is something entirely distinct and unprecedented; it constitutes its state of being crooked (*vakrabhāva*).
This is the grammatical connection [of the sentence], as there is no other verb [to govern it].

Why? Because the excellence of the qualities and ornaments of word and meaning residing in the *mārgas*—the *mārgas* being the *sukumāra* (delicate) and others—is itself a distinct kind of *vakratā* (curvature), a certain unique beauty that exists apart from it. In this context, "the *mārgas*" refers to the *sukumāra* and so forth; "residing therein" means those specific *vakratās* which deviate from conventional usage; and "the excellence of the qualities and ornaments of word and meaning" refers to a certain splendor, which is indeed a particular form of *vakratā* distinct from that [conventional] excellence.
Of what nature is it? It is "thus-endowed-with-life.
That is to say, its life and entire essence consists of that very expression—an unprecedented designation—of some indescribable kind in such a manner.
As to its essential form, he says: "It is a certain skill of the creator."
The meaning is that the *vakratva* (curvature or aesthetic deviation) of a sentence is precisely that certain extraordinary skill (*kauśala*) or proficiency (*naipuṇya*) of the creator and arranger;
it is, in some sense, like that of a painting (*citra*),
just as in the case of a picture (*ālekhya*).
Captivating and heart-pleasing, there is a certain distinct and separate skill belonging solely to the creator, which is apart from the materials employed for the task.
Why is this so? He says: "Because of the splendor of the beautiful carvings, colors, and luster of the panels.
This refers to the beauty—that is, the excellence—of those particular carvings, colors, and lusters of the panels that are truly beautiful and heart-stealing.
The meaning is that it is some distinct reality with a separate form.
A "board" (*phalaka*) is a wall serving as the support for a painting; "sketching" (*ullekha*) is merely the arrangement of lines in accordance with the measurements of the drawing-cord.
*Varṇas* are specific coloring substances;
*chāyā* is luster.

The intended meaning here is as follows: just as in a painting, apart from the collection of implements such as the wooden board, there exists separately the skill of the painter, which serves as the very life-force for all the depicted objects.

In the very same way, from a sentence, there emerges a certain *vakratva* (poetic curvature)— distinct from the collection of contextual objects such as the path and so forth— which is characterized by the poet’s skill, perceivable by the hearts of connoisseurs, and which consists in the manifestation of all the contextual objects presented therein.

And thus, whether in the description of the delicacy of the nature of an emotion (*bhāva*), or in the unfolding of the essential character of sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), or in the composition of the aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) resulting from the arrangement of various ornaments, that supreme excellence of nourishment which brings delight to those who know it [is this *vakratva*].
As for the cause:
whatever variety of *vakratā* (poetic deviation) occurs within a single word or a portion of a sentence, the poet’s skill alone stands as its foundation.

This is because, until the end of the aeon (*ākalpa*), those very modes of *vakratā*—consisting of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), and their inherent natures—remain fixed, being restricted solely to that specific form.
From this very source, there emerges a certain other nature that is distinct from every new description and which produces a wondrous flash of consciousness;
by means of which it is said:
"Though its essence has been seized day after day by the best of poets since the beginning of saṃsāra..."
Even now, the movement of speech continues as if the seal were not yet broken.
Though its essence has been seized day after day by the preeminent poets since the beginning of saṃsāra,
the movement of speech still triumphs as if its seal were unbroken even today.
Thus ends the shadow [of the subject].

Herein, from the very beginning of creation, that movement of speech— which, by the majesty of the individual vibration of the poets' own creative intuition (*pratibhā*), has seized the entirety of its essence day by day, yet even today remains as if scarcely exhausted due to the unfolding of an infinity of ever-new manifestations of intuition— is [the subject].
"He triumphs" means he exists in a state of supreme excellence; even within such a perfectly coherent sentence-meaning, there flashes forth a certain extraordinary manifestation of the poet's skill.

For, by emphasizing the suggestion (*dhvani*) of his own self-conceit, he has stated this as follows: "Though its essence has been extracted day after day by the preeminent poets throughout the duration of the world, even now this [work] remains as if its seal were unbroken."

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because the reality has not been thus fully understood by anyone, nothing at all has been grasped from this [teaching]; therefore, since the ultimate truth revealed by my own intuition shall now indeed have its seal broken, the movement of speech triumphs through the attainment of the fruitfulness of its own supramundane activity.
Although the skill of the poet alone is the life-breath of all elements— be they sentiments (*rasa*), essential natures (*svabhāva*), or ornaments (*alaṅkāra*)—

nevertheless, in the case of an ornament specifically, without its being favored by that [skill], it would be impossible for it to serve as a repository of delight for those who know [poetry], even if it were composed with perfect accuracy while merely manifesting its own form as the intended "ornament" of the object under description. Not even in the slightest degree...
We do not perceive any variety [in the cognition],
because it appears as a generality of other objects fallen into a profuse stream,
just as follows:
Dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, she was slender like a dark vine.

And thus, in this [creation], which captivates with its novel description and possesses a preeminent beauty distinguished by the extraordinary arrangement of its parts, a certain power to delight those who know such things is revealed;
as in the verse regarding her creation: *In the act of creating her...* (Vajrāvalī 3.18)
Thus:
"Just as what [is the fruit] of the tree of youth? (Vajracchedikā 3.19).
Thus,

even when this [poetic figure] occurs as a distinct entity, its inclusion within *vākya-vakratā* (the curvature of the sentence), characterized by its dependence on the skill of the poet, alone accords with reason.
This has been stated as follows:
That other crookedness of speech which is divided in a thousand ways—
in this, the entire category of poetic ornaments (alaṃkāra) will be included.
An example of an essential nature (*svabhāva*) illustration is as follows:

"O gentle one, I know that the sprouts on the vine-cottages along the banks of the Yamunā—the companions of the amorous sports of the cowherd women and witnesses to the secret trysts with Rādhā—are now turning old, their dark luster fading, even though the soft materials for preparing the beds of love-making have long since been exhausted. (Vajrāvalī 3.21)

In this case, although only the mere nature of a thing, as it exists in reality and is perceivable by the sensitive heart (*sahṛdaya*), has been described, nevertheless, because it is presented without being explicitly stated, its very essence is revealed— subtle, beautiful, and characterized by a novel and captivating delineation that is accessible only to the hearts of the rare and discerning, and which functions by merging into another object; such is the nature of *vākya-vakratā* (the curvature of the sentence).
A certain pinnacle of poetic skill is indeed attained;
for no excellence of meaning can be found apart from that [skill].
An example of rasa is as follows:
Whatever the world says of that son of a Kṣatriya as being rich in audacity, he would indeed be exactly like that by virtue of truth; his report is not inconsistent.

For these arms of his—once so eager to exhaust the itching heat of their valor, and which long forgot the tumultuous battles with the celestial hosts—would now be occupied with the discharge of even a single drop of time.

Here, the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) called enthusiasm (*utsāha*), having been elevated to the highest state of nourishment through the speaker’s devotion to praising the extraordinary beauty of the object characterized by appropriate determinants (*ālambanavibhāva*), and through the variety of clever and artful expressions of one desiring victory, is led to the state of rasa; thus, it reveals the poet’s skill, whose very nature consists in the curvature of speech.

The sentence-crookedness (*vākya-vakratva*)—whose life-characteristic is the unique expression (*tathābhihitijīvita*) found in each of the other examples from previous sections—should be investigated by the connoisseurs themselves.

This [discussion] is sufficient to stimulate the various modes of crookedness that possess the quality of appropriateness (*aucitya-guṇa*), even for those who are great in their own spontaneous expression. (VjivC 3.23)
The aesthetic flavors (rasa), essential natures (svabhāva), and ornaments (alaṅkāra) that have existed since beginningless saṃsāra attain,
through this [work], a state of novelty that bestows delight upon those who know them.
These are the intermediate verses.

Having thus delineated the nature of the triad—consisting of the designation, the designated, and the designating—which is useful for poetry, he establishes the classification of the subject matter to be described:
"The states of being, beautiful through the propriety of their unfading intrinsic natures..."
The intrinsic nature of sentient beings and insentient things is remembered as being twofold.
The nature (*svarūpa*) of entities (*bhāva*) whose functions (*vṛtti*) are being described is their movement (*parispanda*).
Of what kind is it? It is twofold;
that which has two kinds or modes is thus described.

This has been remembered—that is, traditionally taught—by the wise. Of what entities? Of both sentient and insentient things. "Sentient" means, in other words, living beings possessed of consciousness.
"Inert" (jaḍānām) means those things distinct from that [consciousness], which are devoid of life-force and sentience.

And this very twofold nature of the substratum (dharmi) is the basis for the twofold nature of the attributes (dharma). Of what kind is its essential nature? It is beautiful through the fitness of its own unwithered intrinsic essence.

That which is unfading, charming due to its fresh and full development, is the ultimate nature (*svabhāva*) of reality (*dharma*). Its *aucitya*—its state of being appropriate, its fitness for the context, and its freedom from the taint of defects—is what makes it beautiful and delicate; the meaning is that it brings delight to those who know it.
He analyzes and examines this very twofold division as follows:
In that regard, it is first distinguished by two modes alone, through the association with predominance or otherwise of lions and the like, or gods and the like. (Vjiv 3.6)

Therein, between the two natures, that which is first—the one related to the category of sentient beings—is divided, attains distinction, and becomes twofold by means of exactly two modes, since there is no other category [of existence].
Why? Because of the connection with the predominance or otherwise of [qualities such as] liquor and so forth, or lions and so forth.
The gods and so forth— namely the conscious beings such as the thirty-three [gods], asuras, siddhas, vidyādharas, gandharvas, humans, and so on—

as well as others such as lions and the like, headed by the maned beasts: from the cause of their respective connection with both predominance (mukhyatva) and non-predominance (itarad-aprādhānyam), according to their respective order.
Thus, the first nature is that of gods and others who possess primary consciousness, which serves as the subject matter for the descriptions of poets;

the second is the nature of lions and others who possess secondary consciousness—beasts, wild animals, birds, and reptiles. This very distinction is specifically elucidated [by the following]: "The primary [nature] is charming through the cultivation of untroubled love (*rati*) and other [emotions]."
The supreme [state] is radiant with the manifestation of eloquence appropriate to its own kind.

That which is primary—the essential nature pertaining to sentient beings such as gods and asuras—being of such a kind, becomes the object of description for poets; that is to say, it comes within the scope of their creative activity.
Of what sort is it? It is "charming through the cultivation of unlabored love and other [emotions].

"Unlabored" means free from artificiality and charming in its freshness; this refers to the permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love (*rati*). Their "cultivation" is the process of bringing them to the state of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth.

"However, according to the principle that 'the rasa must be the permanent emotion (sthāyin) itself,' it is therefore captivating and heart-stealing. Examples of this are found in the fourth act of the *Vikramorvaśīya*, in the lamentations of the mad Purūravas during the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation)."
That she might remain hidden by her power through the force of anger— that she does not become angry for long, that she may fly up to heaven, and that her heart remains moist with affection for me;
yet even the enemies of the gods are unable to seize her while she stands before me, and now she has gone entirely beyond the range of my vision— what kind of fate is this?

In this context, the king— overwhelmed by the onset of the state of desolation caused by separation from his beloved, unable to determine the cause for her non-arrival, and already imagining some reason for her absence that was suggested by her natural delicacy yet set aside by the considerations appropriate to the immediate moment, and which was being sketched out by his momentary conjectures— finds that the possibility of her recovery is impossible; thus, with a mind bewildered by the certainty of despair...
The aesthetic flavor (rasa) has been brought to the highest stage of full development;
and this very [flavor] is further intensified by other sentences, such as:
"If that fair-limbed woman were to touch with her feet the forest grounds where the sands have been rained upon by clouds..."
Because of the weight of her heavy hips, she leaned backward; thus, the beautiful line of her footsteps, marked with red lac, became visible.
In this context, one might imagine the possibility of her reaching [the destination] with the hope that she might perhaps touch the earth with her feet; however,

because her succession of footprints— marked by the extreme pressure of her heavy hips as she leaned backward over forest grounds where the sand was soft from the sprinkling of rainwater, and possessing a lovely gait due to being flushed with passion— is so deeply imprinted, the certainty of despair has all the more fully emerged.
Those [lamentations] served as the occasion for the subsequent sentences, which were like the ravings of a madman;
they are the examples of the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa-rasa*) found in the lamentations of Vatsarāja in the second act of the *Tāpasavatsarāja*,
such as:
Beholding the bath-house with a dejected face, and having wandered through the pleasure-pavilions, he sighed deeply and quickly cast his gaze upon the rows of *kesara* creepers.

"Why do you come to my side, my little son? What is the use of these flatteries? You have been abandoned by your cruel mother as she departed with me for this vast earth. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra 3.27)
In this passage, the poet has most excellently brought forth the convergence of the factors of aesthetic emotion (vibhāvas), etc., which serve as the basis for the full development of rasa.
Accordingly, a statement by the Vidūṣaka is employed to introduce this very speech: "This is indeed the Queen’s pet young deer; it is following Your Honor. (VjivC_3.28)
This is negligence! Indeed, this fawn, acting as a son to the Queen, follows after Your Majesty.
Such is the shadow [of meaning].
By this, the status of the young fawn, the rain-pavilion, and so forth as excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) for the rasa of compassion (*karuṇa-rasa*) is produced all the more clearly.
And thus, immediately after Rumaṇvat’s statement, "This is another sprinkling of salt upon a wound," another sentence was composed with precisely this intent, as follows:

O Queen, why do you not give an answer to that parrot, your playful friend, who—having repeatedly pulled with his beak at the ruby bud resting on the edge of your ear, thinking it to be a pomegranate seed—struck you on the cheek with his foot and now cries out repeatedly in distress? Why do you not respond to him fearlessly?
In this passage, Śuka’s possession of such perverse behavior is presented for the purpose of demonstrating his great affection [for his father].
By the word "this one" (*asau*), there is a reference to the excellence of the tenderness experienced through direct perception by the cheeks acting as cauldrons.
Thus, the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa, having its sole life-force in such an excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), was led to a state of exquisite beauty that has reached its highest pitch.

Thus, examples for the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*) and the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) have been presented due to their delicacy; examples for the other sentiments (*rasa*) should likewise be conceived by oneself.
In this way, the nature of the second type—the non-primary sentient being associated with lions and the like—becomes the subject of description for poets.
Of what sort? "Resplendent with the vivid depiction of the natural disposition appropriate to its own genus.

Its own (svā) genus is that which is individual (pratyeka), belonging to itself, and whose nature consists in the character of a universal (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa); the disposition (hevāka) appropriate to that genus is the movement following its inherent nature; the vivid depiction (samullekha) of that is its correct delineation, or its composition in its actual form—by means of that, it is resplendent and radiant.
That is to say, it causes delight to those who know it;
for instance,
once, while his eyes were closed inside a cave-dwelling on Mount Pāriyātra by means of this [practice].
He was fast asleep, with his two hands crossed and resting upon his chin, which was raised by the tips of his fangs.
In this instance, while the lion is experiencing sleep within the interior of his mountain-cave dwelling, a position appropriate to his own species is depicted.
Or, for example:
"Casting his gaze repeatedly at the chariot following behind him—charming in its neck-bending—he has entered mostly with his hindquarters into his forebody out of fear of the falling arrow."
Behold, its path strewn with *darbha* grass half-chewed and falling from mouths opened by exhaustion, it travels much more in the sky than on earth due to its lofty leaping.
He elucidates this very point by way of another formulation:
"It is beautiful, being bound by the capacity to kindle aesthetic flavor (rasa) in sentient beings—both primarily non-sentient and largely insentient. (Vjiv 3.8)

The very nature of sentient beings who are secondary—that is, those who are not primary—being of such a kind, attains the state of being worthy of description as it serves as a subordinate element to the subject at hand. Of what sort is it? It is charming, being the basis for the power that intensifies the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

The *rasas* are those beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*); their "excitement" (*uddīpana*) is their arousal and nourishment. The capacity or power for that [arousal] is the ability, and by means of that, there is a composition or arrangement; because of this, it is "charming," meaning heart-captivating.
For example: "The male cuckoo, its throat made hoarse from tasting the mango sprouts, sang sweetly."
That very speech of Smara became capable of destroying the pride of the high-minded woman.

And even for insentient things— for insentient, non-conscious entities such as water, trees, flowers, and the seasons— their very nature becomes a fit subject for description when it is rendered charming by its capacity to kindle passion,
as in:
"Even at the first sight, the five-arrowed god [Kāma] consumes my mind, which is difficult to restrain due to its longing for an unattainable object."
How much more so when sprouts have appeared on the mango trees in the grove, their pale leaves having been uprooted by the Malaya breeze?
Or as it is said:
"The *kuravaka* flowers appear with their sprouts ready to burst forth; the lakes shine with their edges choked by masses of moss; and the rivers are marked by parting lines of foam.

Moreover, O slender-limbed one, at this time even the forests, though thickly overgrown with creeping vines, come to possess the playful grace of the bow of the sporting God of Love. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā, 3.34)
Having thus described the nature of things as being based on their inherent and beautiful vibration, he concludes that very point:
"This body of an object, overflowing with loveliness, should be known by poets as something to be accepted as a subject for description. (Vjiv 3.9)
This body of the subject matter—the thing to be described—is to be known as something to be accepted, understood as that which is to be grasped;
being what kind? It is overflowing with loveliness, completely filled with beauty.
Insofar as it is free from any possibility of being set aside, it means that it attracts those who possess such knowledge.
For this alone is the subject matter of description for poets, lying beyond the scope of direct denotation (*abhidhā*).
Thus, for such a thing—which is radiant with an excellence of beauty in its own nature—ornaments initiate another level of splendor.

He examines this very point by way of another method: "Furthermore, another [aspect], which is based on the activity of the means for accomplishing dharma and so forth, and is appropriate for worldly convention, receives the status of being worthy of description. (Vjiv 3.10)
And another [aspect] is that which is suited to common usage.
Furthermore, the very nature of objects—whether sentient or insentient—attains such a description and becomes the object of a poet's activity.
Of what sort is it? It is that which is suited to common usage.

It is suitable for worldly conduct. Being of what nature? It is that which has as its basis the activity that serves as the means for accomplishing dharma and the rest. That is to say, it is so described because its basis is the very activity—its own manifestation—which constitutes the means for the accomplishment or fulfillment of the four aims beginning with dharma.

This is what is meant: in poetry, all entities—whether they be primary sentient beings such as heroes and the like, or even those that are non-primary sentient beings—are to be described primarily in terms of their activity as means for achieving the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*).

Even those entities whose nature is that of secondary sentient beings enter the domain of poetic description by poets primarily through their own playful manifestations which serve as means for dharma, artha, and so forth.
Thus, the lives of kings such as Śūdraka and ministers such as Śukanāsa are described solely with the intent of instructing on the practice of the four aims of human life.

The beautiful form of elephants, deer, and other animals—which possess a consciousness that is not primary—appears in the poetic subject (*lakṣya*) as being described by virtue of their movement being an integral part of battles, hunting expeditions, and the like.

For this very reason, it was established at the very outset that there is a similarity between poets and their poetic instruments on the one hand, and painters and their painting implements on the other, precisely because of the predominance of the delineation of such forms.

Thus, this twofold nature—consisting of the predominance of intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*) and the predominance of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), characterized by innate delicacy and vitality—is the very body of the object under description; it deserves to be the ornamented (*alaṅkārya*) itself, and not the ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
In that regard, it has already been established at the outset how the natural form of a thing cannot itself be an ornament.
Now, he refutes the status as an "ornament" (alaṅkāra) claimed by other theorists regarding that which consists of rasa, whose function is described as the vibration of the primary consciousness:

"It is not an ornament like rasa, because another [element] does not appear [as distinct from it], and because there is no connection between word and meaning for something that is not distinct from its own nature. (Vjiv 3.11)
"An ornament is not *rasavat*.
The meaning is that it is not logical for this ornament named *rasavat*, which produces a [specific] cognition, to possess the quality of being an embellishment.
For what reason? Because nothing else appears apart from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Because no other, external element—distinct from and additional to the very nature and inherent movement of the object being described—is perceived or understood;

this is the intended meaning here: that for all the utterances of great poets, the state of distinction established by the analytical separation of "this is the figure" and "this is the substratum" flashes forth in the mind of any and every cognizer whatsoever.
Regarding the statement "possessing rasa" (rasavat) and "possessing an ornament" (alaṅkāravat), even those with attentive minds do not understand anything at all by this alone.

For instance: if the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, being described as the primary subject, are what is to be adorned (*alaṅkārya*), then there must be some other ornament (*alaṅkāra*) distinct from them.

Or, if the very nature of that [sentiment] is called an ornament because it is the basis for the delight of those who know it, even then something else distinct from it must be manifested as the object to be adorned.

Thus, in the manner of defining and exemplifying the *rasavat* ornament as conceived by the ancient authors of poetics (*alaṅkāra-kāra*), not even a slight trace of such a distinction can be discerned.
And so it is said:
"The *rasavat* is that in which the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and other sentiments are clearly displayed. (VjivC 3.35)
Thus ends the definition of *rasavat*.

In the interpretation where it is explained as "that in which the *śṛṅgāra* and other [rasas] are shown, touched, or clearly manifest," no meaning other than poetry itself is perceived as constituting the sense of the compound.
If one were to argue that this *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure) is indeed nothing but poetry, even that does not possess perfectly clear excellence.

Since one begins by stating that word and meaning, which are parts of poetry, possess their own distinct ornaments, yet concludes now that poetry itself is the ornament, there arises the fault of inconsistency between the introduction and the conclusion;
or, if the compound is taken to mean "that by which the *śṛṅgāra* and other sentiments are clearly shown," even so, it must still be explained: what is this [poetry]?
If it is argued that this is merely the variety of the means of demonstration (*pratipādana-vaicitrya*),
that too is not a correct or tenable justification;
for the variety of the means of demonstration, which serves as the basis for its embellishment, is indeed something other than that which is being demonstrated.
Furthermore, it is not merely being demonstrated;
even if one were to state the variety of ways in which the aesthetic flavors (rasas) are demonstrated as clearly shown, that too would not be easily understood.
In the case of a clear manifestation, it results in nothing other than the complete perfection of the essential nature of the erotic and other sentiments (*śṛṅgārādi*).

Furthermore, if [the view were that] "ornament belongs to the poetry possessing rasa," then since that [poetry] already exists as such, there would be nothing further for it to express by means of this [ornament].
Alternatively, if it were held that the state of possessing *rasa* is imparted to that [poetry] by that very ornament, [then...]

Thus, in that case, it follows that this is not an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) of the *rasavat* [sentiment], but rather that the *rasavat* itself is the ornament; by virtue of its greatness, even the poem becomes *rasavat*.

Or else, because it is an ornament of the *rasavat* poem—which has acquired a connection with rasa through that very [ornament]—it subsequently receives the designation "the *rasavat* ornament," just as one says, "the son of one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice will become [a performer of it]."
That too is not a well-founded resolution,

because the word "agniṣṭomayājī" first attains its established conventional meaning in another context as a characteristic of an existing entity (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) without opposition; it can only subsequently experience that [other meaning] through its fitness for a connection with the sense of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).
Furthermore, it is not correct to argue here as follows:
"Since 'ornament' (*alaṅkāra*) belongs to poetry that possesses aesthetic flavor (*rasavat*), its very nature is established solely through its connection with that [flavor];
and since the possession of flavor by poetry is based on that connection, by whom can this fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) be removed?"
Or, if it is argued that "that which possesses rasa" should simply be called an *alaṅkāra*, even so, there is neither an *alaṅkāra* nor poetry here, but nothing else; thus,
both of those two positions are refuted.
The example is not treated separately because it shares the same security of definition as the definition itself:
"She who was dead, by whom my death was remembered in order to reunite with her after passing away—she very same woman of Avanti has been found by me here in this very birth. (Vajrāvalī 3.36)
In this case, nothing other than the mental state—which constitutes the very body of the subject matter characterized by the intensification of *rati*—is perceived as a distinct, separate entity.
Therefore, it is only logical that [the *bhāva*] itself is the object of poetic ornamentation (*alaṅkārya*).
As for what has been stated by some...
It is the locus of its own words, the stable emotions, the transitory emotions, the determinants, and the dramatic representations.
By this, the definition has already been qualified.
In that regard, the fact that the *rasas* themselves are the locus of their own words (*svaśabdāspadatva*) was previously unknown to us.

Therefore, those very learned ones—whose minds are absorbed in the essence of *rasa* and who know its ultimate reality—must be asked this: does the status of being the locus of their own words belong to the *rasas*, or to that which possesses *rasa* (*rasavat*)?

In that regard, concerning the former position: *rasayanti* means they are "savors" (*rasa*); being the locus of their own words, they abide in those [words]—that is, existing within the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and other [sentiments]—they are tasted by those who know them. This is what is meant: when [the sentiments] are denoted by their own words and enter the path of hearing, they produce for sentient beings the wonder of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇacamatkāra*). By this principle, objects such as *ghṛtapūra* (sweetmeats) and the like, when denoted by their own words, [attain] the excellence of their own aesthetic taste.

"To those who accomplish [this]—to those of noble conduct by whom, for anyone seeking the happiness of utility, the prosperity and bliss of the sovereign wealth of the three worlds would be bestowed effortlessly merely through the mention of their names: homage to them!
It is not possible for that which possesses aesthetic flavor (rasavat) to be their locus."
Since even its own expressed meaning (svavācya) does not serve as the locus for that rasa, how much less so anything else?
Furthermore, its status as an ornament (alaṅkāra) has already been refuted at the very outset.
The remaining [figures], such as *sthāyin* and so forth, have already been explained by the previous definitions and thus are not further examined here;
this also applies to the figure *rasavat*, which arises from its dependence upon rasa.
Thus, a definition has been formulated by some; however, that too is not correct, as it does not withstand critical scrutiny. For instance: "rasasaṃśraya" means that which has rasa as its substratum;
for that reason, this becomes the figure of speech known as *rasavat*.
Nevertheless, it must still be stated: what is this "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) that functions apart from the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)?
If you say it is poetry itself, that too has already been refuted; for since it is contradictory for something to act upon its own self, it is untenable for poetry to be an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Alternatively, "rasasaṃśrayāt" means that which is the locus of rasa, or that which is supported by rasa;
nevertheless, the question remains as to what this [locus] is, and thus it must indeed be explained as something distinct.

The collection of examples for this definition is, for the most part, of the same nature as the preceding one; therefore, it is not considered separately. It is "delightful with aesthetic flavor" (rasapeśala). (VjivC 3.39)
In this reading, nothing further remains to be added.

Now, as for the question: how can that collection of word-meanings (*padārtha-sārtha*)—which is the very nature of the subject matter (*alaṅkārya*) mounted upon sentences expressive of the essence of things (*vastu*), their inherent nature (*svabhāva*), aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and so forth—become an ornament (*alaṅkaraṇa*) by entering into the nature of the *rasa*, when its own distinct movement has dissolved, like substances [that have merged] into the nature of *rasa*? This too...
This is indeed to be reflected upon.
Furthermore, even if one were to accept it in that way, it would ultimately result in a reversal of the primary and subordinate status [of the causes]; therefore, this is of no consequence.
Herein lies another refutation.

He proceeds: "Also because of the lack of connection between word and meaning. That is, because of the lack of connection between word and meaning—that is, between the denoter and the denoted—and because of the absence of their coordination, the presence of the *rasavat* ornament is not possible.

And here, since the suffix *matup* is prescribed in the sense of "that in which rasa exists" (*vidyate tiṣṭhati yasya*), the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed as "the ornament of that [rasa]," or else a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) is formed as "an ornament which possesses rasa."
In that regard, concerning the former position: what other distinct category of object exists apart from rasa, for which this would be an ornament?
If it is argued that it is poetry itself, then even there, what is that object distinct from it wherein the designation "ornament consisting of rasa" (rasavad-alaṅkāra) could find its scope?

No category of object (*padārtha*) distinct from the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) is observed that could be established as the possessor of that quality (*tadvat*), which would then constitute the figure of speech *rasavat*. Thus, in the manner described above, there is no connection whatsoever between the word and its meaning regarding the figure of speech *rasavat*.

Alternatively, if one were to establish a coordination between word and meaning even in the two types of compounds by treating them as the domain of another illustrative example (*nidarśana*), as follows:

Slender as she is, with her sprouts moistened by the water of the clouds, she appears as if her lower lip has been washed away by tears; deprived of her ornaments due to the absence of her season, she seems vacant as her blossoming has ceased; remaining in the silence of anxiety because of the absence of the humming of bees, that fierce lady is perceived as if she has cast me down at her feet and, now filled with remorse, has turned away from me.
Or as the river, with its waves for knitted brows and its rows of birds for a girdle, drags along foam like a garment loosened by her agitation.
Just as one who has stumbled repeatedly goes on according to where he was struck, so too this river, being inevitably impatient, has surely transformed into its present state.
In this case, both the presence of rasa and the poetic ornament (alaṅkāra) manifest clearly;
therefore, the difficulty of discerning between them does not exist in any way whatsoever.

Consequently, according to the interpretation of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) as "an ornament belonging to that which possesses rasa," there is nothing inconsistent regarding either word or meaning.
Since the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is subordinate to the nourishment of rasa, its very composition constitutes the state of being possessed of rasa (*rasavattva*).

Even in the case of the analytical compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*)—where it is understood as "an ornament that is possessed of rasa"—there is nothing inconsistent. Thus, in these two examples, because the creeper and the river serve as excitant determinants (*uddīpanavibhāva*), and because the hero’s internal organ is permeated by his beloved, he becomes identified with them; [is he not] insentient? [No, he is sentient.]

For one who perceives the entire collection of objects as being exactly that [the Self], there is no way whatsoever to apply the poetic ornaments of simile (*upamā*) or metaphor (*rūpaka*), because such application would involve the superimposition of similarity upon them and the attribution of their attributes, which would contradict the nature of those objects.
This is true.
However, in the absence of the designation by the word "alaṅkāra" (ornament), in the case of the *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (adjectival compound),
the use of the term "rasavān" (possessing rasa) alone would result.
If it is argued that there is the apprehension of what is called the "flavorful ornament" (*rasavad-alaṅkāra*),
even that does not deserve to be considered logical, because of the absence of metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the like.
The view that "rasavat" is a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa)—meaning "an ornament belonging to that which possesses rasa"—is also not clearly consistent with the facts.
For every single work of poetry possesses rasa;
since it is precisely because of its excellence that such poetry, which brings delight to those who know it, ought to be composed, [rasa] is its very ornament.
Thus, when this [sentiment] is accepted as the substratum, it is only logical that all figures of speech, such as *rūpaka* and the rest, attain the status of being *rasavad-alaṅkāra*.

Furthermore, since every single figure of speech possesses this quality of *rasavat*, the same principle applies even under the view that the term is a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (adjectival compound). Moreover, even if that were admitted, for those figures of speech whose individual definitions have been set aside and which have acquired their own identity through their devotion to nourishing the subject at hand, there exists—distinct from the excellence expressed by their respective individual definitions—this [excellence of sentiment].
Nothing additional is added;
therefore,
the futility of producing those respective characteristics follows as an unavoidable consequence.
Furthermore, there is no scope for the application of the figure of speech *rasavat* in such a context,
because those who know [the subject] do not perceive it as such,
and because other figures of speech are established as being primary [in that instance].

Alternatively, if the distinction between the scope of figures such as *rasavat*— which has sentient entities as its object— and that of *upamā* and others— which have insentient things as their subject— is established on that basis,
even that does not win over the learned.

For it has already been established by the ancient masters that because even insentient things possess a certain delicacy and sapidity when delineated by a great poet who is capable of heightening the aesthetic flavor (rasa), there would otherwise result either an extreme scarcity of scope or a total absence of scope for similes and other figures; furthermore, it would follow that the flow of great poetry— which is beautiful due to its distillation of sentiments such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra)— would become devoid of rasa.
Or, if it is argued that the *rasavad-alaṅkāra* is established by virtue of its captivating other varieties of aesthetic charm,
as those most proficient [in the field] have stated: "Where rasa and the like are subordinate to another primary meaning of the sentence..."
In that poetry, my view is that the ornament consists of rasa and the like.
Thus,

where another meaning of the sentence is established as the primary element to be embellished, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, being subordinated to it, attains the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
For in such cases, the quality (*guṇa*), having first manifested the underlying emotion (*bhāva*), embellishes the principal element.

Therefore, the manifestation of the discernment of ornaments unfolds: "May that fire of Śambhu’s arrow burn away your misfortune—the fire which was like a lover who had recently committed an offense, and which was cast aside by the young women of Tripura as they wept with lotus-eyes; which, when thrown, clung to their hands; which, though violently struck, seized the hem of their garments; which, when grasped by the hair, was flung down; and which, when falling at their feet, was not even looked upon in the confusion. (Vajrāvalī 3.43)

In this context, because the description of the agitation caused by words such as "sword" and "lotus-eyes"— which serves to proclaim the power of the Enemy of Tripura over the beautiful wives of the Asuras being consumed by the fire of Śiva’s arrows— is the primary motive, the sentiment of *karuṇa* (pathos) is the subordinate element (*aṅga*), and not the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment of separation through jealousy.
Because that [ordinary perception] is not being experienced here;

therefore, this is the ultimate truth in this matter: the extraordinary majesty of the Blessed One, having ascended the stream of beauty nourished by the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of compassion—which is accessible through the excellence cultivated by the poet’s creative intuition—attains an indescribable state of captivating the hearts of those with sensitivity.

Furthermore, since the property of being denotable by the same word is not possible for both fire and the heat of the sun's rays, it is impossible— even with the greatest effort of the Supreme Lord— to establish the identity of these two, whose natures are opposed by such superimpositions of contradictory attributes; for one's own nature cannot be altered.

Nor does the cognition of that experience by those who know it arise merely from the fact that such [an emotion] is not denotable by words; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that joy, dejection, and so forth would result from the mere mention of words such as "jaggery" or "sugar-candy," since they too possess that flavor.
Furthermore, if such an experience were cognized, the fault of the simultaneous presence of two *rasas* (*rasadvayasamāveśa*) would become unavoidable.
Moreover, it cannot be maintained here that the fault of the simultaneous presence of two *rasas* is determined by the relationship of subordinate and predominant (*guṇapradhānabhāva*).
Or, if it is argued that both of these constitute ornaments because they are subordinate to the primacy of the Blessed One’s power (*bhagavat-prabhāva*), that too is not tenable.

For since compassion is real, it would be one alone; and because those two [compassion and power] lack a common root, no similarity whatsoever can be established between them, just as there is none between existence and non-existence. Therefore, enough of this rashness in the cleverness of chewing upon what is inappropriate.

Or, if those who do not place their trust in this illustration, but who—striving correctly to establish the consistency between the definition and the example as handed down in tradition—are reflective and explain another example of the *rasavat* ornament, [what need is there for further mockery?]:

"O pitiless one, will you not go away, leaving me who have finally seen you after so long? What is this passion for exile? By whom have you been driven far away? Speaking thus at the end of his dreams, with his beloved clinging to his neck, the enemy's wife wakes up and weeps loudly, her arm-bracelets empty. (VjivC 3.44)

"In this context, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is that the host of the enemy's beautiful women, having lost their beloveds through your hand and being without refuge due to an onset of grief, undergoes such a calamity brought about by reaching the very pinnacle of the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇarasa*); thus, it is this [intended meaning] alone that constitutes the primary sense of the sentence, while the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) is composed as its subordinate element."
In this context, being primarily concerned with the erotic sentiment of separation caused by travel (*pravāsa-vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*) is not the ultimate reality.

It is called an "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*) because it appears as a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*), its function being the presentation of a multitude of word-meanings mutually connected to one another.

Furthermore, since there is no absence of an object for that [ornament], the impossibility of its definition—caused by the lack of the complete collection of its own causes, such as the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth which serve as the substrata for rasa—cannot occur.
The defect of the coexistence of two rasas is also far removed;

since the actual nature of both exists, there is no contradiction of self when they are perceived through experience, because there is an absence of rivalry. Therefore, that too is beautiful in its capacity to bestow delight upon those who know it.

Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of the rasa of compassion (*karuṇarasa*), both [the following points] are tenable: first, that during the time of dreaming and at the moment of waking, the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth—serving as the causes of the separation caused by travel—are presented as being based upon words; and second, that such a state of that very compassion is logically possible. Thus, the question of how this [compassion] first arises is also addressed.
It is not entirely consistent;

for even if the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇarasa*) is firmly established, the fact that one's enemies and their beloved wives flee here and there— their hearts terrified by the assault of the Great Man’s majesty upon the objects of their flattery— does not transcend the application of logical reasoning, as it constitutes a distinct state of affairs.

For him, whose mind was stilled by one-pointed concentration as he ascended the support of such a state of full development, and whose heart was permeated by the addiction of long-practiced habituation, there occurred after a long time a dream-encounter with his beloved; they began a lovely conversation consistent with their previously experienced history,
