but somehow he woke up, and immediately upon awakening, his inner self was rent asunder by the contradiction between the present reality and the connection of past and future events that had flashed forth.
Since the multitude of the wives of your enemies weeps, this constitutes the very ascent to the stage of the full development of *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment);

for whether it be the beauty of the propriety of such a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) or its entry into the very nature of that [sentiment], how could there be even a scent of *pravāsa-vipralambha* (love-in-separation due to travel) as a distinct operation?
If it is argued that, because the beloved is predominant, the *karuṇa* rasa is called an "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) due to its being subordinate to him, that too is not faultless.
For in both of these examples, the primary meaning of the sentence is composed as having a function that unfolds precisely through the nature of *karuṇa*.
This occurs by way of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) or *anyāpadeśa* (indirect designation), such that the two meanings are perceived as distinct from the literal expression.
Since compassion (*karuṇa*) is a rasa, it is not logically consistent for that which exists as the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) to be expressed directly (*vācyatva*).
Nor is it the domain of "subordinated suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), because the suggested meaning [here] possesses primacy.
This is because it manifests through itself alone;
nor can both be suggested, since the relationship of subordinate and principal (aṅga-aṅgibhāva) would be untenable.
And this has been analyzed by us according to the circumstances; however, that [logical principle] is not the operative factor here, so enough with further elaboration.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "in that poetry, the ornament is rasa and so forth," it would follow that rasa alone is the ornament, and nothing at all would be expressed by the suffix *matup* in the term *rasavat*.
Thus, since there is an absence of a connection between word and meaning, the charge of infinite regress remains; yet even this is of no consequence.

Having thus rejected the status of *rasavat* as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) because it constitutes the very body of the subject matter being described—and because its fate is inextricably linked with that—[the author] now [addresses] *preyas*.
"It is not the case that 'the opposite of the *preyas* would be the *apreyas*';
for [that] *apreyas* would not be [the mere absence of] the *preyas*.
They [the *preyas* and *apreyas*] may exist as distinct figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), even because they are not observed elsewhere. (Vjiv 3.12)
That which has been traditionally handed down by the ancient masters as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) cannot possibly exist according to your [view].

For some have declared the definition of *preyas* to be "the narration of that which is more dear," while others, regarding it merely as an illustration, have considered that very [illustration] to be its definition.
This has been demonstrated just as Vidura spoke to Kṛṣṇa when he had arrived at his home out of affection.
In time, this joy shall be yours again through your very arrival.
Thus;
and this very example is intended by the predecessors as well. And so it has been stated by them:
O Govinda, today a [great] joy has arisen for me now that you have come to my home.
Thus,
that very [position] does not withstand critical examination;
and so, by the passage beginning with "by time" (*kālena*), etc.

That very thing which is described as the object of description is the essential nature of the entity; since that itself is the ornament, nothing remains that could serve as the object to be ornamented.
It is illogical for that very same thing to possess both the status of being the object of adornment and the status of being the ornament itself;

it is not possible for a single entity to simultaneously function as both the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) of one and the same action. Even if such sentences were observed where both [statuses] could coexist—
You know yourself by yourself; you create yourself by yourself;
and through your own creative power, you dissolve back into yourself alone.
Thus it is said;
yet that too is for the most part devoid of logical consistency.
For even though there is an actual non-difference here, linguistic usage proceeds by relying on an imagined distinction based upon a metaphorical existence.
Furthermore, whether because the Supreme Lord consists of the universe or because the universe consists of the Supreme Lord,

even though there is ultimate non-duality, the awareness of difference— which perceives His state as every individual subject regarding the construction of the manifold world with its diverse individual vibrations— never fails to find clear scope for itself, even for the purpose of demonstrating His majesty.

Therefore, since in this case some form of the Supreme Lord Himself is being attained, there is nothing inconsistent in one [aspect] being the object (*karman*) of the action such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, while another is the instrument (*karaṇa*) because it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).
Furthermore, even by means of a conceptual abstraction (*apoddhāra-buddhi*), no division whatsoever can be discerned in the example.
Consequently, the refutation—"because nothing other than its own nature (*svarūpa*) appears"—should also be applied here.

Furthermore, in the view that there is no distinction [between the two], that very thing would be both the object of adornment and the ornament itself; since this contradicts the principle of agency within one's own self—as it is established that "one's own self never climbs upon its own shoulder"—it follows that such a case would be impossible.
Now, he offers another objection: "It would be contradictory."
(Since it is being described by this principle, its opposite, the *preyas*, which is the counter-position to that [the *rasavat*], would also be subsumed under *apreya*;
therefore, it would constitute an *alaṃkāra*).
If one asks, "Even so, what fault would there be?", that too is not correct.
For those [ancient authorities] did not accept it in that way.

Furthermore, having reflected upon the conventional usage of the "ornamented" (*alaṅkārya*) and the "ornament" (*alaṅkaraṇa*) as found in inference (*laiṅgika*), the former scholars applied that convention to poetry by relying merely on a commonality of such a nature.
In the world, the infinite multitude of objects existing within the three worlds is the "ornamented," while the perfected ones, Vidyādharas, and so forth, are the "ornaments."

Ornaments such as bracelets and armlets are only a few; in the same way, in poetry, the body of the subject matter being described is the infinite substrate to be adorned, and likewise, ornaments such as similes are only a few.
If the primary object of description were itself the ornament (*alaṅkāra*), there would follow an infinity of ornaments other than that which is being described;
consequently, because there would be no completion [of the enumeration], there would be no undertaking of *abhidhā* and the other [functions] as there is in the case of *saṃbhāvanā*.
Therefore, the distinction between the ornamented and the ornament in the domain of poetry deserves to be expressed exactly as it is found in worldly convention, neither less nor more.
Right here, he presents another objection: “In the case of another figure of speech” (*alaṅkārāntare*).
There would be *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) and *saṃkara* (conflation). First (the former)...
Since that which is being described is the means for achieving what is called "the more beloved" (*priyatara*), even though it is itself the object to be adorned (*alaṅkārya*),

when another ornament such as *rūpaka* (metaphor) is prescribed, then— upon that being prescribed— there would arise two specific ornaments, namely *saṃsṛṣṭi* (coexistence) and *saṅkara* (commingling), based on the connection with the *preyas*.
This is how it should be.

Among statements endowed with the expressions of the beloved, those who know [the nature of poetry] have never previously employed the technical usage of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) or *saṃkara* (blend), because such an appearance does not occur;
for example:
"The spot on the moon, the base of the throat of Viṣṇu—conqueror of Smara—and the temples of the world-elephants, bearing the ink-like ichor."
O tilaka of the earth's circle, even now they appear as if smeared with darkness; tell me, what has been whitened by your glories?
In this case, the beloved is the object of adornment (*alaṅkārya*) and the "feigned praise" (*vyājastuti*) is the ornament (*alaṅkāra*); however,

there is no appearance of both as ornaments such that the designation of "conjunction" (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) or "commixture" (*saṃkara*) would apply, because no third element appears as a further object of adornment.
He begins to refute this very point by another method: "Also because it is not observed elsewhere.

"Elsewhere" means in another subject matter distinct from the description of the beloved; since the beloved serves as an ornament [only] in that context, the application of metaphors and the like would follow there as well.
And it is not observed to be so anywhere;

therefore, because it is not seen elsewhere either, its status as an ornament is not logically tenable, since even that which possesses rasa shares the same fate as that [ornament]. Thus, its being an embellishment is likewise untenable.
Having thus rejected such ornaments for the Beloved, because his body is the primary object of description, he rejects others that are of the same nature:
"Similarly, there is no status as an ornament for the *ūrjasvin* (vigorous) and *udātta* (noble), nor likewise for the *samāhita* (composed) which is beautified by two modes. (Vjiv 3.13)

"In the case of *ūrjasvin* and *udāttābhidhāna*, which are produced through a sequence of [elements] that do not possess the nature of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), 'ornamentality'—that is, the state of being an ornament—'does not exist,' meaning it is not possible.
How so?
By the term 'tadvat' (like that), there is a reference back to the previously mentioned *rasavat* and other figures."

Therefore, just as in those [previous cases], the meaning is that these two do not possess the status of being ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), like the previously negated state of being an ornament or like *rasa* and so forth.
(Even though) ancient authorities have declared the ornamentation of these two by first presenting definitions and examples,
nevertheless, because it is not logically consistent, [that view is rejected].
This is not tenable; for instance, some have presented the definition and illustration of the first [type] as follows:

"The composition (*bandha*) of mental states (*bhāva*) and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) that proceed through impropriety due to causes such as desire, anger, and so forth, is called *ūrjasvin* (the forceful). (VjivC 3.49)
In this way his passion increased until he proceeded to seize the daughter of the Snowy Mountain by force, casting aside the path of righteousness.
Thus,
some, considering that only an example need be stated because it [itself] constitutes the definition, have demonstrated just that;
for example:
"O Śalya, why does Karṇa, having been driven away like a snake, aim twice at Pārtha with such vigor as if he had returned? VjivC_3.51 //
Or rather,
let there be no fear in your heart that I am one who would do you harm;
my sword never desires to strike those who have turned away from me.
Thus [it is said].

Regarding that, first of all, this must be considered concerning the definition and the example of the first two [types]: what indeed is this so-called "inappropriateness" (*anaucitya*), by virtue of which the composition of *rasa* and the like when they are thus manifested becomes an ornament (*alaṅkāra*)?

Because by that which is contrary to propriety (*aucitya*), not only is there a loss of nourishment for those [qualities] being perceived, but rather, their lack of delicacy (*saukumārya*) attains a state of having scope for manifestation.
Thus it has been said:
"There is no cause for the destruction of rasa other than impropriety. (VjivC 3.53)
Thus [it is said].

Or rather, what is intended here is not an ultimate (pāramārthika) impropriety; instead, it refers to something relative to the faultless rasa, which is manifested through the propriety of the determinants (vibhāva), consequents (anubhāva), and transitory states (vyabhicārin), and which pertains to a different context.
And so, the reasoning is set forth: "due to causes such as desire, anger, and so forth."
Even that is not a well-established samādhi;

for, in consideration of the abundant aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) produced by the perfection of propriety, it is appropriate to employ a composition of aesthetic flavor and emotion associated with some degree of impropriety when directed toward the majority of beings who are merely ordinary creatures, and for the sake of causes such as desire;
however, this is not the case regarding the subject matter already cited.

When the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— which is naturally charming by virtue of its inherent delicacy, illuminated by the skill of the innate poetic power, and brought forth by the convergence of the *vibhāvas* such as the *puṣkara*, and which is appropriate for those of refined intellect because its logical inconsistencies are dispelled by marvelous playfulness like the moonlight illuminating a moonstone— attains supreme beauty.
How, then, could that which is withered by impropriety and whose function is restricted by the postulation of causes such as desire attain the status of appearing as an ornament?

And thus, in such a case, it is the great poets who shine most brilliantly when they conceive of aesthetic flavor (*rasavattā*) through the similarity [of the subject] to another object worthy of description.
As for example:
Even Paśupati, longing for union with the Daughter of the Mountain, passed those days with great difficulty;
for what person, however dependent on others, would these emotions not disturb, since they affect even that Lord?
This very point, which has now reached its proper occasion, has been reflected upon by us.
Indeed, we are debating this matter with your honors, who possess minds expert in logic and who know the ultimate truth.
Does this Blessed One, who has been cited here, deserve to be described as having the semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) or not?
What is the use of imagining propriety or impropriety?
In every respect, let it remain exactly as it appears to those venerable ones.

Nevertheless, because such a particular state of his mental activity (*cittavṛtti*) is described as the primary element, it does not transcend the status of being the object of poetic ornamentation (*alaṅkāryatā*).

In passages such as "He joins [the bow] twice," nothing other than the excellence of the speaker’s innate mental state— overflowing with enthusiasm— is presented as the primary meaning of the sentence, since the hero is intent on proclaiming his superhuman prowess.
For instance: thinking that even the mere counting of the repetitions of the act of fixing an arrow might cause him to neglect his own natural movement, he asks, "Why does he [Karna] avoid this?

The perception of pride arises from the word "Karṇa" (the primary sense being augmented by the crookedness of the person). This is the intended meaning of the vocative address "Śalya," which possesses a variety of conventional nuances.

From the context, it is understood that the phrase "for the sake of Pārtha" refers to some general enemy who possesses a different form or character, and for whose sake one might perhaps provide the means of another assistant capable of counteracting him;
thus, [the word] "arrived" (āgata) refers to that specific object.

Even another person, having come of his own accord for the sake of a man's purpose, was rejected through effort and pride; thus, from the context, the perception of an excellence of pride is understood.
This very example is powerful.

Thus, this particular state of mental activity, characterized by a preeminent consciousness and distinguished by an excellence brought about by the primary sentient principle, is primarily described as the very nature of the thing itself; therefore, it is that which is to be adorned (*alaṅkārya*), not the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) itself. This has been stated: "The description of a thing as beautiful through its own noble movement is *vakratā* (poetic curvature), because it is the exclusive domain of figurative language."

Thus, because these are specific modifications of the mind (*cittavṛtti*), it is possible for *rasas*, *bhāvas*, and their semblances (*tadābhāsa*) to be included within one or another [of the poetic figures] according to their respective fitness by virtue of the speaker's intention; therefore, it is logical that they are indeed the objects of embellishment (*alaṅkārya*),
and not themselves the state of being an embellishment (*alaṅkāra*).
Therefore, it does not escape being subject to the same refutations as those stated regarding [the verse beginning with] *rasavad-ādi*.
Consequently, everything said in that regard should be applied here in its entirety.

Similarly, another example—*apakartāhamasmi* (I am an offender)—is understood to have its meaning already established, as it is essentially equal in status and security (*samānayogakṣema*) to this very same principle.
Thus, it is logical that both types of *udātta* are themselves the objects of embellishment (*alaṅkārya*) and not the embellishment (*alaṅkaraṇa*) itself.
Regarding the first of these, the very definition-statement has a difficult-to-grasp application:
"The *udātta* is a subject matter (*vastu*) characterized by prosperity (*ṛddhimat*). (VjivC 3.55a)
Thus:
here, whatever object [is mentioned] is the *udātta*;
when there is an expectation as to what kind of ornament it is, if it is qualified by the term "possessing prosperity" (*ṛddhimat*), then that very [object] is endowed with excellence (*saṃpad*).

Since the very object being described is that which is to be adorned, it cannot itself be the ornament; for this is unavoidable as it constitutes the fault of a contradiction in self-action (*svātmani kriyāvirodha*).
Furthermore, because no other distinct entity apart from its own nature appears, the status of being an ornament is untenable even in the case of the *ūrjasvin* and *udātta* figures.

Alternatively, even if an explanation is made that "the object possessing supernatural power (ṛddhimat) belongs to whomsoever" [in a given context], nevertheless, that object which is characterized as a distinct syntactical meaning (anyapadārtha) and brought forth as the sense of the compound must still be stated. If it is argued that such an object will simply be the poem itself, that too is of no consequence.
For it is well known that "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) refers to something belonging to poetry, and not that poetry itself is the ornament.

Or, if this "ornament" is understood through the sense of a compound as "that in which there is a magnificent object," or "that which belongs to [the poem]," even so, the ornament is something distinct from the subject of description; there is nothing here that is merely a semblance of an ornament.
In either case, the fault characterized by the incoherence of word and meaning arises as an unavoidable consequence.
Furthermore, if the *udātta* (the sublime) were indeed an ornament (*alaṅkāra*),

then because another ornament would be prescribed [in its place], the designation of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) or *saṃkara* (combination)— which is based on dependence upon that [other ornament]— would not be established in the other case.

Since there would be the undesirable consequence that, just as in the case of *rūpaka* and other figures, another subject of description that is contrary to it— namely, one devoid of prosperity— would also be considered an ornament, the status of *udātta* as an ornament cannot be established in any way whatsoever.
Likewise, it follows that the second type of *udātta* is merely something to be ornamented (*alaṅkārya*).
But it is not the nature of an ornament;
for its definition is as follows:
".........and the conduct of the Great-souled Ones."
It has attained the state of being an illustration; it has not become a mere narrative account.
Thus,

let those who know the ultimate reality of the meaning of sentences consider this: whether there exists, in the sentence-meaning under discussion, any positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the mere conventional usage of great beings.

In that regard, according to the former position, because it is not merged therein, even though it is a distinct denotation, its designation as a constituent part (*avayava*)— just like any other category (*padārtha*)— is logical,
as in the case of the hand and so forth in relation to the body; however, it does not possess the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) at all.

In the second case, because there is no connection with that [meaning], its very existence there is impossible—just like the meaning of words occurring in another sentence—and thus there is no further discussion regarding it as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
But surely, even for ornaments such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the like, there is a connection with that [meaning];
therefore, since they too would be connected with it, their status as ornaments would cease to exist.
This is true; however, that which is associated with it is twofold,
by virtue of being a subordinate factor to the intended meaning of the context, like another degree of deficiency.
And it is merely by way of producing its own embellishment, like another ornament.
In that regard, the former position is indeed rightly stated;
for if the mere act of causing its disfigurement constitutes faults in the conduct of a Great Being, then these faults are certainly not difficult to avoid.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that another poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), which functions in opposition to it, would also be considered a [primary] poetic figure.

Furthermore, when other poetic figures are present, it would be fit to be designated as "blending" (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) or "commingling" (*saṃkara*) based on its dependence upon them; and it would function even in other domains, just like other poetic figures.
Even that which was established by former masters here, preceded by a display of great regard due to their addiction to composing examples of perfect propriety,

does not attain even the slightest fitness for those who possess the state of a connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*), precisely because its function is dependent solely upon the intended meaning under discussion.
Just as [the threads] are led away, separated, and pulled apart, so too is there a severance until the attainment of the final state. // VjivC_3.56 //

With their ears ringing from the caves of Mount Mahendra, those dark [mountains], equipped with chisels, have not been traversed by your fame— which, like a single path for the discharge of arrows from the crown of Śiva’s head, dwells there— just as inaccessible fortresses are not entered by the light of the moon.

(Here, the subject matter previously and subsequently described— the characteristics of a Great Man's life— is undermined by the intended meaning of the current sentence, which is reinforced by the figure of *vyatireka* [contrast].)
But it is not merely for the sake of its ornamentation.

Thus, the intended meaning here is this: when a task has been undertaken with unremitting zeal by a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) such as Lakṣmaṇa—having set aside all other wandering activities and having taken the matter into his own hands—it cannot be accomplished by anyone else, apart from another person whose conduct exceeds that [of the first].
"Even though it functions without commonality, it shines forth;
therefore, even in those regions where such great beings have passed away, your supreme majesty is able to prevail and spread.
Thus, it is logical that even one who is thus composed remains only the object of adornment, and not the state of being an ornament itself."
Thus he says: "Even for one who is thus composed.

"In that same way" means by that very manner previously described; the meaning is that for the figure of speech called *samāhita*, there is no "ornamentality"—that is, it possesses no quality of being an ornament. For its definition is as follows:
That which consists of the cessation of aesthetic flavor (rasa), emotion (bhāva), and their semblances, whose sequence is unperceived,
and whose nature is devoid of any other experienced objects— that is *samādhi*.
It is a particular state of the aesthetic moods (*rasa*), the transitory emotions (*bhāva*), and their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), which is the object of the designation "subsidence" (*praśama*).

It is devoid of the waves of the entry of subsequent moods; its fluctuations have come to rest through the cessation of the operation of its own manifestors. Because it is completed by its initial impulses and because it is not manifested from a subsequent collection [of parts], its sequence is imperceptible, and its specific configuration resembles the time of twilight (*sandhyā*).
Even by great poets, its function (*vṛtti*) can only with difficulty be inferred; it is charming by its very nature and possesses a composed ornamentation.
Thus:
The redness in your eyes, turbid with clear tears, has dissolved; the frown, along with the quivering of your lower lip, has subsided.
Although anger remains upon your cheeks, it does not find scope to spread because its latent impression has been weakened by this change of state.
Even that is not correctly established (*saṃpatsamāhita*),
because there is a desire for the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that which exists as a particularity of flavor (*rasa*) and so forth.

And since those [flavors] are particularities of mental modification (*cittavṛtti*), how could that [desire for the essential nature] be possible, given that even what is prohibited is of the same form as them when they serve as ornaments?

Furthermore, because it possesses the nature of a primary consciousness, the objective reality—which is of a different kind [than that consciousness] and constitutes its describable essence—is incapable of enduring an innate manifestor. Due to its very nature of being transparent (*svaccha-svabhāvatva*), its capacity to tolerate contact with other distinct entities cannot be justified in any way whatsoever; thus, no entity other than its own essential nature ever appears, and so forth.
This is unavoidable according to the circumstances.
Furthermore, as for that which has been described by some under another heading as "ornamentation called *samāhita*," its status as an ornament likewise does not exist;
he states this as follows:
“Likewise, even for one who is thus concentrated, [the body] is adorned with two aspects. // VjivC_3.60 //
In these two ways—namely, by the manner previously described and by this other one—the state of being an ornament for one who is radiant and composed is not possible.
Accordingly, its definition and illustration are as follows:
"When someone, having begun some task, [finds] that task again [frustrated] by the power of fate..."
The meditative attainment that accomplishes that [state] is what they call "concentrated" (samāhita).
Thus [he spoke]. This sentence is clear in its meaning:
"He will fall at my feet to refute her authority."
By good fortune, this thundering of the clouds has arisen for the sake of benefiting others.
Let it be that what is stated here— namely, that the primary support for each preceding subject is established in the subsequent one—
is not prevented by anyone from being designated by the term "samāhita" (established).

Furthermore, since both [the cloud and the elephant] possess aesthetic flavor (*sarasatva*) and there is an absence of a primary-subordinate relationship between them, nothing [of the nature of a figure of speech] is established.

Since for both, being a property of the object (*vastudharma*) is equally what is to be described, there will be a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on the cognition "it is as if the deep thundering has arisen" (referring to *ghanagarjitam udīrṇam iva*). Enough of this digression.
Thus, the essential nature of an object—distinguished by the categories of sentient and insentient entities, and naturally charming through its inherent delicacy—has been explained.
Now, that very same nature is considered as it is brought to a state of loveliness when fashioned anew by the extraordinary excellence depicted through the poet’s imagination.
Apart from the superlative beauty produced by the arrangement of such ornaments, the mere fact of being an object of adornment is not the cause of the delight experienced by those who know.
That which is a well-known property of an object, yet does not serve as a basis for poetic embellishment— such a thing, being unfit for description, is thus employed by the foremost of poets.
And as he shines forth with qualities whose functions are marked by the excellence of the supramundane, his state of being new is established.
These are the intermediate verses.
Thus, the ornaments (alaṅkāras) belong to the nature of the poetic meaning (*kāvyārtha*), which produces a novel excellence;
therefore, he now begins with them.

There are two modes of expression: one of these clarifies the [meaning] itself, while the other, existing as a subordinate element, illuminates the aesthetic charm (*vichchitti*) of the poetry. (Vjiv 3.14)
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the designation" (*abhidhāyā*) and so forth:
certain figures of speech, such as *rasavat* and others, when present in a subordinate part, bring about an excellence of beauty for that which is to be adorned;
others, being established as the primary element, manifest their own status as ornaments by illuminating its principal nature—this we shall illustrate through examples.

Now, having analyzed this very point, he investigates it further: "Just as that which is called 'flavor' (rasa) is the life-force of all ornaments, how is it now investigated that it constitutes the sole essence of poetry? (Vjiv 3.15).

"Yathā" and so forth: "Just as that [figure] called *rasavat*"— that is, "in whatever manner," "that" [figure], namely the previously mentioned *alaṅkāra* named *rasavat*, "attains the status of the sole essence of poetry," meaning it becomes the very soul of the poet's craft.

"Life of all ornaments"— it becomes the "life," that is, the animating essence, of all ornaments such as simile (*upamā*) and the rest; "in that manner"— by that method— "now"— at this time— "is investigated"— is analyzed,
being expanded out through the distinction between definitions and examples.
He defines that very figure of speech, *rasavat*, as follows:

The figure of speech which exists equally with rasa (sentiment), by virtue of its being established as possessing rasa, is called *rasavat*, because it is produced for the sake of delighting those who know it. (Vjiv 3.16)
"By means of rasa," and so forth.
That which is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is called *rasavat*.
Indeed, that which possesses such a nature, such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the like, is designated as *rasavat*.
What is its intrinsic nature?
It "functions similarly to rasa"—it functions similarly to *rasa*, such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth; it abides in equality with it.
Just as a Kṣatriya functions similarly to a Brāhmaṇa, that is, like a Brāhmaṇa, so too does this ornament function like *rasa*.

Why? "Because of the prescription of possessing rasa"—that which has *rasa* is *rasavat*, namely poetry; its state or essence is *tattva*; because of the prescription of that—that is, by means of producing aesthetic flavor (*sarasatva*).
(Why so? "Because it produces delight for those who know it"—those who know it (*tadvidaḥ*) are those who understand that [poetry];
because it produces their delight, that is, because it generates joy.

Just as *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) bestows both the state of possessing flavor upon poetry and the delight of those who know it, so too a figure such as simile (*upamā*), by accomplishing both, becomes a "flavorful" (*rasavat*) figure of speech.
Just as the moon seized the face of night with its rising passion, causing its pupils to tremble, so too did she,
out of passion, fail to notice that her entire garment of darkness had slipped away even before her.
In this context, the primary essence of the sentence-meaning consists of the night and the moon, whose delicate natures are appropriate to their own occasion and are thus the subjects of description.
Because they possess such loveliness, the poet has composed a metaphorical ornament (*rūpaka*) that superimposes the conduct of a lover upon them.

And this ornament shines forth all the more intensely due to the power of the specific gender and the striking nature of the adjectives, which are rendered charming by the shadow of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Bringing forth the aesthetic flavor of poetry and bestowing delight upon those who know it, [this figure] has itself attained the status of the *rasavat* ornament.

Just as the capacity to convey the essential nature [of an object] exists even without the use of words such as "beloved of a playful woman," we shall clarify this further during our discussion of *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) metaphor.
Furthermore, the previously mentioned objections (such as *saṃsṛṣṭi* and *saṃkara*) are unable to prevail here;
for it has been refuted by this very example, because [the principle] is observed in other instances, as stated in the phrase "and likewise because it is seen elsewhere."

"Because nothing other than its own nature appears,"— thus, regarding the non-distinction between the object of embellishment (*alaṅkārya*) and the embellishment (*alaṅkaraṇa*), the impossibility of that very thing being the embellishment due to the contradiction of an action directed toward itself when it is the object of embellishment has been refuted by further examples,
as follows:
You repeatedly touch her trembling glance with its flickering corners; you whisper softly into the vicinity of her ear as if revealing a secret;

and you drink the very essence of love from the lower lip of her who waves her hand away. O bee, we are ruined by our search for the truth, while you, indeed, are the one who has achieved his purpose.

The ultimate meaning here is as follows: because it bestows an excellence of beauty, the *rasavad-alaṅkāra*—in which the primary sentiment (*bhāva*) of love (*śṛṅgāra*) is [enhanced] by the superimposition of the behavior of a lover onto the bee—is a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Or, for example:
A row of leaf-designs on the cheek.
In such passages as these,
by this same principle,
[the verse] "kṣipto hastāvalagna" (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.68) [is explained].
In this regard, the rejection of the *rasavat* ornament is improper.
This is true;
however, [it concerns] the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment of separation).
That [objection] is refuted there;
however, since the remainder shares an identical status, its nature as the *rasavat* ornament cannot be denied.
Nor can the consequence of designating it as *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) or *saṃkara* (blending)—based on the requirement for *rasavat* when another ornament is present—be dismissed.
As if grasping the mass of darkness with its rays like fingers gathering a tangle of hair,
the moon kisses the face of night, whose lotus-eyes are beautifully opened.

Here, the convergence of the *rasavad* ornament with metaphors (*rūpaka*) and other figures shines forth most brilliantly. In this regard, the composition of the *rasavad* ornament— characterized by poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) in the phrase "the moon, as it were, kisses the face of night"— is primarily established,
while similes (*upamā*) and the like function as its subordinate elements.

Because the intended excellence of the *kevala* [figure] alone was not fully realized due to the lack of nourishment from the *prastutatarasa* (the relevant sentiment), [the verse reads]: "Autumn, bearing a rainbow upon her pale cloud-breasts that resembled fresh nail-marks, while pleasing the spotted moon, increased the heat of the sun even further. (VjivC 3.70)
Thus,

here the nature of the object, which arises from convention (*samaya*), is perceived even without the employment of words such as "iva" that express it; this is the figure of speech *rasavat*, characterized by poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), which the poet has endowed with a certain loveliness through the composition of words like "sakalaṅka," which, though possessing other meanings, are captivating to the mind.

Because it is arranged in such a way as to be consistent with both the pun (*śleṣa*) and the simile (*upamā*), namely: "bearing the rainbow of Indra, which has the luster of fresh nail-marks upon her pale breasts.

Thus, the manner in which she, while pleasing [him] despite his being stained [with guilt], caused excessive torment to another, is based on the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor); for this superimposition of the manifest conduct of a woman attains a most perfect coherence.

Here too, the connection is exactly as before: the *rasavat* ornament, which functions through suggestion (*pratīyamāna-vṛtti*), holds primacy, while the similes (*upamā*) and other figures serve as its subordinates.

Even in cases where the figures of speech act like the first manifestation of a charming emotion such as love (*rati*), the same principle of integration should be inferred by the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*) for himself.
Just as the Goddess of Spring, having applied a tilaka mark upon her face variegated with the black pigment of bees clinging to it,
adorned her lips— which were like young sprouts— with a passion as tender as the rising sun.

Here, because the figure of speech *rūpaka*— which involves the superimposition of the heroine's circumstances and is aided by the shadow of *śleṣa* (paronomasia)— is employed in such a manner, it constitutes the *rasavad-alaṅkāra*.
Furthermore, even that collection of objects which is for the most part devoid of rasa attains a state of aesthetic flavor (*sarasatā*) solely through this [figure].
As in the phrase:
"the curved [rays] of the young moon."
Thus,

in this way, this [poetic suggestion], which constitutes the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of all poetry, while effecting a certain manifestation of poetic figures— which are otherwise like mere wood or a wall— attains the status of being the cause for producing aesthetic wonder in sentient beings.
This is that which is called "flavor" (rasa), the foremost of all ornaments;
it shines like a crest-jewel, being the sole cause for the excellence of the body.
Today, the entire treasure of the poet’s skill has been clearly unveiled;
it shall now come within the range of the discernment of the wise.
These are two intermediate verses.
Thus, in order to cause the emergence of flavor (*rasa*) in insipid objects, he has employed the *rasavat* ornament.
Now, he begins with the *dīpaka* ornament to illuminate some particular excellence in things that exist merely in their own essential form.

And this has been designated by the ancient masters as *ādidīpaka* (illumination at the beginning), *madhyadīpaka* (illumination in the middle), and *antadīpaka* (illumination at the end), based on the position of the illuminating word at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence;
for it is the verb itself that illuminates, and thus it is called the ornament named *dīpaka*. For example:
Intoxication produces pleasure, which brings forth the bodiless god of love who shatters one's pride;
that [love] gives rise to longing for union with the beloved and an unbearable anguish of the mind.
Spring adorns the women who wear garlands and fine garments,
as well as the foothills of the mountains with the songs of green pigeons and parrots.
The forest regions abounding in crickets, the rivers whose waters are drying up,
and the minds of travelers— all these the heat of summer seeks to bring to their end.

In this context, the "illuminating nature" (*dīpakatva*) of verbs means their quality of being illuminators; for by means of these verbs alone, [other elements] are illuminated—that is, they are made known as being connected to them.

Thus, since every single verb—even those distinct from an [explicitly stated] *dīpaka*—possesses this same uniform character, it follows that there would be a monism of *dīpaka* (i.e., all verbs would be *dīpaka*).
Furthermore, if that which produces an excellence of beauty were devoid of logical justification, its status as an ornament would be untenable.
Moreover, let alone the question of action;
rather, it is simply the inherent nature of whatever element within a sentence to illuminate another word by virtue of its relationship to it.

Since the nature of the meaning of a sentence is based on the connection through mutual syntactic relation (*parasparānvaya-sambandha*), the manifold variety of the *dīpaka* (the "lamp" figure) arises once again.
[If it is argued that] a verb situated at the beginning, middle, or end attains excellence by which it achieves the status of an ornament—[then we ask:
what such a distinct difference (*svarūpātireka*) or specific quality exists among those sentences and so forth?

The division of sentences based on the variety of verbal forms (*kriyāpada*)—namely, their beginning, middle, and end—is possible even in cases such as *arthadīpaka* (illustrative by implication); thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of varieties of *dīpaka*.

Furthermore, the designation "poetry" (*kāvyatva*) applies only when the verbal form occurring within a sentence governed by the *dīpaka* ornament belongs to a class other than the root *bhū* (i.e., it possesses meaning).
Alternatively, if *dīpaka* is defined as a single verbal form that illuminates many factors of action (*kāraka*) sharing the same case-ending, [the same over-extension follows].
In that case as well, it must certainly be stated what the basis is for producing an excellence of poetic luster.

The most learned authorities have already established that it is nothing other than the similarity of the suggested function (pratīyamānavṛtti) attained through the power of the subject matter, whether primary or secondary.
For example:

They know that as *dīpaka* (illuminator) where the objects at the beginning, middle, and end are connected to both the primary and the secondary, and where the qualities of comparison are included within them.
And it has been stated in another work:

"Just as lordly elephants roam about, their hearts captivated by the scent carried from every direction, so too do poets wander through the forest of suffering on the great and uneven path of poetic expression. (VjivC 3.79)
The lords of elephants, their hearts captivated by the scent of rut from the world-guarding elephants, pace restlessly;
likewise, poets find hardship in the forest of the great poet’s path, which is treacherous with its verbal expressions.
Thus is the shadow (chāyā).

Herein, the very nature of poetic beauty— which brings delight to the hearts of the sensitive (sahṛdaya) and which shines forth through a similarity attained by the power of both the contextual and the non-contextual subject— is what constitutes [the essence].
Furthermore, the verbal action (*kriyāpada*) is invariably concomitant with the sentence, being established just like another sentence or like other words within this very same sentence;
this is the meaning of the sentence here.

Just as lordly elephants, whose minds are delighted by the scent of rut from the elephants of the quarters, wander with great difficulty through the forest, so too do poets on the path of the great poets—which is rugged with verbal expression and variegated with *vakrokti* (oblique speech); this is the meaning of the word "iti" (*ca*).
For they, being full of self-conceit and desiring to proceed with a movement that transcends that [path], describe it only with great effort; such is the intended sense.
Therefore, this ornament, whose sole life is similarity (*sāmya*), is captivating because it is suggested; it is a distinct variety [of simile].
For wherever a threefold suggested similarity of function (*pratīyamāna-vṛtti-sāmya*) shines forth, this very principle should be applied.
As for the remainder, it is merely a matter of report, as follows:
The sun has set, the moon shines, and the birds go to their nests.
Thus [it was said].
Now, employing this "lamp" (*dīpaka*) as a distinct poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), the author proceeds in another manner to fashion a certain loveliness of poetry:
"That which brings about propriety, is unfading, and is a cause of delight for those who know it..."
That which illuminates a thing that is incapable of illuminating itself, while serving as the basis for the manifestation of meanings and dharmas, is a "lamp" (dīpaka).
"Appropriate," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "The *vastu* (the thing) becomes the *dīpaka* (the illuminator); that is, the *vastu*, which is established in its own form, becomes the ornament (*alaṅkāra*)."

Because no other action is heard of [in that context], it follows that anything whatsoever exists; thus he says: "It becomes an ornament by illuminating," that is, by making manifest. He specifies what illuminates what: "Dharma," which is a particular kind of motion (*parispanda*).
"Of objects" (*arthānām*) means "of those things to be described.
Of what nature is it?— "Incapable" (*aśaktam*), meaning unmanifest,
because it is manifested by that very [consciousness].
And of what nature is it? "Bringing about propriety" (*aucityāvahaṃ*) means that which brings about propriety, which is to say, magnificence; thus it is so described.
Furthermore, of what kind is it? "Unfading" (*amlānaṃ*), meaning fresh, that is to say, untouched by weariness.
Because its nature is such, it is "the cause of delight for those who know it" (*tadvidāhlādakāraṇaṃ*), meaning the source of bliss for those who understand poetry.
He describes other modes of this very [perception]:
"In some cases, there is a single illuminator for many [objects], or there are many [illuminators] for many [objects]."
It is observed to be of two kinds: either solitary or arranged in a row.
"One" means:
"is seen to be twofold" (*dvividhaṃ paridṛśyate*) = it is observed to be of two kinds; it is discerned in the object of focus (*lakṣye*).
How so? "Solely" (*kevalaṃ*) = without a companion.
“Or situated in a series”: that which is established in a sequence, existing within a similar category formed by other accompanying elements.
How so? “One” (usually):
among many objects, one that is a “revealer” (*prakāśaka*) or illuminator is called *kevala* (the solitary).
Or just as one [perceives] saṃsāra to be without essence.
And so forth.

Here, the author, "resolved to establish" [the truth], has attained the status of the *dīpaka* (illuminator) ornament by illuminating the qualities of the world and so forth, such as their lack of substantiality.
[This is] arranged in a sequence (*paṅktisaṃstha*).
“*Bhūyāṃsi*” means many illuminating objects; “*bhūyasām*” means of many subjects to be described; “*santi vā kvacit*” means they exist or are found in some particular instance.
For example:
“The lion is the enemy of elephants, the moonstone is the enemy of pearls, and the peacock is the enemy of serpents.”

The second [type] is that which "illuminates another illuminator" (*dīpakaṃ dīpayaty anyat tad anyat*); that is, when one thing serves as an illuminator by producing excellence in another.

Thus, this is an ornament (founded upon the artfulness of the first half of the word).

Since the characteristics of a metaphor—whether it resides in a single part or in multiple parts—are observed to be identical to those of the *dīpaka* (the illuminator), its composition follows immediately after that [figure].

By the power of their creative intuition (*pratibhā*), they lead a certain metaphor (*rūpaka*) toward the secret state of being indirect (*vakrabhāva*), aided by the delineation of other figures of speech.

This very ornament, called *rūpaka* (metaphor), poets "lead" (*nayanti*)— that is, they bring to light— a certain "mystery of crookedness" (*vakrabhāvarahasyatā*), which is a transcendental state of ultimate crookedness (*vakratvaparamārthatā*).
In that regard, the supreme essence of beauty, which has ascended to a distinct charm through the crookedness of its composition, appears most vividly.

Of what nature is it? "Assisted by the manifestation of another figure of speech"— the "manifestation" (*ullekha*) of "another figure of speech," that is, of another [figure] such as *sasandeha* (poetic doubt), *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), and so forth, [is present] therein.
"Accompanied by" means that which has an assistant in the production of poetic beauty.
Why do they lead [the poet]? "By the power of intuition"—because it is dependent upon one's own innate capacity.
Thus, the composition of such a subject matter, which falls within the domain of a splendor transcending the world, is undertaken.
Where, due to the absence of such established usage, the introduction of a conventional term might appear like a rash act,
a supreme maturity arises— beautiful through its resonance with the hearts of the sensitive (sahr̥daya)— because it is being enjoined as a restatement aided by another ornament.
For example:
Like the slough cast off by the serpent of the sky, or like the playful forehead-ornament of the King of the Triple Heaven.

Thus, the intention here regarding the manifestation of the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*) is as follows: because the object of description is praised for its extraordinary excellence of beauty, it is impossible to express it by any other means; and even by such a stroke of the figure of speech known as metaphor (*rūpaka*), it is not appropriate to employ it with stability, precisely because such a thing is not well-known in that way.
Therefore, for us, this very nature of the object to be described appears as such; thus, the definition of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) has been cited here as an auxiliary figure of speech.

In its composition as a pure [figure], it is accompanied by the ornament of *saṃdehālaṅkāra* (the figure of doubt) through the poetic charm (*vicchitti*) expressed in the thought: "Because of my being startled, my mind doubts whether this might be such a thing or not.

Having thus examined the metaphor (*rūpaka*), he introduces the *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), which consists in the expression of a similarity with something else: "Even though it is not the subject at hand, when an object—whether the meaning of a word or the meaning of a sentence—introduces a striking beauty (*vicchitti*) pertaining to the subject at hand, it attains the status of being the object of description. (Vjiv 3.25)
Where, based on that similarity or indeed upon another relationship, this figure of speech called Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Unrelated) is described, [that is the definition]. (Vjiv 3.26)
"Aprastuta," and so forth.
"It is called *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise)"—this ornament has been designated by that name by those who know the ornaments. It is an ornament known as *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.

Of what kind [is it]?—“In which” (*yatra*), that is, in which [poem], even a thing not under discussion (*aprastuta*)—that is, one not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*)—“attains the state of being described”—becomes an object of description.
What does it do? “Bringing down,” that is, manifesting, “the charm” (*vicchitti*)—the embellishment—“of the subject matter” (*prastuta*), that is, of the intended meaning.
For there exist two kinds of entities that constitute reality:

first, an object established by the mere word contained within a sentence; and second, an effect pervading the entire sentence, which exists as the primary element characterized by a preeminent excellence of various internal movements. Keeping both these forms of the subject at hand as the intended meaning (pratīyamāna), poets describe another, unintended category of objects in this poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) for the sake of achieving its distinctive charm.
They bring about [the result].

Having done what? "Having resorted to that similarity"—"that" refers to the similarity just mentioned, which assists the figure of speech *rūpaka*; "similarity" (*sāmya*) means equality, having resorted to it—that is, having made it the causal basis.
"Or indeed another relation"— that is, "another relation," namely, by relying on a different [relation] such as the state of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) and so forth;
"the sentence-meaning"— [which is] unreal (*asatya*).

Or [it is that] which, by relying on similarity (*sāmya*) or another relation (*saṃbandha*), leads the unmentioned subject to a state of being described for the sake of enhancing the mentioned subject— this being an effect produced by a sentence characterized as a collection of mutually connected words.
Among these, an example of the praise of an unmentioned object contained within a sentence by relying on similarity is as follows:

where the temples of elephants emerge, and where there are other stalks of plantain and fibers of lotus?
Thus,
here, by resorting to the principle of similarity (*sāmya*), the primary object intended by the poet is perceived through the *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) contained within the sentence.

"That which ought to be expressed by one sentence is conveyed by another;
that by which the completion of the poetic embellishment (*upaśobhā*) is achieved is called *paryāyokta*. (Vjiv 3.27)
Regarding the passage beginning with *yadvākyāntara* and so forth: “*paryāyoktaṃ taducyate*” means that the ornament named *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is thus defined.

“*yadvākyāntaravaktavyaṃ*” refers to a subject matter (*vastu*) characterized as the meaning of a sentence, which is expressible by another collection of words (*padasamudāya*). “*tadanyena*” means by another sentence (*vākyāntara*); “*samarpyate*” means it is communicated.
For what purpose? “*upaśobhāniṣpattyai*,” that is, for the production of a particular striking effect (*vicchitti*).
"For the sake of attainment";
this means it is expressed by a synonym (*paryāyokta*).
Now, one might ask: since this is merely a synonymic indirectness (*paryāyavakratva*), what is superior about it here?

In *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), only the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is the subject matter as the expressed sense (*vācya*), whereas in *paryāyavakratva* (curvature of synonymy), the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is also included as a subordinate element; therefore, it is described separately.
An example is as follows:

By the very force of his command, delivered through the impact of his discus, he rendered the festival of love for the wives of Rāhu’s kin devoid of the unrestrained dalliance of embracing, leaving only the act of kissing.
Thus:
"Where there is praise by way of being expressed for the sake of the intended subject's censure, yet censure by way of being suggested, that is considered *vyājastuti* (ironic praise). (Vjiv 3.28)
“In which” (*yatra*) means in that [context]; “as the expressed” (*vācyatayā*) means by way of being denoted by words; “censure” (*nindā*) means reproach;
“as the suggested, praise” (*vyaṅgyatayā stutiḥ*) means commendation by way of being implied; “for the sake of the charm of the subject matter” (*prastutasya vicchittyai*) means for its beauty.
Thus, this two-fold figure of speech known as "vyājastuti" (feigned praise) is considered [by the ancients].
For example:
"The Lord Hari himself remains awake; he prepares with the multitude of Śeṣa’s heads to bear the burden of the earth, for the sake of the world's stability."
O King, even now, while you have extended such incomparable pride in this matter, not even a single moment’s rest has been granted to those two; what kind of sequence is this?
Or as the mark on the moon. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra 3.102)
And so forth.
In the case of the opposite, this very same [method] is prescribed as an ornament for that which is to be adorned,
as follows:
He is the unconquered victor.
And so forth; or as in the case of the name "Antataru. (Vajracchedikā 3.104)
Thus [he said]:
"Or rather, O well of the desert, the day has ended and we have rested by you; a supreme favor has been done for us, such that we are not able to express our anger out of shame."
By virtue of our good deeds, may you remain a river whose waters never dry up for travelers; and may I, in turn, become a *śamī* tree providing shade upon your banks.
Here, the word "praise" (*stuti*), as before, functions through the figure of paradoxical indication (*viparīta-lakṣaṇā*) to denote even censure.

Having thus explained "disguised praise" (*vyājastuti*), [the author] now treats "poetic fancy" (*utprekṣā*) as being on an equal footing with this [figure], because of the commonality of its non-difference from the introduction and conclusion.

Desiring to speak, he says: "By means of a presumptive inference, or by similarity, or by both, with the wish to demonstrate the excellence of the preeminent qualities of the object under description. (Vjiv 3.29)

Just as [words] such as "like that" (tadiva) or "that itself" (tadeva) are understood through their own meanings implied by the capacity of the signified and the signifier, so too [the meaning is grasped] even without a verbal expression. Vjiv_3.30.
The imaginative association of a meaning distinct from the literal sense of the words uttered is called *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), [an ornament] by those who know the essence of poetry. (Vjiv 3.31)
Regarding the passage beginning with *saṃbhāvanā*:

"Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is the joining of a meaning distinct from the directly delineated sentence-meaning."—as for "directly delineated" (*samullikhita*): it means "properly delineated" (*samyagullikhita*), presented as if it were inherent (*svābhāvikatvena*) to the subject.

The "meaning of a sentence" (*vākyārtha*) is the entity denoted by a collection of words; from that, the "joining together" (*yojanam*)— that is, the establishment— of a "distinct meaning," characterized as the intended purport (*tātparya*) of another sentence.
"Utprekṣā"—the ornament called *utprekṣā*.
It is analyzed as "imagination (*utprekṣaṇa*) is *utprekṣā*. By what means? He says: "by inference through probability (*saṃbhāvanānumānena*)," that is, the inference which is based on probability.
The meaning is this:
the "inference" (ūhana) of an object that is being conceived necessarily brings about its status as a distinct entity from [the perceived object], because one observes an effect identical to it.
He states "by way of similarity" to show that this [inference] is also possible through another mode.
"By similarity"—even by the cause of resemblance—“the joining of a meaning distinct from the expressed sentence-meaning” is indeed *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
Two kinds of similarity are possible: real and imaginary.
Among these, the real pertains to the domain of *upamā* (simile) and other such figures.
In this context, the conceptual [similarity] is relied upon, because the discussion concerns that which possesses excellence,
and because similarity is invariably concomitant with being based on both [the object and its counterpart].

Since no other category of entity apart from those under discussion is possible, and since that [entity]— if it were a property (dharma)— would necessarily be dependent on something else, its existence as a solitary entity is untenable; therefore, some other substrate for it must be postulated.

As for that [other entity], the question "what is it? remains unanswered, resulting in a lack of definitive proof. Even if one were to postulate some single [entity], it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of a connection with qualities (*guṇasamanvaya*) and because it cannot be apprehended, the wise hold that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), postulate another real substratum (*dharmin*) as the basis for similarity.
Therefore, it is clear that [the definition] refers to "by way of similarity with such a subject.

In some cases, even by means of an unreal (avāstava) bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), he sets forth another variety of this [figure] as described above: "Or by both"—that is, by the conjunction of two causes characterized by both probability (*saṃbhāvanā*) and inference (*anumāna*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*), the application of another object distinct from the subject at hand is *utprekṣā*.

He states by what intention these three types were composed: "With the desire to demonstrate the heightening of excellence through description"—that is, with the longing to convey the attainment of the highest limit of the subject's preeminence.
How so? "By means of two modes: 'as that' (tadiva) or 'that very thing' (tadeva).
"As that" (tadiva) means as if it were the non-contextual (aprastuta).
The connection of a similarity with the subject at hand is for the purpose of demonstrating its excellence;
"that very thing" means that the non-subject itself is treated as the subject.

The application of another underlying intention (*tātparyāntarayojana*) for the purpose of attaining an ascent through a stream of excellence regarding the subject at hand, preceded by the expansion of its own nature [of the subject] and the superimposition (*samāropa*) of that unmentioned nature upon it.
He states by what means the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is manifested: "by means of 'iva' and so forth"—that is to say, by words such as *iva* when employed according to their respective fitness.

Regarding the term "expressed" (*vācyā*), he sets forth another alternative: "by those same [words] when they are either employed [directly] or function through implication (*pratīyamānavṛtti*), their own meanings being suggested by the power of the relationship between the signifier and the signified."

In this regard, an example of inference based on probability (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*) is as follows: "As if practicing a spell for the bewilderment of kings, the fish-bannered god [Kāma]—with bees that have crept close to his ears out of greed for the floral crest and have whispered secret words—[is at work]. (Vajrāvalī 3.106)
An example of imagined similarity is as follows:
"The loud laughter of Tryambaka, as if accumulating day by day. (VjivC 3.107)
Or as it is said:
"Like the shedding of the slough by a serpent in the sky. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.108)
And so forth.
An example of actual similarity (*vāstava-sādṛśya*) is as follows:
"The hand with its ear-like sprouts, and the eyes with their pupils, are exceedingly restless."
Dwell in the divine play (līlā) of the Hindus; he remains amidst existence and the like.
(Chāyā? An example of both [types] is as follows:
"Thus, the forest is sharp and red, and it resounds with the cries of the ignoble;
nearby, the enemy's army rises, clinging to the mountain peaks, while all the sweet-sounding [birds] have fled. (VjivC 3.110)
(Chāyā? "Tikkhāruṇaṃ tam" means: "ārāt" means from afar; "bheda eva" means piercing itself is the tearing apart; that is the meaning.
For in the world, a sharp object such as an arrow is seen to have a small amount of blood clinging to it when it has torn open a limb.)

Thus, while there exists a resemblance between the attributes of that [object] and the attributes residing in the pair of eyes—namely, the quality of being sharp and red—the attribute of the subject matter (*prastutavastu*) is here conceived as the attribute of the non-subject matter (*aprastutavastu*); therefore, this is a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on the proof of both.
Or, for example:
"The fragrant sighs of the women flash forth during their momentary separation from him."
They have dragged out the heart-seated essence, like the nectar of the flower-arrowed god of love.
In moments of separation, the fragrant sighs of those lovely women waft forth for him like droplets of nectar from the flower-arrows lodged within his drawn-out heart.
Chāyā (Shade/Reflection). Here, an example of actual similarity is as follows:
This beautiful mango creeper, bent by a cluster of blossoming, lovely flowers, was shaken by that deer-eyed woman.
I suspect this is not the threat of Māra, who crushes those separated from their lovers, directed against each flower of his bow.
One should not mistake this for *apahnuti* (concealment), because it prescribes another object that excludes the meaning not explicitly stated (*asūtrita-artha-vyatireki-vastvantara-vidhāna*).
For its primary origin and life-force is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), and not *apahnuti*, which is merely a subordinate element of the latter;
this very point will become manifest immediately hereafter.
Regarding the phrase *tadiva* (like that), the disputants provide the following example:
"In the spring, this Malaya breeze—intoxicated by the breath of the serpents clinging to the sandalwood trees—causes travelers to faint. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.113)
Or as in:
"O Queen, by your lotus-face... (Vajrāvalī 3.114).
And so forth; or as in:
"O timid one, you [were] by a demon" (Vajracchedikā 3.115).
And so forth.
Regarding the phrase "that very [thing]," there is no illustrative example for its expressive function.
For instance—
“Having raised each petal one by one. // VjivC_3.116 //
And so forth.
He begins another method for this [topic]:
"In the same way as the appearance, [it is] appropriate to the cognizer according to the power of his own vibration."
Even though an entity is devoid of action, agency is attributed to it with respect to that action.
"Like the reflected sun," and so forth.

This other variety of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is observed: "in an action"—that is, in that which has the nature of something to be accomplished—"the attribution of agency"—the superimposition of independence.
Of what? "Of an entity"—that is, of an object.
"Even though inactive"—even though devoid of action. Of what nature? "An excellence of its own nature."
It is appropriate and fitting for that [consciousness].
Why? Because "it appears thus to the cognizer" (*boddhuḥ tathā pratibhāsāt*).
"To the cognizer" (*boddhuḥ*) means to the experiencer; "thus" (*tathā*) means in that manner.
"From appearance" (*pratibhāsāt*) means "from cognition.

As it was said previously: "With the desire to demonstrate an excellence that has been observed, by those who speak [of it] as 'it is like that' or 'it is that very thing,' even without an expressive word"—this should be connected here as well.
An example is as follows:
"Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.117)
Or as it is said:
"Her limbs seem to swim in the ocean of her stumbling, stainless loveliness. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.118)
Just as it is said:
The moonlight seems to glide through the sky, to multiply among the night-lotuses, and to reflect upon the surfaces of their cheeks, pale as the stalks of withered reeds;
it seems to blossom in the waters, to laugh in the dwellings white with plaster, to flutter in the sprout-like folds of the banners, and to dance in the wind-swept ripples. (Vajrāvalī 3.119)
Since Daṇḍin has already provided an enumeration here of the words expressive of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), it is not set forth again.
This *utprekṣā* brings forth a certain excellence in the object of description that is beautiful due to its departure from [its ordinary] nature.

This [poetic imagination], which is essentially synonymous with other ornaments (*bhūṣaṇa*) such as *pratibhā*, itself assumes the role of the primary cause for their initial manifestation, since it is upon it that specific aesthetic refinements (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) depend.
It [is the source] of the supreme splendor of the beauty of ornaments such as *apahnuti*.
Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) expands by virtue of being the life-force of the first mental impression.
This is an intermediate verse.
Having thus explained *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), he introduces *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), which finds its occasion in the manifestation of excellence and dissimilarity:
"It is said that *atiśayokti* is the lifeblood of all poetic ornaments."

When some extraordinary excellence of the qualities of the subject being described—which bestows delight upon those who know them—is conveyed through poetic distinction (vicchitti), [it constitutes the figure of speech known as *udātta*]. (Vjiv 3.33)
"It is called *atiśayokti* (hyperbole)"—the poetic ornament known as *atiśayokti* is thus designated.
Of what nature is it? "In which there is an excellence"—an excellence that has reached the highest pitch, something that transcends the path of conventional usage.
"It is presented through strikingness"—it is conveyed by means of a clever artifice.
Of what? "Of the qualities to be described"—that is, of the movements related to the intrinsic nature of the subject matter under discussion.
Of what kind? "Bestowing delight upon those who know it"—that is, producing joy for those who understand poetry.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is simply that the beauty of its own movement brings delight to the connoisseur.

Therefore, those who have shown great regard for the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), which nourishes that excellence— those figures whose nature is such that they possess heightened splendor when thus manifested— bring the ornaments of the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) to the highest state of beauty.

"Being of such a nature, with their splendors thus aroused," all three of them, "with their excellence of beauty fully kindled," "nourish"— that is, they manifest— "supreme *vakratā*," the extraordinary state of *vakrabhāva* which constitutes the secret essence of poetry. For example:
In a house where moonstones have turned it into a cloudy day,
the female crane cries out again like a deceitful messenger with a crooked gait, following the royal swan with her voice while abandoning him, as she is filled with doubt by the moonlight.
Or as it is said:
"Hidden by the moonlight, which moves with the hue of a flower in the sky, the *saptacchada* trees were inferred by the humming of swarms of bees. (VjivC 3.122)
In this case, the excellence of the nature of the entity (*bhāvasvabhāvātiśaya*) has been brought to its highest degree of nourishment.
Or, for example:

"For him whose sun of majesty blazes forth, the excellence [of other luminaries] is rendered useless even upon the moon—the mountain that supports the world and illuminates it—let alone among other radiant beings."
In him, born of a lineage of kings whose glorious deeds were renowned throughout the three worlds, even the sun and moon themselves assumed a diminished luster.
And just as on the ground where the immersion in frosty water has ceased, which has become stainless by the touch of the morning sun,
there arises some indescribable sprouting of limbs, their bodily color dispelled by the rays of the sun.
In this case, in the former instance, there is the excellence of the full development of the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor);
likewise, in both the first and the other [latter] instances, there is the nourishment of the figure of speech *rasavad-alaṅkāra* (the sentiment-filled).

And thus, by superimposing the activities of a beautiful woman—such as bathing in water and so forth—upon her who has her stains washed away by the cleansing of cool water, whose garment is covered by fresh sunlight, and whose stainless nature is made manifest, [there arises] something indescribable...
Tenderness has been bestowed [upon her],
as it is said:
"The new risings of the Lord of Herbs (the Moon) can be used for the purpose of fashioning an ear-ornament for you."
Their hands, tender as young grass-blades and lacking boldness, were unable to cut [the lotus stalks] even with the hollows of their fingertips.

Here, the extraordinary beauty of the vibration of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) shines forth. Thus, a certain unique excellence now unfolds in the rays of the moon at their fresh rising, which have displayed such tenderness, that they most fittingly deserve the artful arrangement of an ear-ornament (*karṇapūra*), praiseworthy for its contact with the cheeks and the curls at the ears.

The Lord of Pārvatī, as he presents [the mirror] to his beloved, is perceived as one whose mental state is stirred by aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*) through the sight of the beauty of her moon-like face and the sight of the rays of the moon risen at that very moment. Thus, the primary subject matter, which is the object of adornment, is established as a subordinate element (*aṅga*).

Even this class of ornaments (*alaṅkāravarga*), when composed as having a somewhat extended scope, manifests with an intensified state due to the greatness of its delicate arrangement; thus, although it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), it attains, as it were, primacy, and appearing as predominant through the power of its composition, it has been explained.
Now, he examines the artistic arrangement (*vinyāsavicchitti*) of the class of ornaments that shine forth through similarity (*sāmya*):
In order to establish the captivating nature of the intended movement of a thing, its similarity to something else possessing superior excellence is *upamā* (simile). (Vjiv 3.35)

Where, through the mention of a common attribute, or within the meaning of a sentence due to its connection with that [attribute], a word such as *iva* also expresses a verbal action by way of poetic charm (*vicchitti*), [that is a simile]. (Vjiv 3.36)
Regarding the phrase beginning with "vivakṣitā" (intended to be expressed): "yatra" means in which; "vastunaḥ" refers to the subject matter under discussion;
"kenacit" means by some other object that is irrelevant to the context.

"Similarity" (*sāmyam*)—that is, comparison—is called the figure of speech *upamā*. To the question, "For what purpose is there similarity with something irrelevant? he says: "In order to establish the captivating quality of the intended movement. "Intended" (*vivakṣitaḥ*) refers to that which is meant to be spoken; "movement" (*parispandaḥ*) refers to some particular attribute (*dharmaviśeṣa*). Its "captivating quality" (*manohāritvam*) is its power to gladden the heart.
"His accomplishment" (siddhiḥ)—meaning his perfection—is for that purpose.
By what kind of other object? "By one possessing its excellence"; here, the word "its" (tat) refers back to "captivating beauty."
"Excellence" (*utkarṣaḥ*) means pre-eminence (*atiśayaḥ*);
he who possesses that is so described, [meaning] "by him who possesses that excellence."
Because it possesses an excellence of captivating charm.

The intended meaning here is this: for the sake of establishing the beauty of the intended attribute (*dharma*) of the subject under description (*varṇanīya*), a similarity with an irrelevant object (*aprastuta*) as the possessor of that attribute (*dharmī*) deserves to be logically consistent.
It was not stated [in the definition] "by means of an attribute" (*dharmeṇa*).
Because that [similarity] cannot exist in isolation,

it follows that this collection of similarities (*sāmyasamuccaya*) results effectively in a comparison between two subjects characterized as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*).
He states that such a simile is established by the term "action-word" (*kriyāpada*), and so forth:
"Action" (*kriyā*) refers to the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*). [By the word "action-word"]...

What is intended here is the mere general category of denotative words (*vācaka-sāmānya*), and not exclusively the verbal form (*ākhyāta-pada*). For even where an action exists only in a secondary sense, that too is indeed a denotative word for comparison.

Thus, in the case of *pācakaḥ* ("cook"), the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—namely, the capacity for cooking—does indeed exist there as its primary function, though it is subsumed within the derivative form.
As in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*) and "a cook" (*pācaka*),
so too here in "he cooks," although the action (*kriyā*) is predominant, the meaning of the *kāraka* (participant) is also internally contained.
Thus, this [speech-sound]— this very thing— which vibrates in accordance with both forms and is the pulsation of the verbal form— [is that which is referred to by the pronoun] "that."
"Speaks"—that is, expresses.
How? "By means of charm"—by way of the excellence of ingenuity.
The sense is that it is impossible for an expression to delight those who know [the art] if it is devoid of charm.
A verbal suffix does not express that [similarity] alone; rather, even particles such as "iva" (and so forth), any specific word endowed with the capacity to convey it,
and compounds such as the *bahuvrīhi* do so as well.
The suffixes such as *vati* and others also express that [likeness] through a particular poetic figure (*vicchitti*).
The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Under what condition?

Regarding the phrase "in the statement of a common property" (*sādhāraṇadharmoktau*): "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) means identical—that property which follows both of those two, namely the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*).

When such a property is stated, there is a simile (*upamā*) consisting of a noun (*subanta*) [functioning] as the agent of two actions—the action of possessing the property and the action of following—which differ in their agents.

Where? "In the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārthe*)—a collection of words (*vākya*) is that which has mutual syntactic connection; its denoted object, as the thing to be embellished, is the subject or domain (*viṣaya*).
How? "By connection with that" (*tadanvayāt*)—"that" (*tat*) refers back to the word-meanings (*padārtha*).
“Because of the coordination” (*samanvayāt*) of those word-meanings, that is, because they are mutually connected;

for in a sentence many word-meanings occur, and therein, by virtue of the power of their mutual connection, [a certain relation] is established between some [meaning] and one or another [other meaning].
(Regarding the distinction between simile and poetic fancy:
Thus, when there is this equality of things in common,
he explains what kind of difference exists between the objects of simile and poetic fancy:
Even when there is similarity between the subject and the object of comparison, [the latter] falls within the scope of a different intended meaning.

Although a relation of similarity exists in *utprekṣā*, its "intention" (*tātparya*)— which functions as something distinct from the individual word-meanings and constitutes the very life of the sentence-meaning— is itself another entity that is the "range" or object of perception for those who know it; such is the internal manifestation [of it],
and thus it has been illustrated accordingly.

Because here both the basis of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), whether functioning as the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the object (*karman*), are connected with equal status;
