thus, "comparison" (*upamiti*) or "simile" (*upamā*) is established as a mere abstract state (*bhāva*).
And so, of the subject being described—[which is otherwise] exceedingly difficult to describe—...
The intended meaning of the definition is "that in which there is no equality.
It establishes both points with certainty,
as understood from the non-primary verbal expression.
An illustration of the categories [of meaning] is as follows:
"O lotus-eyed one, your face, which resembles the full moon, nourishes the desire of the flower-bowed god to conquer the three worlds. (VjivC 3.126)
An example of a simile based on the meaning of the word to be explained by the particle *iva* and so forth is:
"The cluster [of flowers] being drunk by the bees" (VjivC 3.127).
And so forth.
An example of a simile based on a word-meaning conveyed by a verbal form (*ākhyātapada*) is as follows: "Then, with the movement of the dawn... and so on. (VjivC 3.128)
An example of a simile based on such a statement is as follows:

"With her face pale as a *ketaka* petal, her slender body like a fragile stalk, and adorned with ornaments that were but slight, she mocked the night at dawn, when the young moon's orb was barely visible among the few remaining stars. (Vajrāvalī 3.129)
An example of a simile based on a category of objects explained by the word *iva* and so forth is as follows:
Kissing the surface of his beloved’s cheek, which was bristling with thrills, the moon caused her eyes—glistening with the touch—to close like buds;
it was as if the moon were touching the lotus of the night-lily, whose sweet sleep was awakening, while causing the lotus that had set to close. (Vajjālagga 3.130)
An example of a simile based on such a statement is as follows: "This Pāṇḍya king has a long necklace resting upon his shoulder and has applied fragrant unguents of yellow sandalwood."
With its ridges reddened by the morning sun,
it shines like the king of mountains with the outpouring of waterfalls.

Although in both of these two sentences there is a mutual connection— characterized by the integration of similarity— between each of the subjects of comparison (*upameya*) and their respective objects of comparison (*upamāna*), nevertheless, in the former case, the determination of the sentence-meaning is preceded by the determination of that integration of similarity.

In the latter case, however, there is first an ascertainment of the sentence-meaning, followed by an ascertainment of the concordance of similarity; whereas in this [former] sentence, there is compounding (*samāsa*) and so forth.
Because it is independent of other cognitions regarding its object, the mutual concordance of similarity also emerges immediately following the comprehension of the word-meanings.
The designation of "simile of objects" (padārthopamā) is applied here.
It should not be understood that the completion of the sentence-meaning occurs within this first half alone, because the intended meaning of the poet's expression has not yet been fully realized.
In that regard, there is the principle that "poetry consists of [the word] along with its ornament.

However, in the other case, because it is preceded by the determination of the sentence-meaning— which is based on a connection characterized by mutual syntactic relation— and because the comprehension of the mutual correspondence between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) occurs [therein], the designation of "sentence-simile" (*vākyopamā*) attains its propriety.
(Examples of similes conveyed by verbal expressions have been stated in the *Upamāvārttika* and other works; therefore, enough of this digression.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it has already been stated that the cognition of a simile occurs through other words such as *yathā*, even when distinct from [the particles] *iva* and so forth. (This applies whether the simile is expressed within a compound or not.)
Or both, as follows:
"Her face has the luster of the full moon, and her eyes are like blue lotuses."
And as it is said:

"As she departed, repeatedly turning her neck and bearing that face which resembled a full-blown lotus, the sidelong glance of that long-lashed-eyed woman—smeared as it were with both nectar and poison—is deeply embedded in my heart. (Vajrāvalī 3.133)
An example of a simile where the object of comparison is established through a causal condition (*pratyaya*) is as follows:
"Like a lotus fiber dyed with madder, the leader of the planets moves at his own will toward the state of touching the western mountain, gathering his rays;

for a moment, with the circle of wind-like clouds whirling around him like a parasol made of lotus pollen, that Blessed One, his light diminished even from here, sinks into the ocean. (Vajrāvalī 3.134)
Or as follows:
having heard the words of Kālanemi, the deep-throated and irresistible roar [arose], the herald of his arrival before the city.

The wrath of the great lord of the asuras is observed to be acting with unrestrained force, agitated by the destruction of the fierce pride that had expanded through the paralysis of his fortitude, much like a wild elephant.
For example:
"Having heard this, the daughter of the ascetic [cast] a restless upward glance at the eager [youth]."
At that time, when the flowers of the *atimukta* cluster had fallen away, her heart was bewildered as she went and came.
Or as it is said:

"When Rāma, with his innocent mind, broke the worn-out bow of the bull-bannered god [Śiva] as easily as a lotus stalk, was not the lord of the rākṣasas thereby mocked, even slightly, by him who bears the burden of fame bestowed upon him by the three worlds? (VjivC 3.137)

In the example of suggested simile (*pratīyamānopamā*), the perception of the simile is established even without the employment of verbs or other expressive rules that explicitly state it; this occurs solely through the power of the expressed meanings of both words—which possess a relationship with another rasa and whose movement is neither deficient nor excessive—as follows:
"Though the king had many sons, his gaze never reached satiety upon that particular child."
For when spring has infinite flowers, the swarm of bees is especially attached to the mango tree.

In this context, since even the spring (*madhu*), possessing such an infinite array of causal conditions, will obtain a cognition [of similarity] with that [object] when brought near a mango tree (*cūta*) similar to it,
it is logical that this clearly establishes the manifest similarity between these two;

thus, because of the excellence of qualities such as having innumerable flowers and extreme delicacy, the intended fulfillment of similarity and so forth constitutes the essential purport of the definition of simile (*upamā*).

In this case, it is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) itself that is being presented; nor should the error of mistaking this for an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter) be raised here,
because that [figure] consists in the semantic convergence of the meaning of the sentence.
Because its object is merely the commonality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasāmānyamātra*),
the *prativastūpamā*— which is based on the presentation of a similar thing (*samānavastunyāsa*)— does not deserve to be mentioned separately by this same logic,
since it shares the same status (*samānayogakṣema*) as the previously cited example.
And thus, regarding its definition and illustration, the *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) occurs through the presentation of a common subject, as follows:
"How many virtuous men are there who possess prosperity shared with the good?
Or how many roadside trees are there that bend under the fruit of their own shade? (VjivC 3.139)

In this case, among both types of things that possess similar manifestations, nothing else is perceived as a captivating life-principle that excels or surpasses the similarity characterized by the intended rarity of the poet’s vision.

Thus, since it has been established that *prativastūpamā* (the simile by parallelism) is included within *pratīyamānopamā* (the implied simile), we shall now consider the inclusion of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile) and other such figures within the category of *upamā* (simile). This [reciprocal simile], which consists of both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, exists as a distinct variety because its general characteristics are not otherwise present. (Vjiv 3.38)
Regarding "upameyopamā" and so forth: "upameyopamā" means a certain poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) called "commonality"—that is, it is not distinct [from other figures].
Why? Because the simile (*upamā*) is already under discussion.
For what reason?
Regarding the phrase "because the characteristic remains non-otherwise": a *lakṣaṇa* is a unique designation for its own essential nature (*svarūpa*);
because that [nature] is established as non-otherwise—that is, because no additional entity exists apart from it.
Thus, in the analysis of the compound (*vigraha*) "that in which the object of comparison (*upameya*) is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)," [the term *sva* refers to that very nature].
That which becomes the object of comparison is the upameya; that which is the standard of comparison is declared to be the upamāna.
"Whether it be sleep or even the slumber of one whose heart has fallen into the state of grief—these are the grounds for the consolation of love. (Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇīvyākhyā 3.140)
He states whether or not this [type of] *etadādi* can be established as a variety of *tulyayogitā*:
"That which is called *tulyayogitā* is not a distinct ornament;
for in it, many or two objects possess equal connection. (Vjiv 3.39)
They attain the status of being qualifiers because their primary importance is set aside;
[for] when a thing is described as the principal subject, what could it be, and of what would it be an ornament? (Vjiv 3.40)

This figure of speech called *tulyayogitā* (Equal Treatment) is not [merely] an ornament; for in it, two or many objects possessing equal application (*tulyayogin*) attain the status of being modes [of description] and are led toward the state of being the subject of description (*varṇanīyatā*).
Here, the object to be described is primarily described [as such].

What could be the ornament of what? What would serve as an adornment? The meaning is that, since each thing is determined by its own specific predominance, nothing whatsoever belongs to anything else;
or rather, it is stated that everything might potentially be an ornament for something.
In this regard, even this [objection] is not tenable.
Why? Because of the "removal of primacy," that is, the removal of the state of being the principal element on all sides;
for when something serves as an ornament, it necessarily functions as a subordinate member (parāṅgatva).
By that, the primacy of the object is set aside;
for a primary object cannot, by the very same form through which it experiences primacy, simultaneously experience subordination as a subordinate member.
Because it is impossible for two mutually contradictory things to exist in one place without a difference in their form;
or, if it is argued that both primacy and subordination can coexist in a single person, such as a king's attendant, then in that case a duality of forms would have to be admitted.

And likewise, among the king’s attendants, there exists a twofold nature: the state of being a servant with respect to the master, and the state of being a master with respect to one's own servants. This is entirely appropriate because two such natures exist, characterized by a duality of mutually dependent relations. Thus, in this case as well, when another essential nature is present, who can prevent its being an ornament?
This is true.

While its status as an ornament is not denied, its character as a variety of *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) is, however, set aside; thus he says: "Or rather, if their status as subjects of description (*varṇyatva*) or their equality is further excelled [by another factor]."
For these subjects under discussion, that [analogy] clearly serves as a comparison.
The phrase "the state of being describable" (*varṇyatva*) and so forth means that by the word "or else" (*athavā*), another alternative is established.

Even when there is no state of being describable—that is, even when they are not the objects of description—if there is a "similarity" (*sāmya*), meaning resemblance, between these subjects under discussion (*prastuta*) and something else, and if that similarity at some point "surpasses" (*atiricyate*), meaning it attains a state of superiority over what is being described due to its own excellence; [then this constitutes a further variety].

To the question "What would follow from that?", he says: "That clearly becomes a simile (upamiti). The meaning is that it is both manifest and an ornament; because of its correspondence with similarity (*sāmya*), conjunction (*samanvaya*), and so forth, it is nothing other than a simile itself.

Likewise, regarding the "cumulative simile" (*samuccitopamā*): when it is connected with an object being described by means of a cumulative [set of attributes], it is called a "cumulative simile" (*samuccitopamā*) because the simile is accumulated therein; it exists as something equal to that state.

The mention of a simile here refers to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), not to a "compound simile" (*samuccitopamā*). Because it is the subject under discussion, the standard of comparison—by virtue of its excellence in conjunction with the qualities of similarity—is employed for the purpose of ornamentation, as follows: "In the festival of the full moon, the girl bestows upon her lover a mirror that is pleasing to the eye; she dispels the darkness of the night and brings forth many delights. (VjivC 3.141)
The point is this: even though it is described here in this manner, because of the excellence of the similarity, it ought to be considered a simile (*upamā*) alone.
For example:
"To the people dwelling in Sāketa, both of them were objects of praise for their noble character."
The king is one who desires nothing more than what is to be given to his guru, and he is one who bestows even more than what is requested by those in need.

An imagined point of comparison (*upamāna*) whose nature is exceedingly charming due to its exquisite beauty and tenderness shines forth for the purpose of attaining a superiority over the intended object of comparison (*upameya*), as in:

“If the two separate streams of the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā were to fall from the sky, then [only] by that could his chest—dark as a *tamāla* tree and adorned with a string of pearls—be compared. (Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī 3.143)

(e) This is an illustration of both [types]. Thinking that even in the case of *ananvaya* (the "non-comparison"), because of the greatness of the delicacy being described, even a conceptual comparison (*upamāna*) is not tenable, they describe that comparison as one in which the distinction is superimposed upon the very nature of the object itself, as follows:
In the experience of that [previous object], entities such as the moon become light; yet the mind, when compared to your face, turns away from even the lotus of the nectar-ocean.
Thus the mind concludes that your face is the ultimate limit of the essence of beauty; it itself forms the resolve to attain such excellence of comparison through its own radiance.
Thus, such is the manifold diversity of the various modes of expression, but not so that of the different types of definitions.
The infinity of the modes of expression arising from creative intuition cannot be clearly described, just like the diverse playfulness of a beloved woman.
An intermediate verse:
*Tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) is also not distinct [from this], as it is included within this very category. Thus, its definition and illustration are as follows:

Even when there is an inferior [subject], if one intends to express equality of quality with a superior [subject] through its connection with an action occurring at the same time, that is called *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing).
Thus it was established by them,
because of the absence of equality or superiority.
For example:

"The Himalaya is the Residue (Śeṣa), and you are the Great One (Mahān); both are heavy and steadfast, having never transgressed the bounds of propriety; you sustain the Earth as she wavers. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā, 3.147)
Regarding this definition, he first establishes the inclusion of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) within *upamā* (simile):
"The basis of simile is the conjunction of similarity between an object possessing an excellence (*atiśaya*) and another object whose excellence is established;

however, here [in *tulyayogitā*], the connection of simultaneous actions with the intent of expressing equality of qualities conveys no significance other than the comparison between the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*)."
The illustration (*nidarśana*) is also of this same nature.

Apart from the similarity consisting in the application of *śleṣa* (punning) and so forth to the subject being described—which is the object of description—nothing further appears as distinct. Therefore, because of the greatness of the appearance of the application of *śleṣa* to the intended meaning, this is not a separate figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) from *dīpaka*, as has been stated by those who are most proficient in the science.
Even that is not logically consistent;
for instance:
"Whether they saw her or did not see her, they were all robbed at the same time."
The hearts of some were stolen away, while for others it was the fruit of their eyes.
This appears to the discerning as the mere prattle of someone who is ignorant of even the basic discourse on poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
For this *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), intended to convey through a clever turn of phrase the excellence of a young woman’s beauty, flashes forth in the poet’s mind;
or rather, it is possible that it constitutes *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) by virtue of being the subject of another type of illustration.
For example:

"The delineation of the meaning of poetry, private conversations, staying in seclusion, soft singing up to the throat, and the sharing of the sorrow of a trusted friend. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra 3.149)
It is now analyzed that the *ananvaya* (non-parallelism) is also included within *upamāna* (simile) itself. Accordingly, its definition and illustration are as follows:
"Where there is the relationship of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) between that very same thing and itself..."
They call it *ananvaya* (non-connection) when there is an intention to express dissimilarity.
Your face alone possesses a circle of betel-stain, the radiance of shimmering teeth,
and eyes with the hue of blue lotuses.

Both of these— the fact that its characteristic is non-different [from that of simile] and its capacity to produce a variety of expressions through association with that [simile]— establish its inclusion within the category of simile itself.
Regarding that, it is argued that because the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is established therein,
it is impossible for the *ananvaya* (non-correspondence) to possess the characteristics [of simile] along with another simile; however, this is not a valid solution,
because [the author] accepts a duality of superimposed forms (*samāropitarūpa*).

For you, the basis for the application of the term *ananvaya* (non-parallelism) is similarity (*sāmya*) itself, which is grounded in the relationship between the standard of comparison (*pramāṇa*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*);
however, for us, that [similarity] is established even by means of the simple [negation of difference]. Thus he says:
Poets know that which is equal to a fabricated simile as *ananvaya* (non-connection).
That in which the "simile" (*upamā*) is "fancied" (*kalpitā*)— that is, "depicted" (*ullikhitā*)— is so described.

Poets— that is, those who know [the matter]— know— that is, recognize— the figure of speech called *ananyaya* (the "without-correspondence"), which is "equal" to that fancied simile, being neither deficient nor excessive.

And thus, in the case of imagined similes (*kalpitopamā*), there arises a correspondence between the object described and its own beauty that has reached the height of excellence. Since all existing things lack the capacity to convey such superlative quality, poets of beautiful intent are seen to depict various non-existent, purely imaginary points of comparison according to their own taste.

Furthermore, the relationship of subject and object (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between those two, based on their mutual similarity, results from the fact that [the former] is described as being "unreal" (*asadbhūta*); there is no other cause for their charm whatsoever beyond this.
And thus, they call that which has been described as it was stated above "the simile of the object compared to the standard of comparison," providing both its definition and an illustration.
Fragrant, delighting the eyes, and rosy with the intoxication of wine, your face is like a lotus;
and the lotus is like your face.
Nor is the definition here the cause of a different figure of speech than the simile (*upamā*),
because that has been refuted by the principle previously stated.
Furthermore, the relationship of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) would occur here by way of exchange (*paryāyataḥ*).
In the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), both the appearance of difference and the appearance of non-difference are valid.
Furthermore, it does not constitute a separate poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) merely because its intended meaning consists in the exclusion of other standards of comparison.
In instances such as "the moon is the face," because there is not even a trace of the nature of anything other than the object of comparison,
it is merely the manifestation of a variety of modes of expression brought forth by the maturity of poetic intuition (*pratibhā*); it does not constitute a distinct figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*),
since such a variety is observed even in other types of expressed meanings.
For example:
"By that beautiful [glance] which opened simultaneously, let these two immediately attain a mutual likeness."
Your eye, with its pupil both quivering and soft, is like a lotus with a hovering bee within.
For example:
"To the people dwelling in Sāketa, both of them were objects of veneration;
the king was one who desired nothing more than what was due to his preceptor, and the seeker was one who gave more than was requested. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.155)

In this case, because both [the subject and the object] are under discussion, there is a state of similarity between the two things being described, but not the state of being an *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure).
Or, for example:
He who effortlessly shattered the bow of Śiva, and he who effortlessly gratified the Moon-crested Lord—
between him and this [Arjuna], there may be friendship; in either case, O friend, it is praiseworthy for both of them today.
In this regard, what was stated previously should be considered.
Although it was explained during the definition of simile (*upamā*) that "mere state" (*bhāvamātra*) constitutes an ornament residing in both [the subject and the object],
nevertheless, because the object of comparison (*upamāna*) was not the primary topic there, its status as a subordinate element (*parāṅgatva*) was appropriate.

Furthermore, in this context, the primacy of the subject under discussion has already been examined as to how it is so. By this same principle, it is now established that *parivṛtti* (exchange) does not exist as a separate figure of speech.
And thus is the definition of transformation (parivṛtti):
"The reorientation of objects is considered to be transformation. (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi 3.157)
Thus:
"Parivartana" (exchange) is the displacement of one object into the space previously occupied by another;
this is designated as the poetic figure *parivṛtti*.
And that [deflection] is of many kinds: for a single subject, when there is an opportunity for a suitable object, it shifts to another object.
As in:
"Speak little, O Bṛhaspati, preceptor of the gods; this is not the assembly of Indra. (Vajrāvalī 3.158)
In some cases, within the scope of a single object that possesses a sequence of combined attributes, one attribute is displaced by another;
as for example:
"He turned away from her lower lip, which had shed its redness, and from the ball, which was stained with the cosmetic ointment of her breasts."
Her hand, which had been accustomed to grasping blades of kusha grass, was now made to hold a rosary of beads by her.

In this instance, the attribute characterized by the hand-bell of Gaurī has been exchanged; sometimes, when there is scope for two mutually consistent attributes within a single subject (dharmin) that has been indicated, one attribute is exchanged for another.
For example: "Why did you discard your ornaments in your youth? [and so on].
The bark garment, beautiful in its aged state, has been worn by you.
In some cases, even when there are many competing subjects (*dharmin*), all the aforementioned [types of] alternation (*parivarta*) occur.
And thus, the author of the *Lakṣaṇa* has shown an example right here: as follows—
By your arm, O King, as it delivered a stroke of the weapon,
the long-earned fame of those [enemies], white as a water-lily, was snatched away.
Thus, he states that it is not logical for *parivṛtti* (exchange) to be a poetic figure:
"The turning away of one thing which is the turning toward another..."
That would not be an ornament, because it would be a mere transformation as before.

Regarding the passage beginning with *vinivartanam* and so forth: "The exclusion (*vinivartana*)"—that is, the negation—"of one thing" (*padārtha*), "is not the occurrence (*vartana*)"—that is, the establishment or the ornamentation—"of another," which is distinct from it.
Why? Because both are "subject to transference" (*parivartamānatvāt*), meaning they are expressed primarily [as the subject of the statement].
How is it "as before"? Just as previously, due to the predominance of each [factor] individually and because of the lack of restriction or certainty— just as nothing is an ornament for anything—
so too has this been examined here.
Nor does their state of mutual ornamentation consist merely in that limited form; for if that were the case, it would entail the consequence of the loss of their primary status.

Furthermore, when there is a state of similarity despite the non-cessation of distinct forms, this occurs as a simile; and this is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), just like *samuccitopamā* (cumulative simile), as before.
For example:
"The mighty-armed one shared [his grief] with compassion, thinking, 'She might go away in sudden agitation.'"
He regarded the earth, which had recently been brought under his control, like a bride who has just taken her new husband's hand.
Here, by means of evenness,
the king's effort regarding the enjoyment of the earth as his bride is perceived as being full of passion.
Since both are being described, even when there is a reversal [of roles], it is still a simile (upamā) because of the perception of similarity;
for example:
This battle, which brought an end to the lives of the warriors, brought joy indeed to the soldiers; for here,
through their devotion, the heads [severed] by spears were like fresh lotus garlands upon the edges of new swords.

In this context, the cause of attractiveness is merely the appearance of similarity; therefore, in such a subject matter, the application of aesthetic charm is invariably [based on] similarity (*sāmya*). This is *alaṅkāra* (ornamentation).
They employ suggested ornamentation (*pratīyamāna-alaṅkāra*), and not merely that which is directly expressed (*abhidhīyamāna*).
Furthermore, the state of being suggested is also observed in the case of *parivṛtti* (exchange).
Just as it was described—
having occupied that leaf-hut pointed out by the head of the clan,
accompanied by his devoted wife, he spent the night lying on a bed of *kuśa* grass, the end of which was announced by the recitation of his pupil.

In this [verse], all the words are composed such that they each imply other words capable of being substituted in their respective places; therefore, because these meanings are suggested (*pratīyamāna*), they also produce delight for those who know them. And how could a consistent substitution not be possible? Otherwise, it would be untenable. (True.)
This is correct.

We do not assert that transformation (*parivṛtti*) is absolutely non-existent; rather, our intention is that it does not constitute an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) because it is merely something to be described.
Moreover, mere suggestiveness (*pratīyamānatāmātra*) is not the sole means of establishing a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*),
because it can also occur in the case of a mere object that serves as the substrate of a figure (*alaṅkāryavastumātra*).
This very point is illustrated by the following example.
Nor is it tenable to say that whatever is perceived [as such] is an ornament because it produces delight for those who know [it],
since even that which is the object of ornamentation (the *alaṅkārya*) is seen to produce delight for those who know it;
furthermore, the threefold division [of poetry] into mere matter (*vastumātra*), ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth would be untenable.
Furthermore, if *parivṛtti* (exchange) were a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), no other ornament would be required for its embellishment,
as in the verse beginning, "Why have you cast off your ornaments? or "Tell me, if the night with its bright moon and stars at dusk is fit for the dawn."
Or, if it is argued that even with respect to an ornament, one composes another ornament out of dissatisfaction [with the first], that too is not logically sound;
because [the rule applies] only when there exists another object to be adorned upon which the ornament may be applied.
In that case, another ornament arises from dissatisfaction, but not with respect to anything else.
According to the principle stated previously, when the status of being an ornament for each of the two is individually precluded, the adornment of exchange cannot occur.
In this case, only the state of being an ornament remains.
Therefore, the poetic figure known as *upamā* (simile) has been employed for the sake of embellishment.

Thus, the meaning of the sentence here is as follows: the taking up and wearing of the bark garments appropriate for old age, preceded by the removal of the ornaments suitable for the time of the emergence of youth.
In the night at twilight, with its moon and stars clearly manifest, it reveals a certain quality that delights those who know it—a quality resembling the union with the dawn (*aruṇa*).
This is the ultimate truth here: the arrangement of ornaments must be fashioned according to the lines delineated by the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Also by way of the variety of modes of the crookedness of speech appearing through inspired intuition—as in:
"By the dispersal of the dream... (VjivC 3.165).
Because it demonstrates that specific meaning through the very act [of comparison] itself,
this should be known as an illustration (nidarśana), even though it is devoid of words such as "yathā" or "iva."
Thus, even *nidarśanā*, being characterized in this way, is simply a form of simile (*upamiti*):
"This sun, its radiance dimmed, desires to go toward the setting mountain."
"Rising leads to falling"—thus did the Blessed One awaken men.

In this context, the phrase "tathaiva" (just so) refers to a poetic figure (*vastu*) characterized by the determination of another intended meaning attributed to the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*). This occurs because the *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is perceived through the power of employing a sentence capable of conveying that [meaning], even without an explicit indicator of similarity such as "tadiva" (like that) or "tadeva" (that very thing). For example: "The lightning flashes like a dart, and the nights seem to pierce my heart; the autumn wind, with its loud roar, mocks me, and the cuckoo triumphs over my separation. (Note: The provided Sanskrit verse contains orthographic errors and fragments; the translation above interprets it based on the standard conventions of *alaṃkāra-śāstra* regarding *utprekṣā*.)

In this context, having heard the sound of thundering, some women—on nights when flickering lightning flashes—behold the clouds; yet, because this falls outside the scope of determining the women's actual intention, and because the meaning of the sentence would otherwise be inexplicable, one must follow what was stated previously:
"That moon, with the beauty of its half-risen orb... and so forth.
She drew away the splendor of the forehead-slab of Kāmapāla, which had been surpassed by her own gentle radiance.

In this case, the beauty of the half-risen lunar orb—which transcends the splendor of the forehead-slab of Kāmapāla through its similarity—becomes a cause of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) only by means of another attribute that possesses a distinct function; otherwise, nothing at all would be possible. A verb with multiple meanings does not attain such a capacity for conveying [the sense] as the simile does.

Consequently, because its meaning has already been conveyed, the word [expressing it] is not employed; thus, although the function of "locus" does not apply directly to the eyes, it attains the status of their qualifier through a succession of metaphorical transfers (*upacāra-pāraṃparya*).

In this way, first, by means of the mere quality of the proximity characterized as the relation between property and property-possessor (*dharma-dharmin-bhāva*), which is itself defined by the indication of its own denotation (*svābhidheya-lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇā*); and then, by means of the very proximity based on similarity (*sādṛśya-nibandhanā*), it acquires a function in that which resembles them—the eyes—by way of an excellence in the shadow (*chāyā*) of the eyes.
Precisely because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in this compound, the word *nīlotpala* is placed first according to the rule *saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau*.
In the case of *indumukhī*, she is so described because her face is like the moon (*induriva mukhaṃ yasyāḥ sā*).
This is based on the principle previously stated regarding the causal condition (*nimittabhāva*) for the similarity in the configuration of the entire lunar disc as perceived by all the world.
The word *indu* itself functions as the qualifier; thus, the formation of the compound is justified in the same manner as before.
Alternatively, in the analysis "she whose face is like the moon's face," the word *indu* serves as a qualifier for that part of the whole—the face—just as in the expression "the village is burnt."
The remainder should be understood exactly as previously stated.
In the expression "tiger among men" (*puruṣavyāghra*), even a common attribute is implied,
because the relationship of comparison between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is not possible without such a connection.

Since its meaning is already understood through the force of the connection between the words (*padābhisaṃbandhasāmarthya*), the general term (*sāmānyaśabda*) is not employed because its purpose has been fulfilled.
This is what was stated [by Pāṇini]: "A thing compared is compounded with *vyāghra* and so forth, when the general term is not used" (*upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge*).
In the case of *indukāntamukhī*, meaning "she whose face is as lovely as the moon," the logical justification is given because the general term is actually heard [in the compound].

In the phrase "induriva kāntamindukāntam" (as lovely as the moon, moonstone-like), once the compound has been formed by the rule "upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ" (comparisons [are compounded] with words expressing common properties), the subsequent analysis is: "she whose face is moonstone-like.

Since the general term [kāntam] is applicable in both the compound (*vṛtti*) and the analytical sentence (*vākya*), its status as something heard [in the compound] cannot be determined by any logical principle, because it is that very word which is compounded with another word.
But since it is not [expressed] by anything else, how could its status as being understood (*pratīyamānatā*) be postulated for that which is heard as a verbal form?
Thus, depending on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), in some cases there is the state of being implied (*gamyamānatā*), and in others, the state of being actually employed (*prayujyamānatva*).

In such cases, because [the universal]— which is based on similarity and denotes the relation between both [the individual and the universal] as its object— is already understood, it is not explicitly employed. For the employment of a word is indeed undertaken for the purpose of conveying meaning.
If it has already been understood from a different enclosure fashioned by the poet’s skill, then what is the use of employing the word?

Likewise, where a sentence— possessing a charm that is neither deficient nor excessive, capable of conveying through both sense and sound the similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, beautiful with its graceful clarity, and elegant in its composition— is heard immediately upon being uttered, [there too the word is redundant].
Following the sequence of phonemes, the apprehension of meaning—which is like a mental image—gives rise to the cognition of the ornament;
in that case, particles such as *iva* are not employed because their meaning has already been conveyed.
For example:
Even though he was a king who possessed sons.

Even in cases where the understanding of the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) emerges through the greatness of an extraordinary correspondence of similarity— evoked by the poet’s skill in the transformation of word-meanings and so forth, even in the absence of the basis for distinguishing other figures of speech—

there too, it is the very brilliance of the poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) resulting from the variety of modes of expression that brings about the aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*) for those connoisseurs who perceive it. Thus,
there is the status of being "implied" (*pratīyamānatva*) when the ornaments are present even though words such as *iva* (like) that explicitly denote them are not employed— as follows:
"Indeed, these are great streams of nectar, not garlands of blue lotuses"—
where such [an expression] is used as an ornament (*alam-karaṇa*), there the *iti* and other particles may be employed in many ways due to the variety of modes of presentation.

And likewise, when a comparison (*upamā*) has as its object the meanings of words, and the words for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)— which reside in different parts of the sentence— are employed to express their mutual similarity, then within that very same sentence, a particle such as *iva* is employed again to denote the relation of similarity between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison which reside between the breasts. (Even though) the relation of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is complete for each pair, [the particle is used again].

Nevertheless, when the meaning of the sentence is established and the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is possible, one should follow the very first-mentioned reasoning.
For example:
"Then Raghu set out toward the northern quarter, like the sun."
As if wishing to extract the essences from the northerners with sharp arrows.

In some cases of object-simile (*padārthopamā*), the correspondence of similarity between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), situated within a single part of the sentence, is expressed verbally.

In that same sentence, when it is joined with a denotative word (*vācaka*), the relationship of standard and object of comparison can occur for one of those two [terms] in relation to another substratum (*dharmī*), because it is based on a further property (*dharma*) that grounds their similarity.
According to the principle previously stated, the word "atha" (then) and others are employed as if to restate that [preceding state];
for example:
"Then, having emerged from the mouth of the great seer, which was beautiful like the beginning of day, like the sun from its orb..."
A radiance, white as sparks of fire, entered the face of Pārtha like a shimmering lotus.

In certain cases of object-simile (*padārthopamā*), where the number of subjects (*upameya*) and objects of comparison (*upamāna*) is equal, one first relies on the duality inherent in the two groups— having resolved the intended difference in the number of the groups— and then employs a single expressive word to state the relationship of subject and object through their mutual correspondence. Since the attributes of the collection are preceded by the collection itself, these [attributes] subsequently [apply] individually to each of their respective correlates.
The relationship between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison is established through the power of the connection with a common attribute;
for example: "kissing the cheek. (VjivC 3.174)

In such passages as these, the relationship of simile (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between two things arises through their mutual connection with a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharmasaṃbandha*) by means of two modes: [first], by the word *sparśollasad* acting as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), and [second], by both being established as the substrata of that attribute.
In some cases of simile based on the meaning of words (*padārthopamā*), a single object is presented as the primary subject by virtue of being qualified by various types of word-meaning attributes.

When that which is described as the locus of the quality being expressed (the *upameya*) attains the status of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) by means of its own specific qualifiers consisting of those very [qualifiers],
then, because both of them are connected through such mutual similarity as their common property, the relationship of *upamāna* and *upameya* arises.
To express this, only words such as "as if" (*iva*) are fit to be employed.
Regarding the expression of the mutual similarity between the qualifiers of that [subject], the same reasoning previously stated should be followed,
as in the example beginning with "This is the Pāṇḍya king."

Thus, in this view, all of this is established through the variety of modes of expression and the variety of expressive powers. However, because the definitions of similes and so forth are so well-constructed, they are cast far aside and are not enumerated [as defects], unlike those [interpretations] such as the "interpretable meaning" (*neyārtha*).
"When a quality that captivates the mind is intended as the object of expression, then these faults become cast far away. // VjivC_3.176 //
This is an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*).

Having thus explained the ornament called *upamā* (simile), whose life is the similarity between the expressed (*vācya*) subject and the expressed non-subject (*aprastuta*), he now explains *śleṣa* (punning paronomasia), which consists primarily of a common luster and whose entire essence is the similarity of the expressive words (*vācaka*):
"That state of being denotable by a single word is maintained for two meanings."
The ornament called *śleṣa* (punning) consists in the identity of the expressive words and the expressed meanings.
Regarding the phrase "being denotable by that single word" and so forth: the word "that" (tat) refers back to the expressive [word] whose function is established through punning (*śleṣa*).
By that, there is the expressiveness (*vācakatva*) of that very word already mentioned, which consists of a linguistic unit (*pada*).
By that, "denotability" (*vācyatva*) means the state of being the signified (*abhidheyatva*).

“Of two meanings” (*arthayoḥ*) means of two things being expressed, which are real and constitute the essential nature of the intended meaning of the sentence. That in which [these two] are held together is the figure of speech called *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
“Possessing such expressive words and meanings” (*tādṛgvācakavācyatā*): that which appears like that is called “such” (*tādṛk*);
it is thus described as being both “such” (*tādṛk*) and an “expressive word” (*vācaka*).

By that [term], *vācyatā* means the state of being denotable (*vācyatva*), i.e., the state of being expressible (*abhidheyatva*). That in which there is the capacity to denote such a meaning is also called *śleṣa*. That which is experienced as "like that" due to the identity of sound is said to be of that nature.
Furthermore, that very [word] is differentiated by the distinctness of its properties, such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth.
In this regard, the similarity between the two consists precisely in their mutual dependence;

for instance, when one relies on the fact that "whatever is the denoter of this [object] in one case, it is exactly the same in the other," whether this occurs within a single word or in some portion of a sentence where the function of a real entity (*vāstavapadavṛtti*) is established.
That state of being denotable by a single word belongs to both.
Now, even though there is no difference between those two in terms of being denoted by such a denoter, how can it be called *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone?
Therefore, because that [meaning] is perceived through three modes and through three types of word-meanings.
There is semantic punning (*arthaśleṣa*), verbal punning (*śabdaśleṣa*), and punning on both (*ubhayaśleṣa*).
To the question of what serves as the means of conveying such a [pun], the poets say: "The meaning of another word (*padārthāntara*) is its conveyer."
They assert that the expressive power of words is another [factor], such as "and so forth" (ādi).
"Another category of meaning," and so forth.

"Another category of meaning" (*padārthāntara*) refers to something distinct from the words joined in *śleṣa* (punning). "Another" (*apara*) means that which possesses the capacity to convey it—that is, the expounder or communicator of this *śleṣa* ornament. "The poets who know it" (*tadvidaḥ*) "assert" (*pratijānate*)—that is, they perceive it.

The specific indicator (*vācakaviśeṣa*)—namely, particles such as *iva* and so forth, or that which is distinct from other word-meanings, or merely the capacity of the expressed meaning itself—is the sentence once it has been presented.
One asserts that this [sentence] possesses the power to convey the intended meaning through its own inherent capacity;
the connection is that it is "the communicator" (*pratipādaka*).

In all three of these modes, when two meanings are described as being predominant, there is an ornament consisting of the manifestation of a similarity characterized by being expressible by such words— a similarity obtained through the power of the sentence and perceived [by the reader].
However, when the expressive word is present, it is merely the expressed meaning itself.

When there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate status between the contextual (prastuta) and non-contextual (aprastuta) meanings, there is likewise a coordination through a similarity consisting in being expressible by such words.

Even when one of the two is primarily described as the subject of description, it should be understood— by means of the *locana* [commentary]— that the other is coordinated as the object of comparison (*upameya*),
provided that one word applies to both meanings, whether of the words themselves or their referents.
The similarity between the two illuminations unfolds here due to their being mutually dependent.
An object different from that [perceived object] is understood through the recollection of a similar word;
since the word itself has arisen and perished, it is memory alone that expresses everything.
In this regard, an example of the first [type] is as follows:

Victorious is that speech of poets and beloved women, which—by means of a striking charm marked by the seal of sweetness and intent upon conveying their own inner intention—scratches something ineffable within the hearts of those with noble minds; it has ascended to the ultimate pinnacle of the transformation of the latent impressions of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and is deviously clever. (VjivC 3.177)
An example of the second [type] is as follows:

"May that Mādhava, the giver of all, himself protect you—he by whom the body of the conqueror of Bala was formerly made female by the Destroyer of Manobhava; he who wears a serpent as his armlet and supports the Gaṅgā; whose praiseworthy name the immortals call 'the one who took the moon-crested head,' and who brought about the destruction of Andhaka. (Vajrāvalī 3.178)

An example of a pun (*śleṣa*) whose meaning is unreal (*asatyabhūta*) is as follows: "O Keśava, because my vision was obscured by the dust raised by the cows, I saw nothing at all; for that very reason, O Lord, I have stumbled. Why do you not support me as I fall? You alone are the refuge for all helpless women whose minds are distressed in difficult circumstances. May Hari, thus addressed with a hint of irony by a laughing cowherd girl in the cow-pen, protect us. *Vajrāvalī*, 3.180.
Having thus described *śleṣa* (paronomasia), which is composed by an intellect capable of the variety of sentence-construction and is to be relished,

he now describes *vyatireka* (distinction), which shares the same cause as simile, metaphor, and paronomasia because it is based solely on similarity: "When there is the denotation of the word *tat* (that), and when there is a similarity of attributes existing otherwise,
the setting apart (*vyatirecana*) from another [object] is for the sake of establishing the excellence of the subject at hand."
Whether it be expressed through words or understood through implication, it is called "negative concomitance" (vyatireka).
The phrase beginning with "satī" [means]:
having analyzed the compound as "that which is both *sa* (it) and *śabda* (word)," the word *sa* refers by its own power to the word that serves as the cause for the pun (*śleṣa*).

When that [word] is the "object of expression" (*vācyatve*), meaning it is denotable, and when there exists a "similarity of attributes" (*dharmasāmye*), meaning a mutual resemblance in their movement, [there occurs] conceptual construction (*vikalpanā*).
Because such denotability by words and similarity of attributes reside in both [the subject and the object], and because both are under discussion—

namely, those two, the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*)— there is a "separation" (*vyatirecana*), that is, a setting apart, of one from the other, namely the subject of comparison (*upameya*) from the object of comparison (*upamāna*), by means of some attribute according to the speaker's preference, through its "abiding otherwise," that is, through its existing in a different state than the intended [attribute].
Therefore, that "vyatireka"—the ornament named vyatireka—is "abhidhīyate," that is, it is called;
for what purpose? "For the sake of establishing the excellence of the subject at hand."

"For the sake of establishing the excellence" (*utkarṣasiddhaye*) of "the subject at hand" (*prastutasya*), that is, the matter currently being described, for the purpose of bringing about a superior luster;

that [excellence] is twofold: "verbal" (*śābdaḥ*) or "implied" (*pratīyamānaḥ*). "Verbal" means that which is expressed by a word capable of conveying it, as established by the tradition of poets. "Implied" means that which is understood solely through the power of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-sāmarthya*).

Among these, the first degree of comparison is the *upamāvyatireka* (superiority over the object of comparison), as follows: "Ordinary people indeed compare her cheeks to the orb of the moon; yet, when analyzed according to ultimate reality, the wretched moon is merely like [her cheek]. (VjivC 3.181)
In this very way, people compare the moon's orb to her cheek;
yet, when analyzed from the perspective of ultimate truth, the moon is as wretched as a mere moon.
Or as it is said:
"Desiring to behold the heart-stealing play of your eyelashes with a thousand eyes..."
The swarms of bees do not rejoice in the ponds, though they are beautiful with the blooming of blue lotuses.
Or as it is said:
"Since he has already attained prosperity, why would he cause me distress by churning the ocean again? I do not even imagine that he, whose mind is ever-active, would now fall asleep.
And why does he, followed by the lords of all the islands, build a bridge once more?"—as if bearing such doubts within him, the trembling of the ocean appears as you approach. (Vajrāvalī 3.183)

In this case, since the undertaking [of the work] would not be possible without superimposing the nature of Nārāyaṇa upon that which is being described, it is merely a *rūpaka* (metaphor) perceived through the superimposition of his true identity;
how then can it be justified as *vācyavyatireka* (the expressed distinction)? This is true as you have stated.
However, the reasoning here is stated:

therefore, the object being perceived is of two kinds; [the first is] that which falls within the scope of the expressive operation of a word whose own meaning has become subordinate to the act of communication.
Or rather, its object is the capacity of such a meaning.

Regarding this, having considered that "analogy is expressive," the former sages did not record it [as a separate means of knowledge], relying solely on the capacity of the expressed meaning as the cause for the establishment of the intended meaning.
However, the operation of the expressive word is established in quite another way.
And thus, words such as *prāptaśrī* (one who has attained fortune) are composed with their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) implied;
being intent on establishing the subject's divinity as characterized by a more distinguished prior activity, they clearly convey a *vyatireka* (poetic contrast) based on metaphor (*rūpaka*).
This has been stated as follows:
"That particular kind of poetry in which the meaning or the word manifests that [intended] meaning while subordinating their own literal senses is called 'dhvani' by the wise. (VjivC 3.184)
Therefore, nothing is untenable.
An example of *śleṣavyatireka* (pun-based contrast) is as follows:

Hari, whose hand is the Sudarśana [discus], has conquered the three worlds with the playful grace of his entire body; he has overspread the world with the charm of his lotus feet, while [the other] has a praiseworthy remaining body and possesses beautiful eyes.
May she who, possessing a face like the moon and bearing eyes whose very essence is the moon, appeared to her own body as something superior—she who is like Rukmiṇī—protect you.

He states another perspective: "When one [thing] is distinguished from another due to a specific difference from a movement that is commonly recognized in the world, that is exclusion (*vyatireka*), provided there is no intention to express it [as a positive entity]. (Vjiv 3.49)

Regarding the passage beginning with *lokaprasiddha*: "The other" (*paraḥ*) refers to that figure of speech called *vyatireka* (distinction). Of what nature is it? It is "the distinction" (*vyatireka*), which is the setting apart (*pṛthakkaraṇa*) of "one" thing.

From what [is it distinguished]? "From the activity common to the world" (*lokaprasiddhasāmānyaparispandāt*). That is to say, from that "activity" (*parispanda*), or operation, which is "well-known in the world" (*lokaprasiddhaḥ*)—meaning recognized by the world, being universal, and common to all.
For what reason? "Specifically" means due to some particular excellence.
How [is it said] "by not intending that"? "That" refers to the reference to similes and so forth; "by not intending those" means that which is prescribed without intending them.
The intended meaning here is this: since this very [intended] thing is the universal, those others have been previously mentioned as its particulars in the context of the introduction.
An example for another [type of case] is as follows:
The ground was carpeted with flowers as his bow; the well-arranged rows of bees were its string; the season of spring, with the rising of the full moon, was the time for his assault;

his weapons were the blue lotuses, ketakī blossoms, and other flowers; and the warriors were the lovers themselves. What a wondrous and graceful manifestation of desire, eager for victory, is this of Madana throughout the three worlds!

In this case, compared to the practice of desiring victory [in battle] which employs a collection of implements such as weapons well-known to all the world, the practice of Manmatha’s desire for victory is distinguished by its delicate implements.
Now, one might object: "Since the earth and other elements are described as having the form of bows and so forth, is this not simply a *rūpakavyatireka* (metaphorical distinction)?
This is not so.
For in the case of a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*), after performing an identification with form (*rūpaṇa*), a distinction from that very [form] is established;
in this case, however, the distinction is made from the common understanding (*sāmānya*) well-known to the entire world.
Furthermore, let it be understood that the attribution of the nature of water and so forth to the ground and other such things serves merely as the cause for another qualification.

Having thus examined the method of exclusion (vyatireka), he now examines contradiction (virodha), which is appropriate at this juncture because it is closely intertwined with paronomasia (śleṣa): "Contradiction, moreover, is that which, by bringing together words expressing mutually opposed meanings, delineates the logical consistency of the cognition [produced]. (Vjiv 3.50)
"Contradiction," and so forth:

that ornament which, through the perception of mutually contradictory meanings, illustrates the logical consistency of "words expressing contradictory things"— that is, words denoting opposing entities— by presenting them through another expressive word or by the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*), such that they are established as being tenable through reasoning and a particular mode of presentation.
It establishes a connection;
because it possesses the nature of a word-meaning, it effects a coordination, and that which expresses a contradiction is so called.
For example:
“Even a bad husband is dear to his wife; even a great fault is the locus of all arts. // VjivC_3.187 //
In this context, contradiction is understood through the word "also" (api).
In some cases, contradiction is perceived through the force of the meaning (arthasāmarthya), as for example:
“Gaurī and the others were created by you. // VjivC_3.188 //
Even when there is a commingling of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other figures, contradiction (*virodha*) can occur.
For example:
"In my head, which has the appearance of a whorl and possesses various waves, there is a special radiance that shines forth because it is not abandoned."
One should consider for oneself that these same varieties also occur in *rūpaka* (metaphor) and other figures.

Having thus examined contradiction (*virodha*), he now formulates an investigation into *samāsokti* (speech of brevity) and others, on the grounds of their potential inclusion within the shadow of contradiction:
"Samāsokti and Sahokti (conjoint expression) are not considered to be [independent] figures of speech."
Because it is a distinct ornament and because it is devoid of beauty, thus [it is not so]. Vjiv 3.51.
Regarding the passage beginning with "samāsokti" and so forth:

this figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) called "condensed expression" (*samāsokti*) that has been mentioned is "not considered to be an ornament" (*nālaṅkāratayā matā*); it does not appear as a true embellishment (*vibhūṣaṇabhāva*).
Because it does not occur as something separate, for what reason? "As another ornament" means in the sense of being a different embellishment;
and likewise, "due to the absence of beauty" means by way of being devoid of loveliness.

This is what is meant: if beauty (*rāmaṇīyakatva*) is present, it is included within that other ornament established by another category; if there is an absence of beauty, its result is a state of being devoid of splendor (*śobhā*). And so, the definition and example [are as follows]:

When another meaning, possessing similar qualifiers, is understood from what is stated, that is declared to be *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) because of its condensed meaning, as for example: [VjivC 3.190]
This tree has been born tall, possessing many branches, straight, free from serpents, firm, and bearing many great fruits; yet it has been felled by the wind.

In this case, since both the tree and the Great Being (mahāpuruṣa) are primary subjects, there must be another word denoting the substantive for the side of the Great Being, as the qualifiers belong to that side;
or else, the substantive is postulated by way of being implied through the impossibility of the qualifiers otherwise.
However, since no such conceptualization at all flashes forth, the lack of aesthetic beauty is quite evident.
The method for bringing these two, which possess such natures, down into a single sentence by way of their predominance must be stated;
for without a mutual relationship of expression, nothing of this is possible.
Nor can their connection be established by the logic of "May Umā, the form of the enemy of Kama, protect the world," [as they lack such a relation].

Since in that case the capacity for protection exists in both supreme lords, and since such a purpose is appropriate and thus worthy of being prayed for, and since it can be expressed by such words, nothing is untenable. But in this case, without a mutual connection, there is no basis whatsoever for two [entities] descending into a single sentence at the same time; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Furthermore, if some person were thus brought down by fate in such a manner, [the objection would hold].
Just as this tree is perceived [to be shaken] by the wind, so too is the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) clearly established;
therefore, it is not a separate ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
By what can existence be prevented?
Or rather, if the Great Being is perceived [as such], then the tree is established as the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
Thus, this is an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise);
therefore, that very point remains established once again by means of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).
If both meanings were intended, the inclusion of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) would be unavoidable;

thus, by that [definition] as well, the same conclusion follows. Furthermore, there is another illustration which establishes *samāsokti* (speech of brevity) as a distinct figure of speech: [Example: "The moon has risen, and the night has become full of joy; the lotus-ponds have closed their eyes, and the bees have fallen silent. In this verse, the description of the night (*rātri*) and its attendants is superimposed upon a woman (*nāyikā*) and her attendants. Here, the qualities of the woman—such as her face being like the moon, her body being like a lotus-pond, and her eyes being like bees—are suggested through the description of the night and its attendants. Therefore, this is an instance of *samāsokti*. It is not *dīpaka*, because the common property (*sāmānyadharma*) is not explicitly stated. Nor is it *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, because the subject matter at hand (*prastuta*) is not merely suggested. Nor is it *vyatireka*, because the excellence of the subject matter at hand is not established through contrast with something else. Nor is it *pratīpa*, because there is no subordination of the subject matter at hand to the non-contextual (*aprastuta*). Nor is it *tulyayogitā*, because there is no mention of a common action (*kriyā*) or attribute (*guṇa*) shared by both the contextual and the non-contextual subjects. Nor is it *ākṣepa*, because there is no denial of the literal meaning. Nor is it *arthāntaranyāsa*, because there is no generalization (*sāmānya*) or particularization (*viśeṣa*) expressed in relation to the subject matter at hand. Nor is it *vyājastuti*, because there is no praise or censure concealed under a pretext. Nor is it *vyājokti*, because there is no concealment of one's own intention. Nor is it *utprekṣā*, because there is no imaginative attribution (*adhyavasāna*) of a non-existent quality to the subject matter at hand. Nor is it *atiśayokti*, because there is no exaggeration (*atiśaya*) of the subject matter at hand. Nor is it *apahnuti*, because there is no concealment of the subject matter at hand. Nor is it *bhrāntimān*, because there is no perception of the non-contextual subject as the contextual one. Nor is it *ullekha*, because there is no description of the subject matter at hand from various perspectives. Nor is it *svabhāvokti*, because there is no description of the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the subject matter at hand. Nor is it *asambhavadvastusambandha*, because the relationship between the non-contextual and the contextual is not impossible. Nor is it *asaṅgatyalaṅkāra*, because there is no incongruity (*vaiṣamya*) between cause and effect. Nor is it *vibhāvanā*, because the effect is not produced despite the absence of its causes. Nor is it *viśeṣokti*, because the effect is not produced even when the causes are present. Nor is it *samādhi*, because there is no ease (*saukarya*) in the accomplishment of an action. Nor is it *yathāsaṃkhya*, because there is no correspondence between the order of things. Nor is it *paryāya*, because there is no succession of one thing by another. Nor is it *parivṛtti*, because there is no exchange of things. Nor is it *kārakadīpaka*, because the common property is not expressed through a single case-role (*kāraka*). Nor is it *śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇā*, because the common property is not conveyed through paronomastic adjectives. Nor is it *sahokti*, because there is no simultaneous mention of two things. Nor is it *vinokti*, because there is no description of a thing as lacking or possessing another. Nor is it *samāsabhinna*, because there is no splitting of a compound. Nor is it *udātta*, because there is no description of greatness (*udāttatva*). Nor is it *bhāvika*, because there is no vivid presentation of past or future events. Nor is it *preya
The twilight is full of passion, and the day is its forerunner;
oh, how strange is the course of fate, that even so, there is no union!
In this case, since the twilight and the day are primarily the subjects under discussion,

the perception of the narrative of a beloved woman— possessing identical adjectives— does not transcend the nature of implied simile (*pratīyamānopamā*), as it conveys that state through the connection of similarity between the two subjects.

Alternatively, if the narrative of the beloved woman is what is primarily perceived, then the twilight and the day are being described [by means of her], and thus it is simply the figure of "Praise of the Unrelated" (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*).
“Furthermore, *sahokti* (concomitant expression) is not considered a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) for the same two reasons previously stated. Thus, its definition and illustration are as follows:
“Where two actions occur simultaneously, based upon two entities...”
When two things are expressed by a single sentence, that is considered *sahokti* (simultaneous expression), as for example: [VjivC_3.193]
With the quarters of the sky turbid from falling snow, the nights grow longer along with the passion of lovers, providing the occasion for deep embraces.
In this context, the composition of captivating charm through the correlation of mutual similarity is nothing other than *upamā* (simile); in its absence,
as in "The teacher recites together with the pupil," [there is no simile].
In cases such as "the father stands with his son," that [figure] would exist even in the absence of beauty.
Thus, having set aside the status of these two as ornaments based on mere logic, he states what is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Among those, first, regarding *sahokti* (concomitance):

Where, for the sake of establishing the subject matter to be described, there is a simultaneous expression of multiple meanings by means of a single sentence, that is considered by the wise to be *sahokti* (concomitant expression). Vjiv 3.52.
“Where,” and so forth:
that is the figure of speech Sahokti (Coupling);
it is “regarded” (*matā*), meaning it appears as such.
The meaning is that it is "approved by the wise," that is, by those who know it.

Of what nature is it? It is that "in which" (yatra)—meaning in which—there is a "simultaneous" (yugapat), that is, at the same time, "utterance" (ukti)—meaning the expression—"of the meanings" (arthānām), that is, of the entities that constitute the intended purport of the sentence-meaning, "by means of a single sentence" (ekenai va vākyena), that is, by a single collection of words (padasamūha) that is itself undivided.

For what purpose? "In order to accomplish the subject matter to be described" (*varṇanīyārthasiddhaye*) means for the sake of the accomplishment (*siddhaye*), that is, the fulfillment, of the "subject matter to be described" (*varṇanīyasya*), which is intended as the primary theme. This is what is being said: where even a thing that ought to be mentioned in another sentence is expressed by that very same sentence through a striking turn of phrase (*vicchittyā*) for the sake of establishing the subject at hand. For example:
Cast your sword from your right hand upon the Śūdra ascetic for the sake of restoring life to the deceased child of the twice-born;
how can there be compassion in the hand of Rāma, who was skilled in exiling the Queen while she was distressed by her heavy pregnancy?

In this case, for the sake of establishing the primary meaning, that matter which would otherwise be expressed by another sentence has been composed with poetic elegance within a single sentence alone.

Even if a deed characterized by deceit must necessarily be performed because it is just, yet remains as if unfit to be done due to its being an object of compassion, one should still not neglect its execution;

for how could there be any room for compassion in you, who are like the hand of Rāma— the son of Daśaratha— intent on following what is fitting when he was ready to exile the Queen, distressed by her heavy pregnancy?
Therefore, there is one thing: even though he is not subject to execution, you must hand over your sword to protect the life of this Brahmin child.

Second, if you think that what is just and even mandatory should not be done by one of noble mind due to such compassion, nevertheless, you are in the hands of Rāma—the crest-jewel of the merciless—who was capable of exiling the Queen while she was burdened by her full term of pregnancy.

"How much killing of a sage is there in you?"—through this intensification of the erotic sentiment of deception (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*), a certain poetic curvature (*vakratva*) arising from the semantic richness of the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *rāma* flashes forth in both instances.
And so it is said:
"Let him be told his entire reproach; O friend, harshness toward a lord is not proper."
"Bring him here after conciliating him; or else, how can he be won over by causing him displeasure?"

"What is the use of going? It is not right to approach her. What kind of pride, O beloved who considers yourself so fortunate, can women possess?"—in conversations such as these, lovers gathered together cultivated a firm resolve of many flavors.
Here, by means of poetic charm (*vicchitti*), that which expresses the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) is composed;

for instance, although both the heroine and her friend are bound [as subjects], because each is intent upon her lover and the mediation of his union respectively, the entire sentence is perceived as the expressive word (*vācaka*).
Or as it is said:
"O Lord of all kings, I have seen in a forest region a woman, beautiful in every limb and delightful, who is separated from you. (Vajrāvalī 3.198)
In this passage, two sentence-meanings are composed for the purpose of enhancing (*vicchitti*) the development of the predominant sentiment of love-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
Now, one might ask: since multiple meanings are possible here, why does the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) not enter into it?
It is explained as follows:
in that case, since *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) occurs when there is a primary status for either one of two [meanings], whereas here such a state does not exist; therefore, it is not *śleṣa*.

In many or even in all cases, there is a subordinate status [of the elements], because they terminate in being directed toward the primary sense. Furthermore, in that case, by means of a single word, there is a simultaneous illumination of two objects—like the light of a lamp—or an illumination of two word-meanings; therein the general meaning unfolds.
But in the case of *sahokti* (concomitance), such a thing becomes a subordinate factor through a single [word].
Furthermore, by means of the sentence, the illumination of another object is enjoined through repeated recurrence;
therefore, in this case, repetition attains primacy for the word.
If it is argued that the inclusion of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is possible within this single part of the sentence, namely "O Lord of all kings," even so there is no fault;
for one ornament sometimes serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to another ornament.

In this case, while *śleṣa* (paronomasia) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) within a portion of the sentence, the primary status (*mukhyabhāva*) belongs instead to *sahokti* (concomitant expression).

(Now, one might object: "If, through such repetition, another matter is understood, then because the concomitance (*sahabhāva*) [required for] *sahokti* would be absent, the loss of the distinctness of meaning (*arthānyatvaparihāṇi*) would necessarily follow."
This is not so; for it has been stated that there is "simultaneous mention" (sahokti), and not "simultaneous cognition" (sahapratipatti).
Therefore, it is understood that this very expression of absolute coexistence (*atyantasahabhāva*) results from the comprehension of excellence; thus, there is nothing incoherent.
Some call this *samāsokti* (synecdoche), while others call it *sahokti* (concomitance).
Because of the connection with their respective meanings, other learned ones consider these two to be distinct.
This is an intermediate verse.
Thus, even though they are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), due to the majesty of their excellence of essential nature and because they possess the general character of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*),
having now mentioned certain ornaments, he proceeds to discuss those very same kinds of subordinate elements precisely because they are embellishments.
In this regard, he first states the definition of an illustration (dṛṣṭānta):

"When, based on a similarity of entities, one thing is presented as being like another, provided that words such as 'as if' (iva) cannot [otherwise] be used, that is called an illustration. (Vjiv 3.53)
"Similarity of the object," and so forth:

"The presentation"— that is, the composition— of "another" thing, distinct from the subject matter being described ("than which"), namely another entity with a different function, is called the poetic figure named *dṛṣṭānta* (the Exemplum).

How so? "Relying on the similarity of the entities" (*vastusāmyaṃ samāśritya*) means relying upon—that is, taking as the basis—the "similarity" or resemblance between two "entities" (*vastunoḥ*), namely the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).
The term "entity" (*vastu*) is employed for the purpose of making it clear that [the comparison] is devoid of similarity in terms of gender, number, case-ending, and essential form.
"In that case," [meaning] "in the absence of words such as *iva* and so forth which express similarity" (*sādṛśyābhidhāyinām*), when there is no possibility of [such particles] at the beginning;
thus, the direct denoter (*vācaka*) of the simile (*upamā*) is distinguished hereafter,
as follows:
A lotus is beautiful even when entwined with moss; the dark spot on the moon’s surface enhances its splendor.
This slender woman is exceedingly lovely even in her bark garment; for what indeed is not an ornament for those whose forms are naturally sweet?
(Here) only three quarters constitute the illustration,
because a different ornament may occur in the fourth.

Having stated the simile (dṛṣṭānta), and since the occasion for ornaments related to it has arisen, he states the "corroboration by another fact" (arthāntaranyāsa), which possesses a similar aesthetic flavor.

The arrangement of another sentence-meaning based on the equality of the primary intended meaning is to be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration), which is employed for the purpose of providing support. (Vjiv 3.54)
Regarding the phrase beginning with *vākyārtha*:
“*jñeyaḥ sor'thāntaranyāsaḥ*” means that the ornament named *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter) is “to be known,” that is, it is to be fully understood.

Of what nature is it? It is "the presentation of another sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthāntaravinyāsa*). A sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is an object denoted by a collection of words mutually connected; "another sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthāntara*) is one distinct from that [primary meaning], because it is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛtatvāt*), being different from the matter under discussion. Its "presentation" (*vinyāsa*) is a specific placement—that is, its composition in such a way as to bring delight to those who know it. For what reason? "Because of the equality of the primary intention" (*mukhyatātparyasāmyataḥ*).
"Principal" (*mukhya*) means the primary subject matter because it is the topic under discussion;
its "intention" (*tātparya*) is that toward which it is intended; "by virtue of the similarity" (*sāmyataḥ*) means by way of resemblance to that.
How is it that "it is presented as a deliverer"? It means it is formulated as a deliverer, that is to say, by way of connecting it with its logical justification.

In this context, when a general property (*sāmānya*) is to be established, a particular property (*viśeṣa*) serves as its proof; or, when a particular property is to be established, a general property serves as its proof,
because these two do not deviate from one another.
