For example:
"Without doubt, she is worthy of being taken as a wife by a Kṣatriya, since my noble mind desires her;
for the inclinations of the inner sense of the virtuous are the authority regarding matters that are subjects of doubt. (Vajrāvalī 3.201)
Or as it is said:
"For what indeed is not an ornament for those whose forms are sweet? (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.202).

Having thus stated the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth), he now states the *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis)— which possesses a similar aesthetic effect— by means of its connection with a sentence concerning a specific case: "The *ākṣepa* [is characterized] by the shadow of negation, in order to manifest supreme splendor."
This should be known as "insinuation" (ākṣepa), which pertains precisely to the subject matter at hand.
"By the shadow of negation," and so forth.
"It is to be known as *ākṣepa* (paralipsis)" means that this too is to be understood as the figure of speech *ākṣepa*.
Of what nature is it?—"The *ākṣepa* of the very subject at hand" means the rejection (*apākaraṇa*) of the very matter under discussion; that is to say, the turning back even of the intended meaning.
By what means? "By the shadow of negation" (*niṣedhacchāyayā*), that is, by the strikingness of prohibition.
For what purpose? "To manifest supreme luster" (*kāntiṃ prathayituṃ parām*), meaning to reveal an excellence of beauty.
As for example:
"O handsome one, wait a moment until I have steadied this heart that causes such separation;
then I shall speak. Or rather, depart—what can we say?"
O fortunate one, linger for a moment while I steady this heart, distressed by separation; or rather, depart—what more can we say? (Thus the shadow speaks.)

The meaning of the sentence here is as follows: "O fortunate one" (*subhage*) is an address intended to convey the state of having many lovers. This [response] of the heroine is not merely hinted at; for it—

When expressed directly, it does not achieve such a striking effect upon the consciousness as when it is apprehended through mere implication (*ākṣepa*) by means of the variety of expression; for the latter necessarily nourishes the production of delight for those who know [the art].
Having thus described the nature of implication, he states the remaining general points to be discussed regarding these [figures]:

These three—the example and the others—whether the reason exists or does not exist, may be employed according to one's intention regarding the subject matter to be stated or already stated. (Vjiv 3.56)
"Regarding the phrase 'to be stated,' etc.: those whose objects are both what will be stated and what has been stated are 'those whose objects are both to-be-stated and stated.
The connection [of the sentence] is that these three—beginning with the example (dṛṣṭānta)—are possible as the domains of both what is yet to be explained and what has already been explained."
"By what cause? means "by the desire to speak"—that is, by the wish to express according to one's own creative intuition (*pratibhāsa*).
This is the intended meaning here: that this is merely a variety of arrangement and there is no further distinction in its definition.
He speaks of another specific feature of the middle [type] to state it: "Whether the cause exists or not," [meaning] "in the case of the cause."
"In the case of a reason" means when a word expressing a reason, such as the particle *hi*, "exists"— that is, is employed—
or "alternatively," at some time, "does not exist"— that is, is not employed.
Thus, *arthāntaranyāsa* exists in two ways: by the explicit statement or the non-statement of the reason (*hetu*).
The meaning is that the mere *arthāntaranyāsa* itself constitutes an ornament.
No instance of this type has been presented here that differs from those previously mentioned; therefore, it must be inferred by oneself.

Thus, having described the ornament characterized by the excellence of its shadow, which is indicated by the negation of specific intrinsic natures, [the author now discusses] the shadow stimulated by the negation of causes.

It expresses an excellence: "Vibhāvanā is the manifestation of the object of meditation through some particular distinction, preceded by the relinquishing of its own cause for the sake of increasing its luster. (Vjiv 3.57)
Regarding the phrase "by its own causes," and so forth:

the "intense contemplation" (*bhāvanā*) of the "object" (*artha*)— that is, the subject matter under discussion— by means of "some particular" (*viśeṣeṇa kenāpi*), that is, by way of a non-worldly transformation of form, is called the poetic figure "Vibhāvanā" (the Poetic Figure of Manifestation).
Thus, the meaning here is as follows: what is that which is brought about (*bhāvyate*) without [an apparent cause]?
It is *vibhāvanā* (the description of the marvelous), characterized by an action consisting of the operation of an efficient cause capable of producing it.

“Preceded by the abandonment of its own cause” means: where the first thing—namely, the abandonment (*parityāga*), i.e., the relinquishing (*prahāṇa*)—of its own cause (*svakāraṇa*), which is the specific ground (*nimitta*) for that particular excellence, has occurred. That is the sense.
For what purpose? "For the nourishment of beauty" means for the increase of splendor.
This is what is being said: so that the subject being described may be led toward a state of transcendental distinction.
For example:
Then she attained that age which follows childhood— a natural adornment for her slender frame, a cause of intoxication known as no wine, and a weapon of Love distinct from his flowery arrows.
In this context, the poet’s intention is to describe the excellence of the extraordinary and innate [nature] of the subject by means of the abandonment of artificial causes.

Thus, having examined *vibhāvanā*—in which the nature [of the cause] is not perceived because the cause is impossible—he now describes *sasandeha*, which conveys an excellence through the presentation of doubt regarding its own nature, as it consists in being an object of deliberation:
"That in which a certain form is imagined because of the possibility of another imagination..."
These [poets] call that *sasandeha* (doubtful) when it is employed for the sake of creating a striking poetic figure (*vicchitti*) based on doubt.
Regarding the passage beginning with *yasmin*:
“*Yasmin*” means in a particular poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).

“*Utprekṣitam*” means that which is conceived through the inference of possibility and the correspondence of similarity, by way of superimposing another nature; “*rūpam*” refers to the form characterized by the movement of objects, which “*sandeham eti*” (falls into doubt).
One encounters a doubt.
For what reason? "Because another poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is possible"—that is, because there exists another [fancy] concerning the same object that surpasses the excellence of the first.
For what purpose? "For the sake of charm" (*vicchitti*), meaning for the sake of beauty.
Thus, they describe this variety of expression as "expression involving doubt" (*sasandehābhidhāna*),
as for example:
"Are the various trees and mountains colored [by twilight], or is the sky bent down, or has it been suspended?"
Has the earth been filled with unevenness, or have the quarters of the sky been withdrawn by darkness?
Or as it is said:

"As they plunged near their beloveds with eyes half-closed and squinting, their limbs trembling and their breasts heaving from their labored breathing, it was unclear whether it was fatigue or passion that spread over them. (Vajrāvalī 3.206)
Or as it is said:

"Indeed, for one who does not perceive the deer-like speed [of the senses] and whose mind is sluggish due to the company of worldly folk, the qualities of virtue, though sharpened, slip away in vain; alas, they do not delight him. (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.207)
Or as it is said:

"Is this the unique jewel in the world-treasury accumulated by the Creator through the great wealth of beauty? Or is it the lotus of the lake of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the very limit of delicacy? Or is it a fresh reflection from the ocean of loveliness, or of the moon? I cannot determine with certainty what your face, so exceedingly radiant, resembles. (VjivC 3.208)
The single variety of *sasandeha* (the figure of doubt) arises from its being rooted in poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

Having thus described *sasandeha*, which is beautiful through doubt regarding the essential nature [of an object], he now describes *apahnuti* (concealment), which is charming through the concealment of that essential nature: "In order to present another form for the object under description..."
When there is a denial of its own true nature within a [context], that is considered *apahnuti* (concealment).
"Another sun," and so forth.

As before, this [figure] is rooted in poetic fancy (utprekṣā). Because it involves a probable inference and a connection based on similarity, it pertains to "the object to be described"—that is, the subject matter at hand.
“Anyat” means something entirely new;
“to impart a form” means to superimpose another form;
“denial of its own nature” (svarūpāpahnavaḥ) means the repudiation of its own essence. This is possible.
“In which [verse], ‘this’— that is, this very kind of statement—
is considered ‘denial’ (*apahnuti*) by those who know it;
as for example:”

This is the radiant sun, the foremost of luminaries, who provides eyes for the entire world; this is not the moon, whose most lovely face brings delight to the eyes. Rather, he has been appointed by me to take turns with the pitiless Mind-born God to pierce the hearts of those separated from their lovers, and to lead his victorious flower-arrows to the state of having sharpened tips.
An example of the denial of a mere attribute while the subject remains in its original state by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*) is as follows:
"Your status as one whose arrows are flowers, and the moon’s possession of cool rays—both of these are seen to be untrue in the case of people like me.
The moon emits fire with its frost-filled rays, and you too make your flower-arrows as hard as adamant. (Vajrāvalī 3.210)

In this instance, by virtue of the variety of expression (*bhaṇiti*), a negation that is not based on verbal testimony (*aśābda*) has been established; for, having set aside the delicate performance of effects—which is the nature appropriate to qualities such as being "the flower-arrowed one" (*kusumaśara*)—there is described instead the performance of effects that are contrary to it and terrifying.
And in some cases, negation occurs through the connection with similarity (*sādṛśya-samanvaya*), as follows:
This pale parasol, radiant with expansive light, does not rise in the expanse of the sky as the full moon of his body—possessing a beauty of perfect nourishment—seeks to conquer the world;
rather, it is now the fitting canopy for Māra, who is intent solely on the effort of shattering the pride of people swollen with vanity through the splendor of the evening twilight.

Having thus described how each ornament, by virtue of its independent nature, produces aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) with respect to its respective object of embellishment, he now describes that same quality when they are combined:
"Where ornaments shine while functioning in mutual association—just as word-meanings [contribute] to the sentence-meaning—that is designated as 'blending' (*saṃsṛṣṭi*). (Vjiv 3.60)
“rājanti” and so forth:
“yatra” means in which;
“alaṅkārāḥ” means the ornaments, being endowed with the excellence of the subject matter, “rājanti,” that is, they shine.

"Saṃsṛṣṭi is so designated"—this ornament is called by the name *saṃsṛṣṭi*. How do they "shine"? He says: "Insofar as the word-meanings [are present] in the sentence-meaning"—that is, in the reality characterized as *tātparya* (intended meaning)—"in such a manner" (*yathā*), that is, by which mode, "the word-meanings," whose own natures are distinct and which are denoted by the words that constitute parts of the sentence, exist.

For although [words] manifest by their own nature, they possess a nature based on a relationship characterized by mutual connection; thus, while experiencing dependence upon the primary [meaning], they convey that very [primary meaning] which consists of a collection and has as its purport the sense of a single sentence.
In this manner, when there is a non-contradictory co-inherence between these two, they function through mutual connection as related members.

The intended meaning is this: because their capacity is understood through mutual connection, even those figures of speech that reside only in a single part of a sentence— which is itself a constituent of a larger, distinct sentential meaning— manifest as dependent upon one another, bringing about a certain aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) that pervades the entire sentential meaning by means of a mutual interrelation perceivable only by connoisseurs.

Just as—embraced by the twilight in a state of deep meditation, which has spread wide with glances from the sun reddened by fresh saffron and met with her trailing garments, the arrival of evening now shines upon the *kurabaka* tree like the Goddess herself; it offers its longing to the tree, whose bees of darkness fall away, agitated by the sprout-like rays of the moon. (Vajrāvalī 3.212)

In this case, a certain striking elegance of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthavakratā*) manifests itself, acquired through the excellence of mutual interaction between the metaphors (*rūpaka*) and other figures, which have each fulfilled their own individual functions.
Or, for example:

"O Kingly Lover, just as a plantain tree is brought to witheredness by you—whose essence is gained through the movement of your eyes that vomit forth the fire of poison—so too has she, who is as tender as a sprout, been reduced to such a state."
Even now, in the dense groves of Kailāsa, which are marked by the playful smiles of the rays of the moon that is the crest-jewel of the Lord, it does not sprout again.

Here, as before, the distinctiveness of *vakratā* (poetic curvature) produced by the excellence of the mutual intermingling of figures such as *rūpaka* (metaphor) and others is perceived. Having thus explained *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction), he now describes the figure *saṃkara* (commixture), which produces a similar kind of aesthetic splendor: "This collection of ornaments has attained a state of commixture with one another."
When multiple [meanings] flash forth within a single sentence, that is designated as *saṃkara* (conflation).

"Alaṅkāra... and so forth. "This collection of ornaments"—that is, this multitude of ornaments such as *rasavat* and the rest—"which possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, is called by the name 'conjunction' (*saṃkara*)," meaning it is designated as having the name "conjunction. Of what nature is it? "Having reached a state of being mixed," that is, having attained a state of intermingling.
Having ascended to the state of appearing as a powerful entity—
performing what? "Sphuran" (throbbing), that is, manifesting its own throbbing while approaching the state of being perceived—
it attains a state of intermingling within the sentence.

Since no specific distinction for their coexistence is possible, any poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) mentioned within [the preceding discussion] that, according to its occurrence, becomes commingled with another ornament attains the designation of "commixture" (*saṃkara*).
Consequently, the term "commixture" applies to the entire collection of ornaments.
For example: [Example omitted as per instructions.]

O Lord, in this region of the sky, your creeper of fame—whose roots grow in the belly of the underworld with the exceedingly white hoods of the lord of serpents, which displays the beauty of emerging young sprouts in every direction through the tusks of the elephants of the quarters—now bears this fruit: the orb of the moon, moist with nectar, appearing like a cluster of blossoming stars.
In this context, the poetic figure of *rūpaka* (metaphor), namely "the creeper of fame" (*kīrtivallī*), does not attain logical propriety without the suspicion that it is already established as such.

Therefore, the poet intends here a suggested (*pratīyamāna*) *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), based on the inference of the greatness of that [fame] arising from the manifestation of such activity— the very basis for the suspicion—
since for both of these [the metaphor and the fancy], their own essential nature cannot even be attained without mutual corroboration.
Regarding the term *vaśyati* ("it will be understood"): in cases where two [figures] are mixed, the expression of such a mixture proceeds precisely from their mutual compatibility (*saṃvāda*).

For example, in a portion of a sentence such as "like the shedding of the slough by the sky-serpent," because it is impossible to employ the expression with total certainty, the opportunity for the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) to acquire its own nature is provided by the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) "like the shedding of the slough."
The same applies to *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because here too the designation of the *saṃkara* (commixture) ornament is employed.

Now, by this same logic, should not the mention of the *saṃkara* ornament proceed in such instances as "In the creation of her... (*asyāḥ sargavidhau*) and "Is it from the tree of youth? (*kiṃ tāruṇyataroḥ*)?
It does not proceed,
because here, since the capacity of the object is understood,
there is no possibility of doubt without the occurrence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
And likewise, in the case of the other [type of *rūpaka*], the reality (*tattva*) of both these is equal.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that when a *sasandeha* (doubtful figure) is internally established as an ornament for those two, there is a charming beauty like that of a necklace consisting of strings of gems.
In the case of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture), there is a captivating quality like a garland of gems possessing various kinds of luster.

Since the ornament of *saṃkara* (combination) possesses a state comparable to incomparable beauty due to its abundance of variegated arrangements of jewels of diverse luster, everything has been fully analyzed.

Having thus defined the ornaments according to their occurrence, he now begins to address the defect of the definition’s lack of pervasiveness (*avyāpti*) regarding certain [ornaments] that have not been defined, on account of their being other ornaments or their being devoid of beauty.
Thus: [he says... "by way of being another ornament" and "due to the absence of beauty."
Whatever ornaments there may be, they do not function as ornaments in the slightest degree.
"Ornaments," and so forth:

"whatever ornaments" other than those previously mentioned "are not accepted as ornaments even in the slightest degree"—that is, they are not admitted as embellishments—for what reason? "Because they are themselves other ornaments"; that is, an ornament distinct from [the primary] ornament is "another ornament."
"Distinct from them";

"by way of being that" (*tadbhāvena*) means by way of having that as its intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāvatvena*), that is, by way of non-difference from it, meaning as one of those very things previously mentioned. "In that way, by way of being devoid of splendor" (*śobhāśūnyatayā tathā*): "splendor" (*śobhā*) is radiance; "devoid of that" means lacking or abandoned by it; "the state of being devoid of splendor" is *śobhāśūnyatā*; by that, acting as the cause.
It is not only for those two reasons;
even on account of their being objects to be adorned—that is, as things to be embellished—it is untenable for them to function as ornaments.
And thus—
That which was previously declared by the ancients to be the figure of speech *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence in order) is not accepted as a figure of speech even for two reasons. Vjiv 3.63.

"The ornament known as *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence in order) has been handed down by earlier authorities; however, that which some have designated by its own name as *tulyakrama* (parallelism) is not an ornament for two reasons: because it constitutes a different type of ornament, and because it lacks aesthetic beauty."
And thus is its illustration:

"The lotus, the moon, the bee, the elephant, the male cuckoo, and the peacock—these have been conquered by you through [respectively] your face, your beauty, your eyes, your gait, your voice, and your hair. (VjivC 3.215)
In this case, since the definition is formulated by the author himself, there is no particular charm due to the absence of a striking mode of expression (*bhaṇiti*).
Even if such charm were present, it is traditionally held that similarity (*sāmya*) or contrast (*vyatireka*) constitutes its very life, and not merely the state of having an equal number [of terms].

If there were only the state of having an equal number, nothing more would be added than what follows from the rule of sequential correspondence—namely, "the designation of an equal number of items follows the order of enumeration" (*yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*)—because of that sequential assignment of numbers.

For certain figures such as benediction (*āśis*) and others, which are considered ornaments, the status of being an ornament is untenable. The definitions and examples of benediction are not recited here;

however, since in those cases the very object to be wished for is primarily the thing to be described, it possesses the nature of the "embellished" (*alaṅkārya*), and thus the defects mentioned regarding the *preyas* ornament apply to them.
One [figure] should not be considered incompatible with another when a different ornament is present;
for there may be both *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) and *saṃkara* (conjunction), even in cases where such coexistence has not been observed elsewhere.
(Intermediate Verse):

Even in the case of *viśeṣokti* (peculiar assertion), since it is included within the figures already mentioned and serves as the substrate (*alaṃkārya*) for other figures, its status as a distinct ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*) is untenable.
Thus, an example of this [is as follows]:
That flower-armed god alone conquers the three worlds;
though his body was taken away by Śambhu, his power was not taken away.

In this case, the sentence-meaning consists merely in the nature of Kandarpa—which is distinct from the victory [of others] well-known to all the world—being treated as something transcendent (*lokottara*).
Thus, [these] are subtle and slight causes [of beauty, but] not ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
And so says Bhāmaha:

Furthermore, the subtle cause (*hetu*) or the slight trace (*leśa*) is not considered an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), because it does not express the intended meaning of the whole through an indirect mode of expression (*vakrokti*). (VjivC 3.218)
And likewise, here is an example of the subtle:
"Having perceived that the lover was thinking of the time for their tryst, the clever woman closed her play-lotus, its meaning conveyed through a glance from her smiling eyes. (VjivC 3.219)
In this case, it is the soul of the description that is subtle, and not the ornament;
why? Because the intended meaning is conveyed directly through denotation (*abhidhā*) by means of such a device.
An example of *leśa* (the "slight") is as follows:
The guards might discover my passion for the princess through the bristling of my hair; alas, I have found this forest to be a cool breeze!
In this case as well, it must be asked: how can this very same matter deserve to be an ornament?
According to the maxim, "Whatever a word is intended for, that is its meaning.
An example of a reason [is as follows]:
This Malaya breeze, which causes the sprouts of the mature sandalwood trees to sway, produces joy for everyone.
Likewise, even this "metaphorical simile" (upamārūpaka) is not a [separate] ornament:
The foot of the Lord of Chariots (Viṣṇu), which serves as a measuring rod for the full extent of the sky,
is victorious— a fresh mirror for the moon-like face of the Siddha women.
In this case, there is no connection whatsoever between the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and the expressive word (*vācaka*) regarding the *rasavad-alaṅkāra*.
Furthermore, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*)," it would have to be intended as a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

Or it may be a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). In that case, regarding the alternative of a copulative compound (*dvandva*), there would be a metaphor in one part of the sentence and a simile in another; thus, there would be no single underlying basis for the composition as a whole.

In that case as well, since each [element] shines forth equally in its own place by virtue of being a vibration, a collective whole (*samudāya*)—which would serve as the substantive (*viśeṣya*)—is impossible without mutual dependence; thus, the alternative of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is untenable.

Even in the case of a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), whether applied to the entire sentence or to a single part, both [qualities] would have to reside simultaneously in one and the same entity, which is impossible, like the coexistence of shadow and sunlight, two things that are mutually contradictory.

When speech adheres to only one side, it is impossible for the other side to find an opportunity even while the nature of each individual signifier and signified is being determined; thus, a compound of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of a collection [of both] is ineffective without mutual dependence.

Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to determine either one of them in that case, and since no fault arises from the conceptualization of the alternative, the conventional usage of "confusion" (*saṃkara*) applies.

In the present case, however, even though such a nature has been established, because there is an intention to express its complete perfection, that which— even while its own self-nature is established— is mounted upon the swing of doubt, must be understood as something merely incidental, determined by the power of the sentence, as if it were sometimes present, though in reality it is non-existent and unstable.

The third [type], consisting of a collection of ornaments that is delightful by virtue of its implied mode [of expression], is to be designated as the "essence of the curvature of the sentence" (*vākyavakratā*). He outlines the nature of this sentence-curvature, which consists of a composite whole:

"It is radiant with qualities such as *lāvaṇya* (grace), adorned with playful gestures through the placement of every word, made charming by a few ornaments fashioned with artistic ingenuity (*vicchitti*)."
Just as a heroine captivates the mind by being exceedingly flavorful and moistening the heart, so too does the eloquent speech of a great poet, which is both noble and artful, possess the same power.
"Beauty and so forth"— by this phrase,
he will provide an illustration for the understanding of the nature of these very sentences.
[He will explain] that which consists of the collection of those [words].
And just as the heroine is able to captivate the mind and heart through her aesthetic flavor (*rasavattā*), so too [is she]—
of what sort?— "Resplendent with qualities such as *lāvaṇya*," [meaning] by means of *lāvaṇya* and other such attributes.

"Radiant" (*ujjvalā*) through "qualities" (*guṇaiḥ*) such as *lāvaṇya*—that is, through qualities characterized by the initial mention [of the subject]—"resplendent" (*bhrājiṣṇu*); "graced with elegance" (*vilāsāñcitā*) through "the placement of every word" (*pratipadanyāsaiḥ*)—"the placement of every word" (*pratipadanyāsaḥ*) refers to the composition of each individual verbal and nominal suffix; [graced] by these, and "adorned with some particular artistry" (*vicchittyā*), meaning by a certain stroke of ingenuity (*vaidagdhyabhaṅgyā*), "composed" (*racitaiḥ*) or arranged, "few" (*alpaiḥ*), that is, limited, "burdens of ornaments" (*vibhūṣaṇabharaḥ*), namely, figures of speech such as simile (*upamā*) and the like.
Speech that captivates the mind—that which delights the heart—when adorned with a measured array of poetic figures (*vicchitti*), becomes a repository of supreme beauty.
What kind of speech is this? It is "noble in expression," uttered with the quality of magnanimity (*audārya*).

Furthermore, when it is "exceedingly flavorful" through its possession of aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*) and so forth, it is "heart-warming," meaning its intention is full of sapidity; even a beloved woman, when graced by such charms, becomes likewise [captivating].
In the case of the heroine (*nāyikā*), "grace" (*lāvaṇya*) and so forth refer to beauty and the like;
"the placement of feet" (*padanyāsa*) refers to the movement of the feet;
and "sportiveness" (*vilāsa*) refers to a particular kind of gesture (*ceṣṭāviśeṣa*). (In the case of speech:)
*Vicchitti* is ingenuity;
*vāk* is speech or sentence; *bhūṣaṇas* are ornaments or poetic figures (*alaṃkāras*).

*Abhidhā* is speech; it is the capacity of the composition. Thus ends the third chapter (*unmeṣa*) of the *Vakroktijīvita*, a treatise on poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṅkāra*), composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Kuntaka.

*Vakroktijīvita*, Fourth Unmeṣa: Thus, after having illuminated the variety of speech (*vākya-vakratā*)—which is like a wish-fulfilling tree for the essence of the entire field of literature—the author introduces the variety of context (*prakaraṇa-vakratā*), which has now reached its proper occasion:
"Wherein the conduct of those who act is adorned by the movement of unrestrained enthusiasm and is characterized by the expression of their own inner intentions. (Vjiv 4.1)
Even when a desire has arisen that cannot be doubted from its very root,
some boundless and unprecedented curvature of the components of the composition unfolds.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yatra" and so forth:
the connection is that "the state of being crooked (*vakrabhāva*)— namely, the crookedness of the parts of the composition (*prabandhāṃśavakratā*) [in a *prakaraṇa*]— occurs."

Of what nature is it? "Boundless"—that is, limitless—"wherein"—in which—"the activity of those who act"—those preoccupied with the undertaking of various occupations—"some indescribable"—transcendental—"unfolds"—emerges.
Of what specific character is it? "Adorned by the expansive grace of the throbbing of unrestrained enthusiasm"—possessing a vast splendor flashing from unimpeded resolve.
For this very reason, there is an incomparable poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) that shines with the reflection of one's own inner disposition, brought forth from the heart—
provided that "the desire, from its very root, is such that its arising cannot be doubted," meaning the intended object is one whose emergence from the core [of the heart] is entirely conceivable.

Therefore, this is the meaning here: where, even when the desired object has not yet been fully revealed, the path of resolve belonging to those whose sole wealth is their boundless honor shines as an ornament for both the context and the composition— a path characterized by an uninterrupted expansion of effort and a striking charm of consciousness that produces a unique aesthetic curvature.

There are mountains by the thousands in every direction, yet these arms of yours are like anthills, though they long for the play of the essence of fierce valor; you have heard the story of Agastya from his own lips—O monkeys, do you truly have no curiosity even to fill a mere puddle at the edge of the ocean?
Following the clamor from behind the scenes, this reply was uttered by the monkeys:
"How many mountains have not been tossed about in the vicinity of the monkeys, assuming the joyful state of a ball out of an intense longing for curiosity?
Yet, even though they possess knowledge of the stories concerning the Lord of Lopāmudrā, there remains a surge of shame due to the touch of the remnants of the Son of the Wind."
In this very context, which is the remnant of the Son of the Wind (Hanumān) and serves as a basis for deliberation, one should recall the various modes of indirectness (*vakratā*).
When Jāmbavān was questioned by Rāma, who remarked, "Noble sir, this resolve to bind the ocean is difficult for them," he spoke these words:
"Even in paths where boundless desires have not yet sprouted..."
The skillful undertake the exertion of what is to be done and they triumph.

Other such examples of this kind, which are beautiful through the grace of their novel and wonderful stylistic turns and constitute the very essence of elegant speech, should be discerned from that same source.

Or, for instance, as in the fifth canto of the *Raghuvamśa*, regarding the Lord of the Earth, who was adorned by a girdle of four [oceans] and who offered all his wealth as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the initiation of the sacrifice known as the Viśvajit.

When the sage— who had uprooted Raghu’s display of ambition by observing the clay vessel presented as a respectful offering during that illustration of the secret of innate nobility, and who was forbidden from entering—
asked, "O learned one, what object is to be given by you to the preceptor, and of what value? (VjivC 4.4)

"Immediately following your question, [the King] offered a teacher’s fee of fourteen crores of gold; having received this, O Worthy One, you should deign to wait for two or three days while I prepare what is required for your sake."

Thus, as the speech— its interior guarded by the weight of its unimpeded profundity— adorns the fire-sanctuary, the determination for victory over Kubera, born from the estimation of him as a mere vassal, attains an indescribable power that delights the hearts of the connoisseurs;
for even the waves of the nectar of well-spoken verses arise from this very source.
These are the things to be tasted.
And something beautiful, characterized by the throbbing movement of life within this context, is cited as an example,
as follows:
The king bestowed that entire heap of glittering gold, obtained from Kubera who was being assailed [by him],
upon Kautsa— like a portion of Mount Sumeru split off by the thunderbolt.
Here, because of the bestowing of all that gold— immeasurable, as it were, through the perception of its resemblance to the foot of Mount Meru shattered by the thunderbolt—

a unique limit of the magnanimity of the treasury unfolds; this magnanimity surpasses even the celestial wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), which do not excel in the distribution of wealth when they are afflicted by the stain of mere conceptualization, while Dilīpa’s son, though beset by such a passion for riches, remains otherwise.

By which [act], the very life-force of that preeminent first utterance beginning with "For the sake of my teacher" was sustained— that utterance which loosened the knots of the pride and gravity inherent in his conception, which longed for an accumulation of peerless fame, and which could not endure any other donor—
and furthermore:
both of them became objects of praise for the people dwelling in Sāketa because of their noble character.
The teacher bestows more than he receives; the king grants wealth even beyond what is requested.
And so forth.
Here too, [we see] Kautsa, who would not accept even gold beyond what was to be given as a teacher’s fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
and Raghu, who gave a hundredfold or a thousandfold more than what was requested— [the two of them], while contending with one another...
The boundless excellence of their desire and magnanimity spread an indescribable seal of great festivity among the inhabitants of Sāketa, the likes of which had never been heard before.

Thus, this distinctiveness of structural ingenuity (*prakaraṇavakratā*) found in the compositions of great poets, which overflows with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), is to be discerned by connoisseurs for themselves.
He elucidates this very point by way of another perspective:
"Even on the path of narrative variety employed within a traditional plot (itivṛtta), another kind of elegance shines forth, distinct from the mere beauty of invented fragments. (Vjiv 4.3)
In such a way that the entire composition appears as if it were alive,
this treatise shines forth, overflowing with a sentiment that has ascended to its highest pitch.
Regarding the term *itivṛtta*:

"In that manner, a crookedness (*vakratā*) arises that is distinct from the beauty of produced parts"—that is to say, by that means, an extraordinary mode of crookedness (*vakrabhāvabhaṅgī*), characterized by the loveliness of artificial arrangements, unfolds and captivates those of sensitive taste (*sahṛdaya*). This is the sense.

"On what [path]?"—on "the path of the manifoldness of the narrative," that is, on the way of the diverse nature of the story of the poem. Of what kind? "Even though employed for historical events"—that is, even when there is an adoption of traditional history (*itihāsa*). It requires such application; therefore, he says: "Just as it is the life-force of the entire composition."
The *prakaraṇa* shines forth as that element which, in whatever manner, appears as the life-giver of the entire work, such as an epic (*sargabandha*) and so on.

Of what nature is it? It is "filled with rasa ascended to its peak" (*kāṣṭhādhirūḍharasanirbhara*), meaning it is completely saturated with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others manifested in their first outpouring.

Therefore, this is the ultimate point here: even in a narrative such as the *Mahābhārata*— which is like a casket containing stories of renowned variety and beauty, and which is sealed by an ocean of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— one must compose those collections of wondrous effects that produce specific sentiments and moods (*rasa-bhāva*), provided they are caused by appropriately matched, incomparable motives revealed by one's own exceedingly beautiful innate intuition, and which lack any conceptualization of superior or inferior excellence.

By employing this particular mode of extraordinary *vakratā* (poetic deviation) throughout his work, the poet brings satisfaction to the entire assembly of poets and connoisseurs. Even within a literary composition (*prabandha*), the nourishment of a beauty made lovely by the cause of refined and novel refinement experiences a charm comparable to that of an ancient, cracked painting whose excellence is made to shine forth by its outlines.

In the drama *Abhijñānaśākuntala*, there is a delightful recognition of a line of incomparable beauty—a pinnacle of charming loveliness perceived in a moment of vision—which, by not being obstructed, serves as the cause for eclipsing all other young women.
It unfolds:

even though the circumstances that caused Duṣyanta’s forgetfulness of Śakuntalā— whom he had long known through various amorous diversions prompted by the height of a mutual love made delightful by the secrets of their conversations, which were sustained by confidence and esteem— had been related, his cruel anger was provoked by what appeared as a very slight offense.
The poet has brought about the curse of the sage Durvāsas, who was averse to compassion;
for in that preeminent dramatic work, Śakuntalā— her inner state overwhelmed by the onset of unbearable sorrow born from the first day of separation from her beloved—
is [described] while he stands agitated at the edge of the courtyard near the hermitage.
"O Great Seer, because of your absorption in anger,
you have been reflecting with undistracted mind [on him] and do not perceive me standing before you, a treasure-house of asceticism.
Even though he has been awakened, he will not remember you, just as a negligent person does not recall a conversation held previously."
Thus was he cursed.
Though being urged by his two friends, who were distressed upon hearing that,
and though about to be exiled, the eminent sage [consented] to the viewing of the ring belonging to his beloved as a condition for the curse.

She made [the river] her garment; and as the daughter of the sage was proceeding toward her beloved, the ring from her hand— whose sprout-like fingers were adorned— fell unnoticed into the water somewhere at the descent of the exceedingly winding, wavy river, where it was swallowed in pieces by a fish, agitated by the suspicion that the shimmering circle of its many rays was a piece of fresh meat, and where it gleamed with the brilliance of rubies amidst the confusion.
After some time, the fisherman, who was its eventual destroyer, returned it once more.

Amidst such a dramatic arrangement—which, like a vessel containing a treasure of aesthetic flavor, possesses a certain elegance throughout the entire play—the King Paurava’s state of helplessness was confirmed by two factors: first, by his understanding of the song containing the reproach of the wandering bee; and second, by the lingering fragrance of the memory of his beloved, which had been cast off by the sage’s curse, yet continued to manifest within him.
And thus,
when a living being, even though currently happy, becomes filled with longing upon seeing beautiful sights or hearing sweet sounds,
it is surely because the mind remembers, from a state of ignorance, the friendships formed in other births that were made firm by habitual attachment.
Here, for connoisseurs, there shines forth a source of wonder entirely distinct from the beauty of the love-letter recalling Menakā, who was so charmingly bewildered;

furthermore, even though she had been turned away, there arose a great outburst of indignation toward her who possessed the token of her deception and whose marriage and conception were announced by the disciples of the Great Sage.

When Bharata’s mother— whose skill in forest excursions was made known by the sweet play of her speech, which produced the resonance of the lute through the excellence of all feminine beauty achieved by [the woman] who had cast off her veil so suddenly that her natural modesty was slightly transgressed— uttered such harshness of rejection toward the king, it served as a premonition of the remorse that would arise from his future curse.

O King, the words of the chamberlain there— describing how [the two lovers] were exceedingly heart-gladdening due to their union with a flood of unrestrained passion mutually manifesting, and how they were simultaneously overwhelmed by the onset of the unbearable fever of separation ignited by the roar of battle for the sake of their reunion at the end of the curse, yet were instantly made to rejoice greatly by the contact of the ring— are most pleasing to those of sensitive hearts.

Having abandoned the practice of elaborate adornment, wearing only a single golden bracelet on his left forearm, with lips reddened by sighs and eyes weary from sleeplessness due to anxiety, he— though diminished like a great gem polished by its own luster— is not perceived as such because of the quality of his inner radiance.
He hates what was once delightful; he is no longer attended daily by his former companions; he passes the nights awake, tossing and turning upon the edge of his bed;
and when, out of courtesy, he utters a fitting word to the women of the inner apartments, he then falters over their names and remains for a long time abashed and embarrassed. (Vajracchedikā 4.11)
Here, the king’s poetic ingenuity (*viśeṣaṇavakratā*) and the verbal ingenuity (*vacanavakratva*) in the word "in the lineages" (*gotreṣu*) produce an indescribable wonder in the mind.

Furthermore, for the king himself, whose eyes were fixed upon the painting he had personally drawn, this was a heartfelt message from his beloved, sealed with her own seal and consisting of nothing but memory.

O bee, I have already tenderly sipped at my beloved’s bimba-fruit lip during our amorous festivals—a lip as alluring as the unblemished young shoots of a tree; if you touch it, I shall confine you within the interior of a lotus.
Thus, [the *utpādya*] should be understood as something to be relished precisely when it has been brought forth.

Furthermore, in the absence of this—this attainment of the beauty of even a fragment of the *utpādya*—the distaste arising from groundless forgetfulness reaches the state of being a cause for the very deformity (*virūpakatā*) of the poetic figure (*rūpaka*), because of the lack of the beauty of even a fragment of the *utpādya*. This should be explained in two ways: namely, that in some cases, that which is non-existent is itself what is to be brought forth (*utpādya*).
In some cases, even that which is inherently proper must be rendered otherwise for the sake of delighting the hearts of connoisseurs;
as, for example, the slaying of Mārīca in the *Dātarāghava*.
This has already been explained previously.

In this way, other examples of her graceful curvature (*vakratā-vicchitti*) should also be discerned for oneself within the compositions of great poets. The words of poets, which are replete with compositions filled with the continuous outpouring of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), possess life; they do not merely rely on the narrative (*kathā*).
(Thus is the intermediate verse.
He further reveals another mode of structural deviation (*prakaraṇavakratā*):
"That which possesses the connection of the fruit, the bond, and the consequence for certain parts of the composition."
The vibration of the relationship between benefactor and beneficiary manifests clearly.
The secret of novel ingenuity is born from a certain poet, appearing in the flash of intuition that reflects an uncommon apprehension.
"Sūte" means she brings forth or unfolds.
What? "The secret of a new sacrifice"—the Upaniṣad of a novel and crooked state of being. "Of someone"—not of everyone.
"Of the poet" (*kaveḥ*)— that is, of the one who composes; in other words, of one who is skilled in the beautiful arrangement [of words] regarding the subject at hand (*prastuta*).
What is this "activity of being the beneficiary and the benefactor"—the majesty of the state of being the recipient of grace and the bestower of grace?
What is he doing while "manifesting"—that is, while unfolding?

Of what nature is he? He is "possessed of the connection to the bond of the fruit," meaning he possesses a concern for the primary effect; the sense is that he is skillful in attending to the task at hand.
He asks how such a thing is so, and says: "appearing in a manifestation that is unique"—shining with the power and majesty of an incomparable unfolding.
Of what? "Of portions of a composition," that is, of the constituent sections (*prakaraṇa*).

The connection is as follows: "of that" refers to "the structural curvature"—that is, the state of being curved—of "the composition," such as a drama (*nāṭaka*) or an epic poem (*sargabandha*). "Wherein the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*) occurs" means wherein the final winding up takes place.

"By disregarding the perfection of rasa in the *itivṛtta* and the *anyathāvṛtta*": in the *itivṛtta*, that is, in history (*itihāsa*), that which is "otherwise"—in another manner—"narrated" (*vṛttā*) or accomplished, namely the "perfection of rasa," the aesthetic arrangement such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth; "by disregarding" (*tadupekṣayā*) means by paying no heed to it, that is, by abandoning it.

Of what [work]? "Of that very one whose form is narrative" (kathāmūrti), that is, of that very body of poetry (*kāvyadeha*). Of what kind? For what purpose? "For the accomplishment of the joy of those to be instructed" (*vineyānandaniṣpattye*), that is, for the production of delight in kings and others who are to be enlightened.

By this it is meant: the poet, setting aside the sequence of aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) occurring in the composition of a particular narrative that forms part of the plot, brings about a conclusion through some other, uniquely desirable sentiment that delights noble persons; thus, he imparts a certain elegance (*vakrimāṇa*) to the literary work.

As in the *Nāgānanda*, there Jīmūtavāhana— the crest-jewel of all those who possess compassion— protecting Śaṅkhacūḍa by the sacrifice of his own body even from Vainateya, the bringer of death, despite his irresistible enmity, did not merely protect him alone, but rather his entire lineage.
Setting aside his skill in matters of fact, the poet imparts a certain poetic curvature even to the title of the primary plot-structure. (Vjiv 4.24)
"Let alone skill regarding things"— let it "be"— that is, let it remain far away—
"regarding things"— namely, regarding the subjects to be explained in the context—
"skill"— that is, aesthetic refinement (vicchitti).

“In poetry, the poet creates a certain kind of *vakratā* (artful deviation). Regarding the phrase “in poetry”—that is, in drama (*nāṭaka*), epic compositions (*sargabandha*), and so forth—he “creates a certain kind of *vakratā*,” meaning he produces it.
“The poet” is one who illuminates the expansion of marvelous creative intuition (*pratibhā*).

By what? By that which is "marked by the name of the primary plot-structure" (*pradhānasaṃvidhānāṅka*): "primary" (*pradhāna*) means that which constitutes the very life-force of the composition; "plot-structure" (*saṃvidhāna*) means the arrangement of the narrative;
and "marked" (*aṅka*) means that which has it as its sign or distinguishing characteristic, or that in which it resides—thus it is so described.
That [quality] and its name—by that as well.
The word "api" (also/even) illuminates wonder.
This is its secret: the curvature (*vakratā*) of a literary composition manifests through the discernment of various objects that have been investigated.
What is wonderful?
Even more wonderful is this: that it is established even by its name, which is characterized by being composed of the most excellent arrangement and endowed with meaningful syllables.
For example— *Abhijñānaśākuntalam*, *Mudrārākṣasam*, *Pratimāniruddham*, *Māyāpuṣpakam*, *Kṛtyārāvaṇam*, *Chalitarāmam*, *Puṣpadūṣitakam*, and so forth.

Such titles of poetic compositions, possessing incomparable descriptions (*vilakṣaṇavakratāsarasā*) and letters that convey an internal, specific relationship, indeed embody a striking artistry (*vakrimāṇam*).
Furthermore, poetic compositions such as the *Hayagrīvavadha*, *Śiśupālavadha*, *Pāṇḍavābhyudaya*, *Rāmānanda*, and *Rāmacarita*,
though simple in nature and bound within a single style,
nourish an invaluable crookedness (*vakratā*) through their mutual distinctiveness. (Vjiv 4.25)
“They nourish” means they cause to blossom;
“invaluable” means immeasurable;
“crookedness” means the state of being crooked.

By what? "By mutual distinctness"—that is, by their reciprocal dissimilarity. What are these? "Poetic compositions"—those preceded by metaphors (rūpaka). Of what nature are they? "Even though bound within a single frame"—that is, joined together by a single narrative theme.

By whom? By "lords of poets"—that is, by those who elsewhere condense an extensive subject matter or expand upon what is concise, bringing about novelty through the synthesis of diverse expressions, denotations, and ornaments. The intended meaning here is as follows: even by many [poets] who carry out a single, particular narrative whose loveliness has blossomed forth...
Many compositions being composed by elephant-like poets, failing to attain even the slightest mutual correspondence, assume a certain curvature that delights the hearts of connoisseurs;
as, for example, within the very same narrative of Rāma, the *Rāmābhyudaya*, *Udāttarāghava*, *Vīracarita*, *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, *Kṛtyārāvaṇa*, *Māyāpuṣpaka*, and others.

For these works, being continuous and excellent, proceed by that very path of narrative; through the richness of their composition, which contains a downpour of unrestrained aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), they manifest at every step, every sentence, and every section with a preponderance of ever-new stylistic turns.

They are radiant, captivating the excellence of the hero’s ever-emerging and marvelous qualities, and even when tasted many times, they produce an excess of joy for those of sensitive heart (*sahṛdaya*).
In the same way, other illustrations may also be brought forth:
"Though their opening is the same, compositions shine forth individually through their own inherent qualities, like living beings with their own bodies. (VjivC 4.56)
This is an intermediate verse.
He further establishes its divisions: "In all the compositions of great poets, there exists *vakratā* (artistic deviation)."
To those who teach the path of policy accomplished through novel means.
"Of the compositions of great poets"—meaning those composed by the most eminent poets who are peerless and skilled in creating new works—"of all" [compositions].
(Of what kind?
"Those which teach the path of policy produced by novel means"—"novel" means fresh.

"Upāyas" refers to the modes of application such as conciliation (*sāman*) and so forth, which are within the domain of those who know them; "accomplished by these" means perfected. Those who teach—that is, instruct—the "path of policy" (*nayavartma*), meaning the way of conduct (*nītimārga*), are referred to as such;
[the word] belongs to them.

What is meant is this: even in all the compositions of great poets, there is indeed found some degree of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arising from the fruit of a principle rendered exquisite by the employment of novel turns of expression, conveyed through the medium of instruction to the subject matter. As in the *Mudrārākṣasa*, where the various operations of policy, elaborated through the power of pre-eminent wisdom, truly flourish.
And just as it has been explained specifically with reference to the *Tāpasavatsarāja*,
so too should other instances be inferred;
for the absence of the excellence of *vakrokti* (poetic deviation) is observed in that which is not true poetry.
How much more so, then, in the compositions of the lords of poets, which are the very bulbs of fame?
This is an intermediate verse.
This treatise is nearly completed.
